item.title: 3rd International Workshop on Global Change, 2011, Tsukuba, Japan
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Before the earthquake, there was this meeting. During the first day, at least, I did learn some interesting stuff. Manabe-sensei spent a lot of time fussing about various convection schemes, as I was told that he would. Mizuta from MRI described the difference bewteen the Arakawa-Schubert and Tiedtke schemes. Arakawa-Schubert employs an ensemble of clouds with simple entrainment behaviour somehow all diagnosed from the cloud top. Tiedtke, meanwhile, has both entrainment and detrainment and various complicated stuff, but only one column of cloud. MRI are looking to combine the best of both. I'm sure there was something else I was supposed to tell Webbo, but I can't really find it in my notes. Perhaps it was the stuff that Hirota mentioned due to the lack of dynamical suppression in some GCMs allowing ITCZ splitting? I'm hoping to meet the lads from AORI / NIES at the CFMIP meeting in June, as our meetings were cancelled due to total destruction. Oh - apparently, NCAR also have CCSM4 now. Will the madness ever stop?

item.title: Held and Shell, (2012), Using Relative Humidity as a State Variable in Climate Feedback Analysis
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: OK - well this paper appears to make sense... Redefine climate feedbacks so that relative humidity is the water vapour variable rather than specific humidity. That means adding a specific humidity depedence to the traditional "Planck" (they don't call it that) and lapse rate feedbacks so that these maintain constant relative humidity. The remaining clear-sky (temperature driven) feedback is then changes in relative humidity. The scatter between traditional feedback terms is then substantially reduced. There isn't that big cancellation between large varying water vapour and lapse rate feedbacks. Instead, the lapse rate and humidity feedbacks are both close to zero. Finally, they admit that their choices are arbitrary (like any other choices) and may only work so well because of the ways models behave at the moment. CLOUD FEEDBACKS are obviously the same, although the non-dimensional feedback term, which scales with the Planck feedback, does get bigger because the Planck term (which now maintains constant relative humidity) is now smaller.

item.title: Zelinka and Hartmann, (2010), Why is longwave cloud feedback positive?
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Why indeed? The paper falls into two sections that I can identify. First, they describe and justify the basic FAT or Fixed Anvil Temperature hypothesis from Hartmann and Larson, (2002) and their updated version PHAT (which might not actually be an acronym, but means that the temperatures of high clouds do actually increase slightly due to processes related to increased subsidence heating). Second, they put it into the context of cloud feedbacks at the TOA and get involved in some kernelly-type stuff. So, to summarise... FAT points out that radiative cooling below a certain temperature is very poor because there isn't much water vapour in the atmosphere. This seems to be confirmed by Salby's book. Convective heating follows radiative cooling. Changing the temperature changes the humidity, and so the level of radiative cooling and cloud formation rises up to a new altitude at the same temperature. And of course, as usual, it's the clear-sky radiative cooling that dominates... As a note for my radiation calculations, it's worth noting that they only use one solar radiation angle for their offline radiation code experiments, claiming that this is fine. Anyway, conclusions from clear-sky radiative cooling / subsidence suggest that FAT isn't quite adequate. They need to employ PHAT:
  • Static stability increases with warming, especially in the upper troposphere
  • More heating the upper troposphere (Don't quite understand the connection, but I guess it sorta makes sense.)
  • Shift in cloud level towards warmer temperature, therefore, as the level of detrainment shifts upwards.
They then move on to cloud feedbacks themselves, and I find things getting less rigorous as the spectre of kernels shows itself. One has to be careful in picking through this section. Overall, though, I think they mean:
  1. (Let's use a numbered list this time.) Everywhere, cloud tops are higher in the warmer climate and nearly the same temperature giving a robustly positive feedback.
  2. However, in the deep tropics, cloud tops are slightly warmer due to this PHAT thing and clear-sky OLR is actually lower due to super greenhouse action here and
  3. There are slightly more high as opposed to low clouds in the tropics as things warm up, which tends to produce lower OLR...
Finally, I think it's worth linking to Dennis Hartmann's homepage as you can click on his photo and he looks slightly surprised.

item.title: Lorenz et al., (2010), Evaporation change and global warming: The role of net radiation and relative humidity
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
First things first, I really need to stop mixing up David Lorenz and David Lobell. It really isn't fair. Plus, there's another guy with almost the same name who I can't even remember at present. Anyway - here they are for future reference. David Lorenz is on the right, although I can't get the captions to work, naturally. Anyway - [caption id="" align="alignleft" width="187" caption="David Lobell"][/caption]
"The results challenge the view that the change in evaporation is predominantly constrained by the change in the net radiation at the surface."
You certainly won't get any complaints from me on that basis. The paper begins by reproducing the analysis of Richter and Xie, (2008) for IPCC models. Taking derivatives of the bulk formulae for evaporation and sensible heat flux allows them to calculate how changes in components leaed to the modelled changes in 20th to 21st century evaporation and sensible heating. The analysis is handicapped throughout by the comparing different parts of transient runs to each other without considering how they are forced or what's in equilibrum or whatever. They show this neatly by repeating their analysis for some period at the end of 2200s and getting rather different results. Still - this makes their point that it's not all about net surface radiation. [caption id="" align="alignright" width="147" caption="David Lorenz. Or is it? (Yes it is.)"][/caption] The turbulent fluxes depend on air-sea temperature difference, near-surface relative humidity and some turbulent transfer constant k. Lorenz finds with Richter and Xie that it's near-surface relative humidity and air-sea temperature difference that change the most in IPCC models. He disputes the findings of Lu and Cai, (2009) that it's all about k. If one wants to "understand" how much evaporation change one gets versus how much sensible change, then one has to constrain at least RH and air-sea temperature difference. As a theoretical paradigm, he applauds the efforts of Takahashi, (2009), (the JAS one) in stating different radiative cooling balances for the boundary sub-cloud layer (that balance sensible) and the free atmosphere (that balance latent). Takahashi sets k constant, in a move that tallies with the Lorenz paper and Richter and Xie, and allows him to predict values for changing RH and air-sea temperature difference. (The Takahashi paper is not really useful for predicting observed / GCM changes, though, as it contains too many approximations.) By way of conclusion, Lorenz et al. admit that there doesn't seem to be much prospect of constraining any of the bulk formula coefficients from current observations - not even relative humidity change.

item.title: Thuburn and Craig, (2002), On the temperature structure of the tropical substratosphere
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Ah - now this is a proper paper. Another one on the "it's basically all radiative cooling" theme. The substratosphere is the layer of the atmosphere between the top of the convective outflow and the cold point above which temperatures increase with ozone heating. The tropopause, which really ought to be defined by the top of the convective outflow (or equivalent structure, if it exists, for extratropical latitudes), is sometimes identified at the cold point instead, which is basically fine in the tropics as the two are pretty close together. Anyway - the substratosphere has some features of the troposphere and some features of the troposphere. It's more or less in radiative equilibrium, which is stratospheric, but the rate at which ozone is removed by transport processes far exceeds the rate at which ozone is formed by photochemistry, which is tropospheric. It exists somewhere between about 200 and 100 hPa. In this paper, they look at the robustness of the substratospheres existence and its location using a radiative-convective model. The radiative-convective model is run for various relative humidites, dynamical forcings, carbon dioxide concentration, ozone, humidity etc. The model is even tried in the extra-tropics, where it's very simple "convective" adjustment mimics eddy-driven heat transports. For me, it did surprisingly well against ECMWF reanalysis. I really must find out if John's still got this model... Stuff drives the levels of the cold point and outflow top up and down. It becomes clear that carbon dioxide driven radiative heating at the top of the outflow (which occurs basically above the layer where there's no water vapour cooling (c.f. Zelinka and Hartmann, (2010)) is important for quashing convection. One interesting aspect is that lowering the ozone layer a bit tends to drive the cold point and outflow top down, as one might expect as their heating descends. However, push the ozone far enough and the cold point vanishes completely and shoots right up above 20km... Things are comparable in the extratropics, with a clear substratosphere that responds in similar ways to changing the forcing. The cold point is not always so clear, particularly in the winter polar latitudes as there ain't no ozone heating, plus the ozone is always a bit lower down in the atmosphere. Finally, I really ought to note that they use what looks they take to be a standard technique for prescribing / thinking about dynamical heating. Upward motion in the substratosphere provides a dynamical cooling and can be prescribed via a specified heating in the model. This makes sense when I consider linked subsidence / dynamical heating in the subtropics. However, that's a balance between heating and cooling. Doesn't the air I import have to be of a lower potential temperature (equivalent potential temperature, peut etre) to provide a cooling. Sacre Bleu.

item.title: Newell et al., (1975), Decreased global rainfall during the past Ice Age
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A bit of tropospheric energy budget antiquarianism. Wonderful, really. This is a paper from 1975 written by Reginald E Newell that uses estimates of changes in tropospheric radiative cooling to predict changes in global mean precipitation during the Last Glacial Maximum. It's one of those proper old letters papers that's only about a page long, says almost nothing about methodology and just gets straight to the point without all our tired modern strictures. He got 10% for the total reduction in precipitation with respect to the present day, which I think is roughly 2%/K. He must have run some sort of radiation code on a 10° x 10° grid, and without considering the effects of changes in cloud cover. The basics of the tropospheric energy budget theory of Mitchell et al., (1987) and others (et al., I suppose) are all there. Newell died in December 2002, which can't be long after John Mitchell told us about all this stuff. His MIT obituary (linked above) said
“Reg had the enthusiasm of a freshman undergraduate even though he was into his 70s,” said Professor John C. Marshall, also of Course XII. “He did, after all, die at his desk working, something that he would not have been disappointed about.”

item.title: Webster and Streten, (1978), Late Quaternary Ice Age Climates of Tropical Australasia: Interpretations and Reconstructions
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Tim Barrows from Geography asked me to read this paper as it expresses the age old problem of why were the New Guinea Highlands apparently so cold during the past ice age? While surrounding SSTs declined by a little more than a few degrees, temperatures in the New Guinea Highlands declined by 7 or 8 degrees. [caption id="" align="alignright" width="370" caption="The Torres Strait: You don't miss your water til your river run dry."][/caption] OK - so a lot of facts were presented in a thick paper. Some things that came through: CLIMAP SSTs, which the authors are not necessarily sure about, show coolings of a few degrees for the tropical western Pacific, Maritime Continent region. Sea level was 200 m lower, meaning that the Torres Strait, which lies between Australia and New Guinea was dry, along with other various shallow channels between the other parts of the region. This has consequences for available moisture. Plant proxies and the like suggest that New Guinea highland temperatures were much lower. This appears to be very solidly backed-up by the snowline being 1-1.5 km lower at the same time. How much this could depend on an increase in precipitation, I'm not sure. Overall, though, pollen evidence indicates that the climate was substantially drier, partly, at least, due to the reduction in available moisture. There's some worthy meterology in there. The part that I find most difficult to accept, however, is the lapse rates bit. The present day situation in the vertical is moist adiabatic. Hence, they find large cooling aloft and small cooling at the surface difficult to accept, but I'm not so sure we ought to accept the moist adiabat as a template for change at the surface at varying altitudes. The authors' favoured explanation is either that cold outbreaks from the midlatitudes increased to the extent that they cooled the highlands, or, locally there was an increase in precipitation lowering the snowline. They seem reasonably confident that the proxy data can't be dismissed, even if they have some doubts over the SSTs. My favourite thing about the paper, of course, is that it brought me into contact with Newell et al., (1975), (below). UPDATE: Tim says the stuff about the Torres Strait is a red herring. (Sorry Fernando.) Most of the heat goes through the Indonesian Throughflow.

item.title: Moss et al., (2010), The next generation of scenarios for climate change research and assessment
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
It really was high time that I, despite myself, learnt about the new RCPs, or Representative Concentration Pathways to give them their full name. Moss et al. describe the old fashioned economics to emissions to climate to impacts way of looking at future environmental change. Noting that the IPCC is no longer in charge of this kind of thing, they describe the new approach that the "research community" now takes. (I wonder who really is in charge?) Old scenarios pretty much assumed that humans weren't going to respond to climate change. The new ones propose that they will, probably aiming to limit global mean temperature change, or a little more realistically, radiative forcing to a certain level in 2100. Impacts people / planners want to know about the next 25 years; scientists want to know about way beyond 2100, particularly with regards changes in sllloowwww climate components. So - like, then, RCPs are defined as things like

RCP x

where x refers to radiative forcing in 2100. Hence, RCP 4.5, is 4.5 Wm-2 in 2100. The idea is that model development, simulation and assessment will all be parallel from now on. Climate modellers model stuff based on the RCPs that we have. Integrated Assessment Modellers develop other ways to get to the right 2100 radiative forcing. The RCPs diverge little before 2035, meaning that decadals can use whichever.

item.title: Raper et al., (2001), Use of an upwelling-diffusion energy balance climate model to simulate and diagnose A/OGCM results
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I'm trying to understand a bit about simple models of ocean heat uptake, as it don't appear that Glen's diffusive / upwelling model is massively choosy over what values one inserts for effective diffusivity. Glen, it seems, is forced to employ a ludicrous range of possible κs (diffusivities) to cover all possibilities, and I'm probably going to have to go the same way in order to satisfy my critics. I'm left wondering whether I'm using the right ocean model at all, although the sort of fits that I'm getting are mostly satisfactory compared with natural variability. This paper by Raper et al., is one of a large number testing EBM fits to GCMs. The EBM does a decent job of reproducing HadCM2 (oh yes) 1860-2100 climate change, but struggles to reproduce a 900 year stabilisation run unless climate sensitivity is able to increase throughout the run. I can't remember to what extent this would be corrected by using appropriate adjusted forcing, and to what extent it's about longer-term adjusting effects in the vein of Williams et al., (200X). Things that might be worth noting from the paper:
  1. Their ocean features a mixed-layer as well as diffusiveness. I wonder if Glen's does?
  2. The ratio of Air temperature change to  Mixed-layer temperature change in HadCM2 and ECHAM1 is robustly 1.2. According to their prose it seems to be due to sea ice.
  3. Murphy (1995) is an earlier origin of transient feedback parameter calculation than Forster and Gregory, although James used ocean heat uptake rather than TOA flux...

item.title: CFMIP / GCSS / EUCLIPSE, Exeter, 2011
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
CFMIP stands for Cloud Feedback Model Intercomparison Project. I have no idea what GCSS stands for, and EUCLIPSE has got something to do with the EU. This was rather a nice meeting. Really very unusually friendly. Some highligts:
  • Sandrine Bony said that Chris Bretherton has found that the degree of convective aggregation strongly affects bulk atmospheric relative humidity. Sounds important!
  • Masahiro Watanabe showed Collins and I some interesting results to do with the relationship between El Nino and some climate change thing. The reason it was interesting was that the three different perturbed physics ensembles he investigated each had its own robust, but completely different relationship across ensemble members...
  • Mark Zelinka and Ben Sanderson each have a new cloudy kernel method for dealing with clouds at TOA. I may unfortunately find myself having to understand at least one of these. They rely on the ISCCP simulator, but I suppose might be adaptable to the surface?
  • I had somewhat extended discussion with Patrick Taylor on a variety of topics. How one defines the cloud masking effect: Pat thinks one really ought to have clouds at control temperatures, although of course agrees that it depends what physically one is interested in. He's also written a paper about water vapour feedback and lapse rate feedback, their global cancellation and substantial differences regionally in CAM3. William naturally claims that "it's well known", but of course there are no references in the published literature. (He's Patrick C Taylor, and he's not to be confused with Patrick T Taylor, also from NASA.)
  • Jon Petch reckons that I can improve my radiation code simulations of cloud by using a correction in time that he uses in space! I have to get the paper from James Manners / Peter Hill once it's ready. Excellent.
Otherwise, if it needed to be said, it's pretty obvious that Webbo loves cloud feedbacks. He could talk about them all night and all day. The more gridboxes, compositing methods, GCMs, LES models, single column models, the better. And the more uncertainty and possible but improbable hypotheses that can be advanced, the better. The LES people are something of a separate community, it seems, basically talking to each other without really setting the scene. A bit like the detectors back in the 90s and 2000s.

item.title: Climate Change and Sustainable Futures Bridging the Gaps sandpit
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Well - this was certainly an experience. I now feel a bit better connected to Climate Change and Sustainable Futures. I've also taken on another project. I ought to be careful about that. There wasn't much money available, and we didn't have much time to put into devising our proposals. Hence, tensions were probably considerably lower than they would be at a proper research council sandpit. Still, I learnt much about how these things might work. My feeling is that there wasn't really any serious getting together beforehand to carve up the funds. Certainly, a couple of people came with what they wanted to do pre-prepared. I don't think there's anything wrong with that, although I didn't feel that these people were really interested in "bridging the gaps". It was inevitable that there would be a large well-designed terrestrial carbon cycle proposal in there somewhere, as most people in CCSF work on the terrestrial carbon cycle. I think the good fortune for the rest of us was that there was only one such proposal. I'm going to be working with Tim Kurz, Duncan Russel and Charles Abraham (with relevant input from quite a few other people) on how do we change people's and corporation's behaviour to make them emit less carbon. Hence, we'll be focusing on energy use rather than changing power generation. I think we will do something useful. Initially, we're hoping to use our £5,000 to pay a graduate student of Duncan's to do a relevant literature review that we can convert into "amount of carbon saved" versus "effort (perhaps amount of £s incentive needed to begin with)".

item.title: Taylor et al., (2011), Geographical Distribution of Climate Feedbacks in the NCAR CCSM3.0
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I met Patrick Taylor at CFMIP. He told me that his paper shows that CCSM3's water vapour and lapse rate feedbacks, although nearly cancelling as with the usual wisdom, are by no means collocated. He uses some kind of offline radiation code calculation that's corrected through some sort of Monte Carlo cloud distribution technique (MCICA) that improves results. Various feedbacks, including clouds, are then discussed. The interesting result is that the water vapour and lapse rate feedbacks are not collocated! Or at least - they aren't in longitude in the tropics. Lapse rate feedback looks like tropical convective climatology. Water vapour doesn't. Preferring to look like changes in high cloud detrainment. Causality is not really discussed beyond mentioning that it would be a bad idea to do so. This is a very decent first paper by Patrick, although I slightly uncomfortable with the strength of some of the conclusions he draws. It would definitely be worth finding out if he wants to take his work further using our data. Oh yeah - I really ought to remember that CO2 forcing does really very little in the high latitudes!

Comparison with William Ingram's thesis

I want to quickly note that William thinks he obviously understands all of this already, and that it's all in the introduction to his thesis. He doesn't, of course, as he's now said now that I've told him what's in the paper... Still - that very thesis contains some interesting information. The evidence, both observed and modelled, suggests that RH indeed does not change very much, apart from a bit of drying associated with deeper convection in warmer climates. It doesn't explain Taylor et al.'s result, but he mentions that different models have different global mean lapse rate / water vapour feedbacks because of different polar amplification meaning different overall changes per degree warming. Where the lapse rate and water vapour feedbacks are principally going on in the tropics, however, changes ought to be fairly consistent.

item.title: Parazoo et al., (2011), Moist synoptic transport of CO2 along the mid-latitude storm tracks
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: In winter, decay and respiration by trees and other plants and stuff like that dominates photosynthesis, meaning that vegetation emits CO2. In summer, photosynthesis dominates and CO2 is taken up. Hence, atmospheric circulation that moves CO2 transports CO2 away from mid-latitudes to the poles in winter and to mid-latitudes in summer. The seasonal cycle in mid-latitudes is damped, while that at the poles is magnified. (Since there wasn't a great deal of vegetation there to begin with, and it sounds like plankton isn't having much effect.) Parazoo et al., examine the circulatory components of CO2 transport due to mean flow, stationary waves and transient waves. The mean flow tends to move about an order of magnitude more than anything else at any one point in space, but has cancelling upper and lower tropospheric components. Wave activity, on the other hand, doesn't suffer from this, meaning that net flow due to wave activity is quite similar. (I assume that eddies dominate heat transport...) Notes that the seasonal cycle is about +/- 2 ppm in the mid-latitudes and +/- 5 ppm in the Arctic, which is larger than emissions at the same time according to the authors, although I'm not sure how that squares with the EOS article I was just reading about CO2 emission. A tree of the kind that might decay or respire in the winter and photosynthesise during the summer...

item.title: Hwang and Frierson, (2010), Increasing atmospheric poleward energy transport with global warming
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
"....(GCMs) project an increase in atmospheric poleward energy transport with global warming... the increase in atmospheric moisture content causes most of the increase in transport."
They look at moist static energy transport in CMIP3 and an EBM that diffuses moist static energy in latitude. Poleward moist static energy (OK - let's call it MSE) flux increases in future CMIP3 scenarios, but differently in different models. They fit the EBM to surface and TOA fluxes and find that they get the (more or less) correct MSE flux. Initially, I wasn't very impressed with that. "Have the authors not just prescribed the answer?" I asked myself. But then, finally, in the conclusions it dawned on me. The point is that the coefficient of atmopsheric diffusion, which stands in for the ability of atmospheric circulation to transport MSE, can be diagnosed from the control and does not change in the perturbed runs. As Mark mentioned to me the other day, although "the increase in atmospheric moisture content causes most of the increase in transport", one need remember that Dargan himself pointed out to me that the moist bit goes equatorward in the tropics! That didn't really come screaming out of the paper as they didn't plot components.

item.title: Ringer and Ingram, (2011), Influence of boundary-layer cloud and convection on the tropical precipitation response to global warming
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: This is the paper of that stuff about the Gregory-Rowntree and Betts-Miller convection scheme stuff that Mark Ringer was always telling me about. All done in HadCM3, naturally. The surface temperature response to a doubling of CO2 has pronounced minima in the tropical Pacific and Atlantic in HadCM3. These are absent in CMIP3. The difference more or less vanishes if you replace the Gregory-Rowntree mass flux scheme with the Betts-Miller scheme. They speculate that this is because the average behaviour of convection schemes mimics the simple, smooth Betts-Miller formulation. They use Vecchi and Soden (2007)'s dynamical precipitation change concept, which is the percentage change in precipitation minus the Clausius-Clapeyron increase in saturation vapour pressure. I'm not sure why this is informative. I'm fairly surprised that William didn't suggest something else. I wonder what radiative cooling changes look like as a function of latitude... Increasing the number of levels to 30 doesn't make a lot of difference to the Gregory-Rowntree results. Most of the differences are in the boundary layer. Changes in stability are similar, but this means that the Gregory-Rowntree boundary layer remains weakly unstable and the Betts-Miller boundary layer remains weakly stable. This means large differences in the frequency of precipitation events. Big reductions in Betts-Miller; small in Gregory-Rowntree. The point of all this is that changes in the basically non-precipitating descending regions are having an impact on the most strongly precipitating regions. Through changes in SST patterns, says Ringer, rather than changes in radiatively driven subsidence. I guess that makes sense because the big differences are in the boundary layer. You don't have any written notes on this one. The paper is submitted to Geophysical Research Letters.

item.title: Jones et al., (2011), A comparison of the climate impacts of geoengineering by stratospheric SO2 injection and by brightening of marine stratocumulus clouds
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
[caption id="attachment_82" align="alignright" width="450" caption="The Dana Anglia"][/caption] Jim Haywood put me onto this one while we were at that Climate Change and Sustainable Future sandpit thing. Two methods of geoengineering the world are described...
  1. Get a pipe and spray sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere. I think Jim said they were actually going to try this, and when I say "they", I think he will actually be involved.
  2. Inject sea-salt aerosols into marine stratocumulus using ships. Here, I drew a picture of the Dana Anglia, so here's another picture of the Dana Anglia.
HadGEM2-AO experiments are performed and the results are compared. Both kinds of experiment are pretty effective at returning CO2 forced temperatures back to control values, although El Joshi take note - the stratocumulus experiment, which feats local forcings of up to 30 Wm-2 in some places, does show some significant departures from fully linear behaviour locally. The impacts on precipitation, of course, are much more extreme, with some serious action over the Amaazon in the stratocumulus experiment, and generally familiar changes in land and ocean precipitation.

item.title: Boer, (2011), The ratio of land to ocean warming under global warming
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Well - I guess I needed to read this one. Gratifyingly, the development of his equations is almost identical to Lambert et al., (2011), so I guess I probably haven't made a mistake. Interesting things in the paper beyond what was in Lambert et al., (2011):
  • Introduces ψ for the ratio of land to ocean precipitation change. Love it - I'll have to return the compliment by using that at some point. Although, unsurprisingly given the sketchy link between heat transport and precipitation change, it isn't massively robust.
  • He introduces a concept called "parallelism", which he says allows him to state that because ocean forced experiments show ocean-to-land ΔA, so will globally forced experiments. Obviously I either don't understand or don't agree with this.
  • α is always negative in his experiments. (Meaning that there's ocean-to-land heat transport driven by warming.) I think that this wasn't the case at least in some QUMP models?

item.title: Banobi et al., (2011), Do rebuttals affect future science?
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
No – No they don’t. Don’t write them.

A paper pointed out by John Kennedy at the Hadley Centre. The authors are ecologists, but they also mention a few findings from other fields. In short, in their field, original papers were typically cited 17 times as much as rebuttals. Only 5% of citations were ever really critical of the paper being cited. (In physics, the number is 14%.)

item.title: Hallegatte, (2009), Strategies to adapt to an uncertain climate change
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Doug McNeall kindly pointed me to this paper when I needed to say a few things about adaptation at the Exeter Climate Change and Technology summer school. Very informative for someone like me that doesn't know much about this kind of thing, and potentially interesting for our Bridging the Gaps behaviour project. Many of the points are obvious, but only once you know them... Building a house for the climate of Seville may be no more expensive than building a house for the climate of Paris. If Paris becomes more like Seville in 2100, then, that doesn't seem too much of a problem. However, what is expensive, is building a house for the climate of Paris and Seville and the conditions in between. This sort of thing goes for a variety of projects. One strategy is to plan for shorter periods. This might also get around the fact that we ought to be already adapting power stations and water projects to coming climate change. Another problem is that, unlike past climates, we don't have a good idea of what the return periods will be like for extreme events in future. Climate change uncertainty makes adaptation even more expensive. Hallegatte describes several strategies to ameliorate problems, and identifies where they might be applied. He comments on the advantages of certain strategies, such as there being "no regret" in employing a given strategy if there is no climate change, or synergy with mitigation. The paper was in Global Environmental Change, where we might send our BTG summary article.

item.title: Friedlingstein et al., (2006), Climate-Carbon Feedback Analysis: Results from the C4MIP Model Intercomparison
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A quick read of this paper summarising results from C4MIP, because I ought to know something about it for my ESPPE collaboration. OK - so C4MIP took a pile of coupled Carbon-Climate models and looked at what was going on with their land surfaces, atmospheres and ocean biogeochemistry carbon cycles. In sum,
"There was unanimous agreement among the models that future climate change will reduce the efficiency of the earth system to absorb the anthropogenic carbon perturbation."
They took a pile of GCMs and EMICs and performed two perturbed simulations with each. One "coupled" straight run carbon-climate A2 simulation and an "uncoupled" simulation in which the radiative effect of CO2 is neglected. I assume they actually mean that the radiative effect of CO2 perturbations is neglected? Anyway, they state that the difference between these two is the effect of climate on the carbon cycle. The models are described, a good many (perhaps mostly EMICs) appear to be less sophisticated on the ocean biogeochemistry side. (We have got Totters, I suppose.) All models are found to have a positive feedback. That is, climate change causes the carbon cycle to produce more atmospheric carbon dioxide. That of HadCM3LC is large at 200ppm. Many models have much much lower numbers, The land may be a source or a sink. HadCM3LC is one of only two models that simulate a sink-source transition. (It's Q10 constant is pretty big, and so the rate at which the land surface spews CO2 back into the atmosphere increases with temperature substantially.) Even though the evidence for this in nature is "equivocal", carbon cycle models produce the land-carbon sink through fertilisation. The ocean, meanwhile, is taking up CO2 at a rate dependent on the difference in surface ocean CO2 and boundary layer CO2. It is primarily, therefore, the rate at which surface waters are transported to depth that determines the rate of ocean uptake, they say. No handwritten notes on this one.

item.title: North et al., (1983), Simple Energy Balance Model Resolving the Seasons and the Continents: Application to the Astronomical Theory of Ice Ages
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Lo - [caption id="attachment_105" align="alignright" width="225" caption="Nicolaus Copernicus"][/caption]

De revolutionibus orbium coelestium

Gerry North's paper on Energy Balance Models and the revolutionary theory of astronomical cycles and ice ages, first described by Milankovitch, (1941), and Hays et al., (1976). The observations from 41 kyr ago feat. an ice-bound North American continent and an ice-free Eurasian continent apart from Scandinavia. Can they reproduce this with a 1D diffusive energy balance model with continents but no detailled ice, ocean, atmospheric dynamics or biology (such as ocean biogeochemistry). The July OC is the perennial snow line; 10C is the tundra line. (Tundra extent can also provide an important albedo feedback, and it's not accounted for here.) The EBM is first fitted to the seasonal cycle of temperature ("fudged", in fact, according to the manuscript). It is then run at various values of insolation. Multiple equilibria are found. At 41 kyr BP (!), an observed-like ice distribution is found. The basic point is that Eurasia is too warm in summer due to its large size to have a proper ice sheet but North America is not. Of course - this paper deals with equilbiria rather than true cycles, which is probably why we are still arguing about this stuff today.

item.title: Colman and McAvaney, (2011), On tropospheric adjustment to forcing and climate feedbacks
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A rehash of Gregory and Webb (2008) using only one model (BMRC), two methods (regression on a slab model and separately applying CO2 and SST forcing) but also using PRP. Both methods reveal that the bulk of rapid adjustment to CO2 forcing is shortwave changes related to changes in cloud cover. Other components of feedback remain "classical" - they scale with temperature. An interesting corollary to this, is that CRF numbers approximate adjustment well, as non-cloud changes that affect SW are small. In the zonal mean, one sees an arc of changes in cloud "extending from the surface in mid-latitudes to around 600 hPa in the tropics." Cloud amount in this model is driven by relative humidity alone, which changes with temperature and therefore heating rates, but also changes with other processes affecting specific humidity. They leave it to future study. Global means hide substantial land-sea contrasts. The lapse rate feedback is fairly small globally, but large and positive over the ocean and largeish and negative over the land.

item.title: Crook and Forster, (2011), A balance between radiative forcing and climate feedback in the modeled 20th century temperature response
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Been meaning to read this one for a while, but I don't think it actually says what I keep referencing it for. We thought that it was the same paper that Mark Webb has been writing with Jonathan Gregory and I, but it isn't really. Instead, they're basically setting about making the same points as Knutti (2008), and Philip Brohan and various people. Namely that the good fit to 20th century data by GCMs is due to compensating differences in forcing, feedback and heat uptake. (Somehow, Reto managed to put a positive spin on this, but I can't really remember how...) Forcing and response are therefore anti-correlated in the 20th century, but correlated in the 21st century leading to those big spreads that we see. They write down a linear model of forcing, feedback and left-over TOA flux to describe modelled global mean temperature change. A 1% run is used to work out the climate feedback parameter in each case. Forcings are from available data. The remainder is then ocean heat uptake. The method's not disimilar to that which we're using in my QUMP paper. They then use a Myles-y/Hegerlian spatial pattern-y optimal fingerprinting technique to work out what the temperature change contribution due to forcing and feedback is. There is then quite a lot of regional type stuff using latitude bands. Particularly tropics versus the arctic (or ar'tic as Zan Stine would no doubt call it). Models tend to underestimate early 20th century warming in the tropics. Not clear why. Also underestimate in the Arctic, but that could be natural variability. What I hadn't realised was that
"Relative warming between Arctic and tropics is highly dependent on the latitudinal distribution of the forcing, which varies between models, and is much less dependent on the Arctic amplification in 1pctto2x [a 1% run]."
Not sure what sort of impact this might have on Joe's proposed PhD project. Perhaps I should have read Shindell and Faluvegi / Yoshimori and Broccoli more carefully... The other thing they say that is quite interesting is that the 1% runs and 20th century runs are in a different order in terms of which warm the most. No paper notes [lace, madam] for this one.

item.title: Frieler et al., (2011), Changes in global-mean precipitation in response to warming, greenhouse gas forcing and black carbon
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
OK - so they've redone Lambert and Allen (2009), except basically better. There's one or two things that we tried that they didn't. But let's be honest, it's basically better. And it's a really short paper too. How do other people do these things? The principle differences:
  • They used some kind of restricted maximum likelihood estimation technique rather than the old fashioned regressiony things that we did.
  • They had a separate regressor for black carbon. Sounds sensible. A large number of other regressors were tried for various other forcings, but they acknowledged that it started to get silly and not really improve matters.
  • They used a lot more GCM data from a lot more scenarios.
Despite these undoubted improvements, they nevertheless noted that
"To our knowledge there is only one approach to extract the individual contributions [due to different forcings and feedbacks] from nine transient multi-forcing 20th century AOGCM runs [Lambert and Allen, 2009]."
which I find fun, and they continued to scale the effects of forcing absorption by TOA forcing as we did. They find a similarish dependence of precipitation on temperature and similar problems with the coefficients of shortwave forcings (e.g. sulphates) too. It all seems fairly reasonable, no doubt. I really must use some more modern statistics at some point. Il n'ya pas de papier ecrits a celui ci.

item.title: General Circulation Models applied to Exoplanets
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
[caption id="attachment_116" align="alignleft" width="218" caption="A transiting presumably super-hot Jupiter."][/caption] A workshop I attended in Exeter. Well - the workshop still continues, but I'm back in my office. We saw a number of talks, beginning with a description of what we can observe and what the state of modelling is. David Sing told us that, observations-wise:
  • Spectra are only available for directly imaged planets - these are normally hot and well-separated from their parent star and therefore young - and transient planets - hot irradiated jupiters close to the parent.
  • They can get composition (or vertical abundances), temperatures, a temperature map(!), perhaps even winds.
  • "We will not be doing Earths."
Much other discussion of various hierarchies of exoplanet models followed from this. Exoplanets generally seem to have some kind of troposphere zone, followed by an isothermally stratospheric-type region above and then a mega-radiatively heated upper atmosphere. Some of the efforts on the second day attempted to "bridge the gaps" between Earth and exoplanet (remember - chiefly giant exoplanet...) modelling. Met Office colleagues were heavily involved. Everybody's favourite tea-maker James Manners pointed out that band models don't band in frequency but in absorption coefficient! I should probably know that. The obviously spectacular Kevin Heng appears to want to observe exoplanets at different stages of their evolution in order to study climatic histories (similar to what stellar astrophysicists do?) Plus he spoke about our kind of atmospheric heat transport except on exoplanets. (The lower down you do the transport the more effective it is.) Overall, their philosophy seems quite different from the way that I have come to think, which is very interesting. Very reminiscent of the atmospheric science that Held and Manabe would recognise.  It was wonderfully bizarre to watch the arguments develop between various attendees. They are very focused on details, which, given the limited knowledge they have of exoplanets, seems strange to me. But I am rather ill-informed, of course, and I'm also like that. I think I now understand why they're so focused on this Held and Suarez (1994) test, which was designed as a way of comparing the performance of GCM dynamical cores. Surely they'd be better off acknowledging some uncertainty in their predictions and just getting on and finding out what kinds of exoplanets are possible?

item.title: Beer et al., (2009), Temporal and among-site variability of inherent water use efficiency at the ecosystem level
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: I'd been badgering Margriet to provide me with some reading material about water use efficiency. I then left the thing on my desk for weeks on end, before reading it on the train but not managing to find the pen that turned out to be in my bag. So this is a bit sketchy. There exists something called water use efficiency, which is defined in different ways, but here and oftentimes elsewhere is defined as the ratio of assimilated carbon by some plant to evapotranspiration. The point about it is that it might provide us with a bulk property that we can attribute to something like a plant functional type that describes how biomes compete with each other and how they interact with their environment. Measuring water use efficiency is not particularly easy. What's available depends on the scale that one looks at and whether ones got the plants in the lab or underneath one of those flux tower things. They also introduce intrinsic and inherent water use efficiency. Inherent water use efficiency, in particular, is a product of the authors' work and is hence shown to outperform other methods as a predictor of gross primary productivity compared with rat regular water use efficiency. It seems that inherent water use efficiency is equal to water use efficiency * vapour pressure deficit. I think Margriet suggested that plants in a given location / climate tend to all have the same (optimal?) water use efficiency.  She's going to look at this sort of thing in GCMs. What's the water use efficiency spatially (or perhaps in latitude)? I'd also like to know how the blinking thing is coded by PFT in JULES. I also wonder if there's such a thing as a limit based on the use of carbon and water by photosynthesis and the amount of respiration they need to do? Alors - there are no written notes on this one. (No pen.)

item.title: Muller and O'Gorman, (2011), An energetic perspective on the regional response of precipitation to climate change
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I feel sure that I've written this one up already, but apparently not.
"but here we show that the energetic approach can be extended to local changes in precipitation by including changes in horizontal energy transport."
Clearly, this statement is true, but the paper makes very little meaningful progress. Sorry - I'm feeling uncharitable because it's Christmas. The paper does make a few minor points worth noting, however. So... they get a load of CMIP3 models under the A1B scenario and compare 2081-2100 with 1981-2000 and look at a tropospheric energy budget equation with dry static energy transport included.
  • Dry static energy transport balances much of the structure of precipitation change. No surprises, really, when we consider that surface fluxes are mostly quite smooth and longwave and shortwave contributions tend to cancel one another.
  • Near the "poleward edges of the subtropics", increases in sensible heat flux decrease precipitation.
  • The correlation between precipitation and diabatic cooling reaches 0.5 at about 7000 km.
No written notes.

item.title: van Haren et al., (submitted?), SST and circulation trend biases cause an underestimation of European precipitation trends
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
This is one that Collins gave to Joe and I from the Geert Jan van Oldenborgh stable. After we'd read it, he confessed that it was a bit of a mess. I have to agree, unfortunately.
"We investigate the relative importance of the two prescribed factors: atmospheric circulation and sea surface temperature in setting the modeled trends. We find that the main factor in setting the trend in winter is atmospheric circulation, for summer SST is important in setting precipitation trends along the North Sea and Atlantic coasts."
So, as per usual, it's GPCP, GPCC and ERA-40 versus CMIP3, but also some regional models including some from ENSEMBLES, looking at the European region. Things are clouded (particularly statistically, which is a big surprise coming from this team!) by investigating different length series for different time periods, but bearrrsically,
  • They use that Annan and Hargreaves reliability thing to state that the models are "unreliable" -> observations are usually above or below the entire range. The high resolution of RCMs is no solution to this problem, suggesting that boundary conditions may be at fault or model error not dealt with by resolution.
  • So what are the key drivers? They diagnose a "component linear in circulation" and subtract it from precipitation change, which allows them to state the conclusions we have in the quote above.
No notes on paper.

item.title: Classical oceanography papers
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
And now some classic (classical?) oceanography stuff from Henry Stommel. The more I read about or from this man, the more ridiculously good he seems. I've been through the following for this term's coming oceanography lecture: [caption id="attachment_131" align="alignright" width="150" caption="Henry Stommel"][/caption] Stommel, (1961), Thermohaline Convection with Two Stable Regimes of Flow: which he wrote second, but makes most sense to think about first. This is the two box thermohaline circulation model that shows stable and unstable thermally driven flow and stable "thermally indirect" saline driven flow. A couple of simple situations are presented to stimulate thinking about various kinds of flow, including a "what density of water the outflow has depends on how long the water stays in your marginal sea for" example. Then it's on to the actual bit. The two box model is a bit more complicated than the one normally presented to undergraduates. Time dependent behaviour is analysed and temperature difference is not prescribed. Everything is non-dimensionalised for heavens sake, and a graphical method is used to obtain solutions to the equations. Familiarish looking roots are obtained... Stommel, (1958). The abyssal circulation: A letter written to Deep Sea Research. This is the article (or an article?) in which Stommel presents his view of abyssal currents, featuring tight western boundary currents that move away from sources of deep water and smooth flow elsewhere that moves towards the poles. Again - the presentation isn't quite that is shown to students. There's no fluids derivation, just a pointer to some earlier work. There is some oxygen based justifaction of Stommel's view of near point sources of deep water and slow upward diffusion everywhere else. But then I read: Lozier, (2010), Deconstructing the Conveyer Belt: which prevents a modern view of goings on. Essentially, we've known just from inspecting the surface wind driven circulation / theoretical considerations that the ocean circulation is really rather turbulent. Hence, "thermohaline cartoons" were never going to be realistic. However, oceanographers appear to be progressively moving to a view that the conveyer belt doesn't even represent things to first order. Again, perhaps unsurprisingly, it looks like the wind driven circulation may interact strongly with any density driven flow out there. In particular - deep water production and subsequent export to the subtropics don't appear to be that well connected. Not only is the thermohaline circulation incredibly unsteady, it's also the case that deep water pathways exist in the ocean interior outside of the boundary current. Still, density driven flow may yet dominate on centennial timescales. And
"There is clear and abundant evidence that ocean waters overturn. Deep water masses, primarily from the North Atlantic, spread to other ocean basins, with a concomitant surface mass flux of ~20 sverdrups. Considerably less certain is the 3D structure of the overturning."
Stommel's brilliant ideas are great for stimulating the discussion, but one needs to be wary of stating them as fact. Notes for Stommel, (1961). None for others.

item.title: Two Geophysical Research Letters papers about polar amplification
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Of the large number of papers I've been through with the ECM3736 students, two of them were about polar amplification. One of them was even quite good. Chung and Raisanen, 2011, Origin of the Arctic warming in climate models:
"There is a debate on whether the snow/ice change feedback or poleward energy transport from lower latitudes generates the observed Arctic warming amplification. There is another possibility that remotely induced warming in the Arctic can be amplified by snow/ice feedbacks."
Indeed, there is. I'm not sure how far this paper goes towards answering any of it. However, it's written very confidently and I went with paper notes. By looking at a couple of CMIP3 models, they conclude that the summer temperature structure of the atmosphere determines how well forced warming from lower latitudes spreads polewards. In particular, one needs a lot of warming in the upper troposphere to spread low latitude forcing competently. They then conclude, based on ECMWF reanalysis data, that CMIP3 models simulate too much warming up here, and therefore that poleward advection of heat is overstated in models. Their other conclusion is that remote CO2 forcing dominates over local forcing in the Arctic in models, and that albedo feedbacks amplify the warming. O'ishi and Abe-Ouchi, 2011, Polar Amplification in the mid-Holocene derived from dynamical vegetation change with a GCM: They've tried to do a lot less than the other paper, with the result that it's a fair bit less controversial, and probably just a bit better. Perhaps I'm going a bit Philip Brohan as I get older. No notes, then, on this one. The crux of it is, if you simulate interactive vegetation in the mid-Holocene then you get much larger land warming than you do without, and that this more closely matches relevant proxies. As I told the third years, I guess this is the kind of timescale on which the vegetation has time to change significantly, or perhaps even equilibriate.

item.title: Goldblatt et al., (2009), An evaluation of the long-wave radiative transfer code used in the Met Office Unified Model
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Suggested to me by Tim Lenton, this paper has been on my desk since the beginning of time. But finally I have it read. The paper describes differences between longwave radiative fluxes simulated by line by line, and narrow and broadband radiation codes. The latter two are Edwards-Slingo as used in HadCM3 and HadGEM1 and (I think) HadGEM2. The paper takes a somewhat haughty tone, which leads to a probable over-generalisation of conclusions based on one atmospheric column in the summer mid-latitudes, but makes some decent points. First, they compare radiative fluxes and changes in radiative fluxes for different types of gases at different model levels in one column. At the tropopause, net fluxes generally work out ok, but individual upward and downward fluxes in the broadband codes are in error by 10% or so. The situation is much worse at the surface, where errors are as big as 50%, and there's no compensating error to sort things out in the net. The newer (ie non-HadCM3) versions of the broadband code are in general slightly worse. That was all for a doubling of CO2. Other bad errors are seen for other gases, and all errors get much much worse if one is prepared to push the broadband codes miles beyond the modes of operations they were designed for. All in all, this leads to extra heating of the troposphere and insufficient radiative heating of the surface. We then encounter some radiative-convective code calculations. If relative humidity is maintained at climatological levels in the single column troposphere, then the HadCM3 version of the code produces a reduction in convective mass flux with CO2 driven global warming. (This doesn't happen with the line by line calculation.) It will be interesting to see if this actually happens in actual HadCM3 anywhere. Collins et al., (2006), was a comparison of lots of radiation codes using a similar method. I don't remember the errors found in that paper being anything like as significant. However, digging the thing out now, the broadband code errors are pretty big. Bigger for some codes! No written notes.

Oh - and remember that none of these studies includes CLOUDS.

item.title: Mann et al, (1998), Global-scale temperature patterns and climate forcing over the past six centuries
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: [caption id="attachment_143" align="alignright" width="186" caption="That tree ring picture of Michael Mann."][/caption] The hockey stick paper. I was bound to read it eventually. I did so as part of the Introduction to research in the mathematical sciences module that I teach. (It might not be such a good paper to do as part of a detection and attribution climate sub-theme, as it gives the students the impression that correlating forcings with temperature is something we do. Perhaps we did use to do it.) So, climate change over the past 600 years (extended to the past 1,000 years in a following paper) using dendrochronology (tree rings), ice cores, "ice melt" and long historical records (such as central England temperatures). Proxies are calibrated to 20th century instrumental data and linked to EOFs of climate change. Climate is assumed to have "weak stationarity" -- that is the same EOFs and relationship to proxies that it has today. The quality of reconstruction declines with time, but they reckon they've got something useful back to 1400. Back to the 19th century can be compared with an "independent dataset". I'm not really sure how it's done before that. I think it's related to how well the proxy data relates to the derived EOFs. Interestingly, quite a few of the EOFs are relatable to physical things rather than just being random mutually perpendicular things. A limited attribution statement is made. No industrial sulphates, but greenhouse gases are fingered as the agent of recent climate change by correlating forcing to response. Response to solar variation seems very weak (0.1 KWm-2), but that could be for all manner of reasons over the whole record.

item.title: Kiehl and Trenberth, (1997), Earth's Annual Global Mean Energy Budget
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A BAMS article by Kiehl and Trenberth that I've probably read before, but read again for the Introduction to research course. The main thing that I wanted to note was that.
"...the largest effect of clouds on the outgoing longwave flux is in the atmospheric window (8-12 [microns])."
Which might just add some hope to building a VAPRP method. Otherwise, the paper is a summary of satellite and surface observations relevant to the Earth's radiation budget. A raditation code is used to resolve some elements of longwave flux. Perhaps slightly suprisingly, looking in one column doesn't appear to make much difference from using a proper global grid in some verificationy stuff they do. Shortwave dominates errors at the top of atmosphere, but due to various uncertainties at the surface, including cloud base height, uncertainty in longwave is very significant at the surface too. Sensible and latent heat fluxes are derived via bulk formulae. In the end they end up with that figure that ended up in the IPCC report and many many talks. No paper notes.

item.title: Barnard et al., (2011), Predicting space climate change
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
This paper caused a bit of a splash on, umm, Geophysical Research Letters. I'm not sure it's all that interesting. I imagine that it's all about the title. Recently, the Sun has been in a state called Grand [caption id="attachment_156" align="alignright" width="300" caption="His prediction? Pain."][/caption] Solar Maximum on a cycle that lasts about 150-200 years. We're now on our way down from that, and various hazards associated with solar activity, or the lack of it, may begin to come into play. Satellites and other electronic systems could experience hostile conditions not seen for a 100 years. (In other words - before they existed.) They examine time series of changes in variables related to the Sun that are called space weather and predict future variations through lining up previous cycle statistically and extrapolating. The indicators and hazards are:
  • Sunspot number. Increases with increasing solar activity.
  • Solar magnetic field, B. Increases with increasing solar activity.
  • Solar Energetic Particle events (SEPs), which is what happens when the Earth gets struck by a coronal mass ejection. As B reduces, their number decreases, but their intensity increases, meaning that there's an optimal reduction from grand solar maximum for maximum pain.
  • Galactic cosmic rays. (But of course.) Decrease with increasing solar activity (due to increased shielding by solar magnetic field).
On top of these, the Earth's own magnetic field has been declining, providing even less protection from hazardous events. The authors state that another event like the Carrington event (the solar storm of 1859) could cost 1-2 trillion dollars and take 4-10 years to recover from, as well as severely irradiating anyone in a jetliner.

item.title: Raper et al., (2002), The Role of Climate Sensitivity and Ocean Heat Uptake on AOGCM Transient Temperature Response
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A paper about possible relationships between climate sensitivity and ocean heat uptake. I'm not sure I follow, actually, but anyway, it's about how physical links between ocean heat uptake and sensitivity may explain correlations between them. This paper is from way before anyone thought that we might be programming these things in subconciously (and that doesn't make it wrong, necessarily). They take CMIP2 models forced for 80 years with a 1%/year increase in CO2. They "know" the forcing, from the Murphy, (1995) method. The forcing due to a doubling of CO2 varies from 3.45-3.74 Wm-2 across the ensemble. Given that the 3.74 is for you know who, it's probable that those numbers were calculated from double radiation calls. They find that values of sensitivity change slowly over 80 years (probably not adjustment as forcing is introduced gradually, although final values do agree with the slab model 2xCO2 change). They parameterise ocean heat uptake as being proportional to global mean temperature change, which they say is ok for this scenario if one neglects various initial mix-layer effects. To the extent this is true, this implies that the spread of transient warmings is smaller than the spread of sensitivities (no surprises, but see paper notes). However, they find that the spread of transient warmings is even narrower than they suspected assuming kappa the same in each model, meaning that there's a correlation between kappa and lambda! Weak lambda (sensitive) is associated with strong kappa (strong ocean heat uptake). They state that this could arise because strong surface warming reduces the overturning circulation, among other features, which apparently increases rather than reduces ocean heat uptake.

item.title: Hill et al., (2012), Parametrizing the horizontal inhomogeneity of ice water content using CloudSat data products
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Jon Petch at the Met Office suggested I read this paper after seeing my CFMIP presentation in order to help me with my radiation code calculations. The paper is an engineering exercise that seeks to better represent real cloud distributions on coarse grids. (They concentrate on ice rather than water because it's easier for CloudSat to see.) Just using mean cloud water to generate cloud doesn't work, because it doesn't get the thermodynamics (e.g. autoconversion) or the radiation right. Clouds need to have appropriate variation in the density of cloud water (well - ice here) present. The authors derive a relationship between Fractional Standard Deviation (FSD) (the standard deviation divided by the mean) and the mean as these things tend to be strongly related. After some tuning, they are able to build a parameterisation (parametrization?) that produces quite accurate FSD for gridboxes of various sizes with different cloud water content. Jon suggested to me that their results, which are for spatial means, could be used to help our results, which use a lot of time meaning. I think he suggested that all I would need to do was scale my cloud water amounts by a constant, but going by this paper, I imagine that that constant would vary with cloud water content. If we want to do this, then I should talk to him.

item.title: Two simple models of ENSO
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Suarez and Schopf, (1988) and Battisti and Hirst, (1989) are two papers about simple models of the El Nino Southern Oscillation. They're none too easy. Especially Battisti and Hirst, which I started with. To an extent, the models, which are both delayed action oscillators, seem plucked from thin air, which is certainly the way Mat Collins put it. This is most certainly the case for Suarez and Schopf. Battisti and Hirst do attempt some justification, but my knowledge of ocean dynamics is far too weak to know if they're doing something sensible. Anyway:

Suarez and Schopf, (1988):

The theoretical basis is that ocean-atmosphere interaction is strongest in the central tropical Pacific. In the west, SST is warm, but gradients in SST are weak and the thermocline deep, so wind-driven anomalies can't influence SST easily. In the east, the thermocline is shallow, gradients in SST are large, but SST is cold meaning that convective interaction between atmosphere and ocean is small. The central area of the Pacific provides a good compromise and hosts the strongest interactions. I have no idea if this is correct. The oscillator equation: Initial pertubations in SST are supported by a coupled atmospheric mode, leading to growth. (The dT/dt and kT terms of the equation.) But once the perturbation gets too big, non-linear damping processes are invoked (cubic term) to bring things back down towards mean climate. Finally, there's the delayed term. Rossby waves are launched westward across the Pacific, are uncoupled in the Western region, and bounce off the western boundary before coming back as Kelvin waves that get re-introduced to the picture in the east. The delayed term interferes destructively with conditions in the west and "shuts down" ENSO. Linear and full non-linear analysis is carried out for complex exponential solutions. Shorter delays mean longer oscillations! Their model seems comensurate with the 2-4 year time scale of ENSO.

Battisti and Hirst, (1989):

They kick off with a fuller exposition of the relevant dynamics, although much is left to earlier work that I haven't read. The dynamical model ends up being very similar to Suarez and Schopf, but is motivated more directly through thermocline depth, upwelling and advection. They admit that nature could be more complicated, but state that in a world like their model, ENSO behaviour and predictability depends on the specification of the basic state. I think I may need to re-read Cane and Zebiak.

item.title: O'Neill and Hulme, (2009), An iconic approach for representing climate change
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Saffron O'Neill has recently joined the Exeter Geography department, and we need her help. Therefore, this paper is great. Tim Kurz suggested that I read it as part of our Bridging the Gaps: 80% by 2050 project. The authors describe an experiment that does a part of what we've been discussing but leaves plenty of nice gaps for us to explore. The introduction describes various strategies for public engagement, and their pitfalls. Piggybacking, for example, relies on getting one's climate mitigation done by pointing out that a given behaviour change saves money. Individuals may resent this, though, or might not like to be perceived as penny-pinching. (Tim has also mentioned this before.) So: O'Neill and Hulme selected icons of climate change by engaging with climateprediction.net participants, focus groups and online surveys. They also derived "expert icons" that might appeal to people like me. Icons were classified by various social psychological dimensions: spatial distance, pragmatic reasoning and intangible (emotional / spritual) reasoning. The layperson icons chosen were the Norfolk Broads (local), London (pragmatic) and, yes, polar bears (intangible). The expert icons were the west Antarctic ice sheet, ocean acidification and the thermohaline circulation. The impact on icons under the "unmitigated" (according to the authors) A1B scenario was projected. Workshop participants were subjected to the information, and the effect on their attitude or "engagement" with climate change measured by survey. Specific results:
  • Participants found local icons more engaging than distant ones.
  • Layperson icons were more engaging than expert ones.
  • The polar bear, despite being an example of "charismatic mega fauna" and a layperson icon, was the least engaging icon all round.
  • Young people think more globally than older people.
The project assesses attitudes rather than behaviours. Tim also highlighted some methodology that he would have done differently. No notes.

item.title: Two papers on AGENT-BASED and VARIABLE-BASED MODELLING
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Agent-based modelling. I didn't even know what it was last summer, but it's suddenly become all the rage as it might be a way of attracting funding for 80% by 2050. In practice, I think this is what Network Theory means for us, but a conversation with Peter Ashwin may yet debunk that notion. Let's take

Smith and Conrey, (2012), Agent-Based Modeling: A New Approach for Theory Building in Social Psychology

first. This is an article aimed at introducing agent-based modelling to social psychologists. It was therefore suggested to me by Tim in order to get me on board, and thinking more in the right way. Overall, I can't say that it's dispelled any of my fears, few of which relate to agent-based modelling itself and most of which relate to how on Earth we can apply it to what we're doing. Smith and Conrey describe my problems neatly in a way I haven't been able to in the group: "For ABM to be a scientific tool... it must, of course, be subject to empirical validation." There doesn't seem to be a way that we can do this at present. Anyway, the paper presents information on agent-based modelling techniques, most of which will be self-evident to a scientist, and compares them to other "variable-based" (ie differential equation) techniques used in social psychology. It is found that the ability of agent-based models to produce complex "unexpected" (ie mostly totally expected) behaviour from a few simple rules trumps variable-based techniques in many cases. It is not restricted to a certain "level" of complexity as variable-based is. They discuss making the automata more complicated (mostly discouraged) or adding noise to the system (can be interesting in the maintanence of minority populations within a model for example). The spread of communications is discussed. Without some knowledge of what our parameters will be, or at least some idea of how a real message would spread, it's difficult to see how we could use these ideas. PDW's suggestion of spreading our own communication looks important, even if we're unlikely to be able to build a competent sample or properly characterise the UK population.

MacCoun, (2012), The Burden of Social Proof: Shared Thresholds and Social Influence

Another one Tim made me read. As he expected, I wasn't overwhelmingly impressed with it. Still, it does say "threshold concepts" and "tipping points" in it. The paper describes some models of social behaviour that can be plotted on graphs against one or two independent variables. The dependent variables typically curve up from the bottom corner to the top corner, meaning that one can fit quite a lot of things to it. Providing that one has enough parameters, the model "does quite well", as they say. The particular, I think "variable-based" model the author lays out is called "BOP" or Burden of Proof or Balance of Pressures. I don't find the model tremendously well-motivated, unfortunately. The individual parameters are not easy for me to understand, but then that may be because I'm not a psychologist. (Although Tim seems to have much the same impression.) He then does a bit of the old agent-based modelling, using BOP to describe the behaviour of individuals and replacing their "mean field" (used previously to simulate social pressures) with "vision" of neighbours or next-nearest neighbours and so on as the case may be. I've started writing like a social psychologist, so I think I'll stop now.

item.title: Two papers on WEATHER TYPES
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Richard Everson and I are working on a grant to do with using novel techniques to process climate data. One such possible source, suggested by Myles, is climateprediction.net weather types or Grosswetterlagen. Hence I've looked at a couple of papers by Paul James on their classification and use. [caption id="attachment_178" align="aligncenter" width="492"] CPDN HadAM3P surface pressure composite.[/caption]

James, 2007, An objective classification method for Hess and Brezowsky Grosswetterlagen over Europe

Grosswetterlagen (GWL) were originally categorised as 29 European circulation types by hand. They are useful because a given weather type is associated with certain precipitation and temperature conditions at the surface. They have advantages over mathematically-derived patterns such as EOFs. Modern classifications are done automatically, but it must be acknowledged that subjectivity may have led to drift of the original classifications over time. James makes composites of every day judged to belong to each GWL and then rederives occurrence frequencies using a correlation technique that compares daily pressures (and geopotential height) to the composites. There are quite a lot of GWLs (29), but a lot of them are quite similar. I wonder if we could come up with a reduced scheme. (I think we'd have to.)

James, 2006, An assessment of European synoptic variability in Hadley Centre Global Environmental models based on an objective classification of weather regimes

This paper came out first, but actually follows on from the other one. The GWL system from above is applied in HadGAM1 and HadGEM1 as well as HadAM3 and the frequency of regime occurrence is calculated. The newer models do better than HadAM3. The frequency of regime occurrence changes under a 2xCO2 climate, unsurprisingly, meaning that the comparison with reanalysis gets poorer. The models also contain overall biases with respect to reanalysis, and these need to be managed. The paper points out that GWL can explain things that simple linear analyses cannot. Overall, this post of mine wasn't terribly informative, but, Grosswetterlagen exist, can classify weather into a number of regimes related to surface meteorological conditions, and their changes in frequency and character could tell us things that EOFs, means and variances cannot. No notes.

item.title: Yan et al., (2011), A record of the Southern Oscillation Index for the past 2,000 years from precipitation proxies
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A paper that Dan suggested Lilo read for her forthcoming PhD. In general, the idea is to get Lilo thinking a bit more generally and a bit more large-scale. Anyway, I too have read the paper. It seems to be the case that more has been done on tropical paleohydrology than I expected and there's more data than I led myself to believe for the last 2,000 years at any rate. The authors introduce El Nino in a fairly standard way, explaining its links to the tropical Walker circulation and the Southern Oscillation (SO). Given the "persistent correlation" between SO and El Nino (it is called ENSO after all...) they define a precipitation index for Pacific paleoclimates based on the anti-correlation between Galapagos (Eastern Pacific) and Tahiti (western Pacific) rainfall (or precipitation-evaporation(?)) proxies. The Galapagos record goes back to 7000 BC (crumbs), the Tahiti record to 25 AD. Resolution is about 10 years. They find that their precipitation data show a trend towards El Nino like conditions as we go back about 350 years. This is in direct opposition to temperature proxies, which apparently show the opposite. According to Yan et al., their results follow a Held and Soden, (2006) type Walker circulation weakens with global warming leading to a more El Nino like state. I'm not absolutely sure they've nailed that on. Does the heat transport actually decrease? Granted, we know that CMIP3 Walker circulations reduce preferentially compared with the Hadley component. And these models also, at least sometimes, produce the El Nino behaviour they suggest. The temperature results, meanwhile are supported by something called the "Ocean dynamical thermostat mechanism", but I've learnt to be cautious of anything with that name. No paper notes.

item.title: Sinha et al., (2012), Mountain ranges favour vigorous meridional overturning
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Bablu Sinha. He who gave the first meeting (COAPEC) talk I ever saw... They took the GCM FORTE and tried running it with and without contemporary mountain topography. Getting rid of the mountains cuts the model AMOC from 18 to 0 Sv. A Pacific Overturning circulation then starts up, with a size of about 10 Sv. And there was me thinking that it was all down to ocean basin topography rather than surface topography! So, they remove the mountains... It causes large changes in surface conditions pretty rapidly. Land areas are actually substantially cooled, because cloudy and moist conditions are more prevalent in most places over land. (There are also areas that warm up, though.) The mountains also play a big role in the surface salinity difference between North Pacific and Atlantic, partly by directing runoff, so that the North Atlantic stays relatively saltier. Removing the mountains rapidly changes surface temperature and salt conditions, but we must wait centuries for circulation driven changes to really kick in.

Succession of processes:

OK - so in the Atlantic.
