Removing the mountains increases precipitation initially (because moist Pacific air can now reach the Atlantic), but strengthen sensible heat flux (and evaporation), because the atmospheric jet and winds strengthen through not being obstructed by mountains. Soon, however, increased precipitation comes to dominate, reducing Atlantic salinity (increasing the saline break) and shutting down the circulation. The consequences in the Pacific are more or less opposite. The jet strength increases, increasing evaporation, increasing salinity and beginning buoyancy driven overturning. The global mean ocean heat flux stays about the same for MOUNTAINS (the control simulation with mountains) and FLAT (the simulation without mountains). I don't really understand how this links with the Seager et al., (2002) paper that they reference about how the Gulf stream isn't related to warm European winter temperatures, but I must. No paper notes.

item.title: Ineson et al., (2012), Solar forcing of winter climate variability in the Northern Hemisphere
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Nathan Mayne contacted me last week in order to suggest a possible collaboration between Astrophysics and me on Solar UV changes. We both read this paper by Ineson et al. from the Adam Scaife stable. A small amount of direct radiance measurements of solar UV changes now exists from the SORCE mission, starting in 2004. Because 200-320 nm UV can vary up to three times as much as other parts of the solar spectrum, but is absorbed in the middle atmosphere its variation may have as yet unknown consquences for the atmosphere and weather. Here they employ a 60-level model taking into account solar max versus solar min UV changes. The focus just on the UV, omitting optical changes, in order that the claim that radiation absorbed at the surface is causing these detected effects can be avoided. In the model world, the differences in radiative heating force the stratospheric equator to pole temperature gradient leading to changes in westerly flow (understandable through geostrophy), which are then amplified by wave activity and transmitted to the troposphere where they manifest themselves as AO/NAO forcing and changes in surface temperature and storm activity. The results are compared to observations / reanalysis of the same region and, well... The authors seem pleased with the results; I find them utterly unconvincing. In particular, the model fields don't even agree to within sign for the latitude-height plots in Figure 3. I guess this is Nature Geoscience, though. Nevertheless, some of the global (or regional) means are ok-ish. Anyway, this leaves, Nathan, Dave Acreman, Isabelle and I with the "what can we add?" question. Things that we came up with:
  • What other data is there on Solar UV changes? Nathan reckons there's the SOHO satellite, which goes back somewhat further. Dave mentioned another mission. I wondered if there's some kind of fitting procedure we can run based on earlier ground based observations that might see UVA / UVB changes. (Although those might be polluted with ozone variability?)
  • Observations of sunlike stars. Can we get snapshots of other stars and see if this helps us. Although Isabelle cautioned me that this might only show up differences between stars along different parts of the main sequence.
  • Include the effect of interactive ozone. Run the whole thing in concert with optical changes, ozone etc. We might have to worry about the ocean model, which Dave keeps saying he'll have a go at...

item.title: Fu et al., (2011), On the warming in the tropical upper troposphere: Models versus observations
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A short paper about the fact that CMIP3 GCMs exagerate observed (MSU) trends in upper versus mid tropical tropospheric temperature change during the past 30 years, and that these, nearly contemporary GCMs, do it a fair bit worse than earlier models. Well - that's basically it. It's noted that ENSO dominates real variability of mid versus upper level temperatures and that ozone and stratospheric aerosol distribution can affect things. They also note that different interpretations of MSU output show considerable differences, although not nearly big enough to cover the model changes.

Surely the obvious question is, "What is the water vapour doing at the same time?"

item.title: Brient and Bony, (2012), Interpretation of the positive low-cloud feedback predicted by a climate model under global warming
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Low-cloud feedback in subsiding regions of the IPSL model. Mark was really very particularly keen that I read this paper, as it ought to tell me how to do things. (Especially when he's not going on about Masa's new CFRAM method.) Basically,
"In a warmer climate, the thermodynamical relationship of Clausius-Clapeyron increases this vertical gradient, and then the import by large-scale subsidence of low moist static energy and dry air into the boundary layer. This results in a decrease of the low-level cloudiness and in a weakening of the radiative cooling of the boundary layer by low-level clouds."
They decompose cloud changes into regimes (composited on large-scale vertical velocity), probability of that regime occurring, and the cloud radiative effect related to the regime. It turns out that the most important change in "the warmer climate" is changes in the cloud radiative effect associated with the weak subsidence regime. The regime is so important because it's probability of occurrence is so high. This is true of AMIP and aquaplanet experiments, causing them to discount land or land-sea contrast effects, and also occurs (I'm using that word a lot) in an appropriately driven single column model. They say that this is how it works in their model and, with caveats, possibly in other models. Adjustment to forcing effects are weak. The single column model experiments suggest to them that SST, rather than other changes in large-scale forcing due to circulation, is responsible for the observed effect, although I find this part a bit dodgy. All these results also go for "atmospheric radiative forcing", which corresponds to the energy budget of the troposphere.

Physically,

it works like this. Low moist static energy (MSE) air is advected into the boundary layer by subsidence. Under climate change, the MSE contrast between the surface and the (subsidence region) upper troposphere increases because moisture increases in the boundary layer so much more than elsewhere. Boundary layer depth also increases due to enhanced shallow convection, which I think reduces moisture import across the boundary layer top into the free troposphere, further accentuating the surface to "aloft" gradient. (I might not have got that bit, though.) They find that the height at which idealised heating perturbations are applied determines their impact on the MSE transport gradient and hence low cloud.

item.title: Held and Shell, (2012), Using Relative Humidity as a State Variable in Climate Feedback Analysis
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: OK - this paper makes sense... They redefine radiative feedbacks so that relative humidity is a state variable rather than specific humidity. To do this, it is necessary to alter the Planck (although they don't call it that) and lapse rate feedbacks so that they maintain constant relative humidity. The remaining clear-sky (temperature driven) feedback is then a relative humidity based water vapour feedback. The result is that the large varying and somewhat cancelling traditional lapse rate and water vapour feedbacks vanish. Instead, both feedbacks are near to zero. They state that their choice is arbitrary, but then so is any other choice of feedback scheme. This one may only work so neatly because of the behaviour of current models, they say. CLOUD FEEDBACKS are obviously the same as before under this scheme. However, the non-dimensional feedback parameter term gets bigger because it is scaled by the Planck term, which is now smaller by virtue of maintaining constant relative humidity...

item.title: Vonder Haar et al., (2012), Weather and climate analyses using improved global water vapor observations
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A paper about the NASA water vapor Project (NVAP) that I read during a CCSF meeting (Hah!). It's a merged dataset that draws on radiosonde, GPS, passive microwave and "hyperspectral" infrared water vapor retrievals to produce both total precipitable water vapor (TPW) and layered precipitable water vapor (LPW) products. NVAP was produced some years ago, but this is a new improved thing that even has a climate stream from which longer term information may be drawn. They haven't yet done trend analysis (there are various artificats to negotiate, so it's not trivial) but interannual variability is already tractable. It's HIRS (right), that provides the vertical information (presumably along with radiosondes, although didn't see that specifically stated?), so it's probably the case that the layered information isn't nearly so good as TPW. HIRS is also given the highest variance, which presumably means it's the noisiest. There's also AIRS data, which contributes to vertical information after 2003.

item.title: Moberg et al., (2005), Highly variable Northern Hemisphere temperatures reconstructed from low- and high-resolution proxy data
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A paper that Dan Charman was interested in for Lilo. It feats wavelets, which probably isn't something to worry about right now. The point is that they take a variety of proxy records and recognise that each has skill at different temporal resolutions. This may lead to earlier studies, such as Mann et al., (1998), enduring various artificats, such as underestimating longer term variability during the past 1000 years. Tree rings, for example, are good at short term variability but not good at long term trends. Lake and ocean sediments are low-resolution, but capture long term trends. It's also the case that regression methods used by Mann tend to underestimate trends when noise is present. Hence, Moberg used some adjustment method suggested by Von Storch to do his calibration to instrumental records. The RESULTS, then. They get a much more pronounced medieval warm period and little ice age than earlier studies. ECHO-G runs are "qualitatively remarkably similar", indicating that estimated volcanic and solar variability predict proxy temperatures.
"As in all paleoclimate reconstructions, there are uncertainties in this one."
Yeah. Anyway, they finish by making that point about how warming post 1990 is bigger than anything in the paleorecord... No. paper. notes. Also - I really want them to bring me the right washing machine next time. No paper notes POSTSCRIPT: I now have the right washing machine.

item.title: Bond et al., (2012), A 61-million-person experiment in social influence and political mobilization
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A social psychology paper fed to me by Hywel... I suppose I eventually had to read one of these things or do some kind of work for 80%. The paper describes the results of posting a message on facebook that suggests that recipients voted in the 2010 congressional elections, allowed them to click a button that says "I voted", and tell their friends and see who of their friends had. The message came in three flavours: (i) "the social message": the actual bit, giving encouragement and allowing them to see who else had voted and press the button (sent to a staggering 60 million people, (ii) "the informational message": only containing the information but no 'social media', and (iii) the control group. (The latter two were only sent to 500,000 people each, for some reason. I suppose they would argue that voter motivation was the prime motivation rather than statistics, and the latter were probably already rather good. (Should I really be getting involved in things that are primarily driven by the former reason?)) Anyway - TURNS OUT - the "social message" is by far the most effective, beating the informational one both for online activity it produced and also, somehow they work out, for the real polls. Shifts are small - only 1% or something. The authors point out that such a shift might have been enough to change the results of *that* Florida poll won by Bush against Gore in 2000. They also examine how the "closeness" of a friend controls their influence on one by noting who appeared in the "look these people have already voted" box. (Closeness was measured by how much recipients interacted with a friend on facebook.) It turned that, although by their definition close friends only make up 7% of facebook acquaintance, they account for almost all influence on others. They finish up by making the rather strong claim that the 0.6% increase in voting compared with the previous election might have all been down to this message. It is Nature, I suppose. Still, they sober things up a bit by conceding that face-to-face interactions outside of Facebook are probably responsible for a good deal of friend closeness. They make the point about how it's not only about how messages impact the individual, but also how they spread. The author list features facebook people, so I suppose that sort of engagement is necessary before being able to do such a thing. No paper notes.

item.title: Things I learnt from ECM3736, Oct-Dec 2012
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
OK, so a quick summary of previously unfamiliar papers that cropped up this year in ECM3736.

Wild et al., (2012): Enlightening global dimming and brightening. A review paper in BAMS on global dimming, aerosols and stuff like that. Partially notable because the precipitation figure looked the way I imagined Joe's NHML precipitation figures should look. However -- it turns out that this is almost certainly due to movement of the tropical ITCZ rather than a reduction in precipitation. Anyweigh... Global dimming happened from 1950-80 (about -4 Wm-2) followed by Euro brightening from 1980-200 (about 2 Wm-2). Asian dimming, meanwhile, tended to continue in India and China, while elsewhere dimming reversed. Diurnal temperature range and PAN EVAPORATION also show indications of these trends. Convection in heavily polluted areas tends to be reduced (opposite of Menon et al., (2002), which we also read -- that paper seems to be an outlier and is interesting for demonstrating conflict...) Previously pristine areas suffer more in general from dimming aerosols because effect of aerosols on CCN tends to be logarithmic. Notes that CMIP3 models don't capture observed dimming driven changes in temperature -- ie they warm too strongly during dimming and too weakly during brightening. I wonder if that's linked to the diurnal cycle thing I saw at AGU? It seems the opposite of Joe's results... There are paper notes too. Also read Lohmann and Lesins, (2002), on aerosols, but it wasn't that interesting. Nicholls, (1997): Increased Australian wheat yield due to recent climate trends. A very simple article about crops and climate in Australia. Notable for being a Nicholls paper, and therefore statistically very careful. It appears that climate has caused about 30-50% of the observed trend in wheat yield from 1952-92. In order to avoid other affects from changing technology or "crop management" or the CO2 fertilization effect!, he de-trends and only looks at year-on-year changes. His multiple correlation on diurnal temperature range (or rather max and min temperature) and rainfall initially reveals roles for temperature but not rainfall. He then does "partial correlation", which I don't yet understand, but it allows him to separate the effects of his different correlators. Results are similar... He finishes by conceding that farmers too might respond to good versus bad years, thus confounding his year-on-year results. No notes. Arrhenius, (1896), will get it's own article...

item.title: AGU 2012
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: The most important thing to remember about this meeting is that there are actual curry houses around JONES and O'FARRELL and they really aren't bad at all. Well - the one I went to twice wasn't, and the others were busier. As for the actual meeting, it was the usual mixture of stuff one had seen 20 years ago, random stuff that I will never have time to follow up on and incredibly specific things detailed on posters. One of the most interesting early talks came from the Met Office's Philip Brohan discussing something that isn't his Old Weather project but is observations from the East India company. It allows him to get a look at the Tambora eruption of 1815 using actual observations and compare to paleo fits. He reckons that GCMs overestimate the volcanic response for 1000-2000 and that paleoproxies don't. Oh - he uses land-sea contrast to guestimate land temperatures! It turns out not to be a problem to produce temperate climates in the Archaean despite the Faint Young Sun as long as you're willing to allow more CO2 and methane into the atmosphere. I asked Ray Pierrehumbert about his steam dominated atmosphere planets during his runaway greenhouse talk. Turns out that "Oh boy" is convection wierd, as you lose most of your convective outflow to rain. It's also the case that hydrogen is a very decent greenhouse gas at high enough pressures. Nearer my field, I was initially fairly irritated to see Angie Pendegrass present the tropospheric energy budget stuff like it is a new invention. However, she spoke to me after my (mediocre) talk and explained she just didn't know how to pitch her talk. We agreed she went a bit low. She's working on using a simple model to explain the effect of things like the lapse rate feedback on the tropospheric energy budget. Xing Qu who I've met at CFMIP, apparently, is working along similar lines to Mark and I some years back with low cloud feedback composites. Let's hope he does better than we did. Yi Ming is trying to use the seasonal cycle to determine the sense of aerosol forcing. However, models seem to drive it the wrong way with respect to observations. (Interesting in conjunction with Wild, 2012?) Gerard Roe, who's always struck me as a bit of a wheel re-inventer, is currently advocating regional feedbacks. By using constant feedbacks with "a time-evolving pattern of warming" he can reproduce the changing climate sensitivity advocated by people like Keith Williams. Of course - for the majority of a model run, I would expect him to be correct by construction or fitting at least. If it takes care of the adjustment phase, however, then it's more interesting, although probably still unphysical given that some of this happens without changes in surface fluxes. Huang: Do I need to be careful about water path in my radiation calculations? Here he finds that the change from water to ice in the warmer climate leads to significant differences in TOA radiation. Brault: A poster about loss of MEGAFAUNA. The simulated reduction of mammoths 20,000 years ago. Makes me wonder what would happen to land cover without present day animals. Are these catered for in land surface schemes in competition parameters somehow? Finally, but perhaps most importantly, I met with Patrick Taylor to talk about tropical lapse rate and water vapour feedbacks. Patrick accepts my land-sea contrast explanation, but points out that there are a number of details in CCSM3 at least that probably aren't controlled by that. We need to repeat my plots for more models and come up with a next goal. I'd say either understanding whether land-sea contrast affects overall or just regional feedback and designing a new more useful measure of feedback are top priorities. It all fits in with PROBEC.

item.title: Chung et al., (2011), Model-simulated humidity bias in the upper troposphere and its relation to the large-scale circulation
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: As part of PROBEC, I wanted to look at observations of water vapour and temperature from satellites. Fu et al., (2011) was my motivation. This Chung paper was suggested by Viju John as one I ought to look at to familiarise myself with some relevant satellite basics. Unlike Fu et al., the paper isn't about trends, but about biases in model climatologies. These biases appear to be connected to large-scale circulation problems, highlighted by analysis of Ω500. There are various problems with the observations and work-arounds that must be employed, but, when all is said and done, the models have a moist bias. (They look at GFDL in particular, but I think this is supposed to be a common problem.) Real circulation is stronger than modelled and the non-convecting upper troposphere is therefore drier than simulated. Finally, Viju has emphasised to me the utility of microwave data over infra-red data. The microwave data also work over land, unlike the infra-red data looked at here.

item.title: Arrhenius, (1896), On the Influence of Carbonic Acid in the Air upon the Temperature of the Ground
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I'm rather surprised I don't have any handwritten notes on this one. Rather surprised. I must have somewhere. Anyway, here it is - the first classic estimate of climate sensitivity. Arrhenius used a one-layer kinda optically thin model of the atmosphere. Incredibly, he estimated atmospheric absorption by CO2 and water vapour by using measurements of lunar infra-red obtained by someone called Langley. Mistakenly, Arrhenius did not realise that an infra-red beam passing through a warm atmosphere can gain intensity as well as lose it by absorption. Otherwise, a large number of his surmises are remarkably correct! He did pretty well with the spectrum, although the text book from which I took the paper, The Warming Papers, edited by Archer and Pierrehumbert, points out that he missed at least one major absorption feature. There's also an appropriate discussion of solar shortwave absorption. He tries to consider some other feedbacks, such as snow and ice and clouds and lapse rate, again in a remarkably sensible way, even mentioning the cloud masking effect. All in all, I think Arrhenius does slightly better than Archer and Pierrehumbert give him credit for, as I'm not sure the Arrhenius atmosphere is quite the one layer beast they describe. (Although A&P's is a very helpful article for understanding the paper.) Finally, there's some fun with geology.
"I should certainly not have undertaken these tedious calculations if an extraordinary interest had not been connected with them."
Arrhenius was interested in the cause of ice ages. He rejected the older but now once again standard theory of Croll that relates ice ages to changes in the Earth's orbit, preferring to think that CO2 variations drove changes. Interestingly, he dismisses the terrestrial and oceanic carbon cycles that we know as unimportant, and says that the balance of atmospheric CO2 must be dominated by
  1. Volcanoes.
  2. Combustion of meteorites in the atmosphere.
  3. (Actually (6)) Weathering.
A very wide ranging and impressively insightful piece of work.

item.title: Evans et al., (1998), Optimal sites for coral-based reconstruction of global sea surface temperature
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: [caption id="attachment_244" align="alignleft" width="252"] Kiritimati (Christmas Island)[/caption] The interesting combination of John Chiang and Lilo recommended I read this one. I've been suggesting we work out where best to next take paleo-observations of hydrology by using statistical [caption id="attachment_243" align="alignright" width="300"] The Galapagos - alright for some.[/caption] techniques. Evans et al. did it years back for sea surface temperature observations derived from coral. Their overall findings are a bit surprising. A couple of sites, usually from the Pacific, do well at capturing EOF SST variability. Using 10 or so isn't terribly much better. This is good news when we consider that, of the 1207 5x5 degree gridboxes in the world oceans, only 65 are suitable for coral observation. If there's a fair bit of observational noise out there, then one is better off resampling corals in the same gridbox at the best sites in order to improve signal-to-noise, rather than going elsewhere. Those two sites "just happen to be" the Galapagos and Kirimitati (Christmas Island), both in the equatorial Pacific. A third site is usually found in the Indian Ocean if observed noise isn't too bad. OK.... So they write a matrix penalty function, minimise it and find the optimal estimate of temperature. I can't follow all of the algebra with one reading, but it doesn't look that toxic. They use 80 EOFs, which sounds like a lot to me, but is apparently appropriate. I can't imagine we could resolve nearly so many for precipitation. There are various minimisation choices, but the trace of the error covariance matrix is the one they use for the majority of their analysis. Various assumptions must of course be employed. None would be surprising to anyone who has read Mann et al., (1998). Overall, they believe that paleo-observations could be as good as the worst directly observed 1860-1900 period, assuming that their calibration etc is ok.

item.title: O'Hagan, (2012), Bayesian analysis of computer code outputs: A tutorial
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A paper that Peter Challenor recommended to Margriet. The paper explains why one does emulation of what statisticians call simulators. It doesn't really explain the how terribly much, because that's not what it's for. So I had to ask Peter. The emulator typically consists of two bits, Peter explained to me, there's a sort of neural network basis function-y bit, and then there's a Gaussian process bit. The Gaussian process bit allows you to fit essentially any simulator, it turns out, but sometimes it's helpful to have some neural network chucked in there too. For strategic parameterisation, I think it would be very helpful to be as neural network as possible, because then one can write down the different parameterisations using the same basis vectors... Anyway, the paper largely discusses the use of the Gaussian process emulator, explaining that, at simulator data points, the emulator reproduces the simulator with zero uncertainty. Away from such points, the emulator glides smoothly between simulator points with uncertainty growing with distance from a point. How smoothly, and how much uncertainty is derived from training data. The main pay-offs, we are told, comes from how very much faster the emulator will be than most simulators that we would wish to emulate and is not that difficult to fit in the first place (few simulator runs), meaning that Monte-Carlo analysis with the simulator to determine some mean behaviour (or whatever) is usually very inefficient compared with emulation (which will be able to reproduce almost the same statistics very rapidly and go much further in terms of number of runs done). According to Peter, discontinuities are increasingly dealable with these days. As O'Hagan states:
"The emulator will smooth these out, leading to locally poor representation of the simulator. This may of course imply better representation of reality if reality behaves more smoothly!"
He also says "myself" half a page after that...

item.title: Krasnopolsky et al., (2010), Accurate and fast neural network emulations of model radiation for the NCEP coupled climate forecast system: climate simulations and seasonal predictions
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Mat Collins suggest I read this when I introduced the concept of strategic parameterisation. He was cautioning me over trying to emulate parameterisations, as apparently this doesn't always work very well. (Peter Challenor has pointed out that it can work very well, though!) Anyway, the paper describes an attempt to speed-up the NCEP climate forecast system by employing a neural network-based emulator to replace the model radiation scheme. Differences caused by emulation are smaller than the size of model versus observed error. They point out that radiation calculations are fundamentally rather slow -- which is why correlated k band models and long timesteps are used. Hence there's interest in doing them even faster. As I keep trying to remind myself: we could emulate Edwards-Slingo! I mean we've already got the thing running offline. Two points to probably note:
  1. "Corners" of the domain might not be well-represented by training data.Could be a problem if one trains on the control and then looks at climate change \ldots
  2. The neural network used here is no respecter of conservation laws. The conservation of energy, for example. If this introduced a bias, I imagine it could be a problem.
Interestingly, this is (another?) neural network-y paper. Peter Challenor and Mat point out that this isn't the only way to fit a linear model. It may very well not be the best way either! This is where those stats guys come in, though.

item.title: Forster et al., (2013), Evaluating adjusted forcing and model spread for historical and future scenarios in the CMIP5 generation of climate models
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Another paper about CMIP5 forcings and feedbacks. This is the "realistic" scenario version (cf Andrews et al., (2012), which is the 4xCO2 version). There isn't terribly much in here that Joe hasn't already worked out for himself, but it was probably still worth a quick read through. They use a standard Murphy (1995) method for deriving scenario forcings and feedbacks from idealised runs (naturally credited to various Forster and Gregory papers here). The most important finding is that CMIP3's sensitivity - aerosol forcing anti-correlation is absent. Instead, there's something of a greenhouse gas - "climate resistance" anti-correlation, where climate resistance is the combined effect of feedback and the "kappa" formulation of the ocean in regulating surface temperature change. We should really think about having a look at how ocean carbon cycle feedbacks correlate with this whole climate resistance thing. One imagines that they tend to reduce the spread of climate response. Perhaps Margriet and Ben would be interested in having a look in QUMP?

item.title: Cawley and Dorling, (1996), Reproducing a Subjective Classification Scheme for Atmospheric Circulation Patterns over the United Kingdom using a Neural Network
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Quite a long title, that one. I've been trying to find out more about weather types. By chance, this paper came up from a computer science conference journal, which is not only weather types, but also machine learning and involves Steve Dorling, who is coming down for Grand Challenges. It turns out that many years ago, he and a computer science colleague used a machine classifier to describe daily British Isles weather patterns. The thing does pretty well - better than some other standard technique, but still struggles to classify 50% of days correctly. (Apparently it is better at westerly flow.) One thing I need to find out from Steve, or someone, is why subjective weather types are preferred by some people, such as Paul James, and perhaps Steve himself, whilst David Fereday and his Met Office colleagues prefer empiricism.

Having also spoken to Richard,

The things that we can add to this kind of analysis would seem to be:
  • Patterns that change into the future. We can start with Grosswetterlagen, or use empirical clusters like Fereday et al. (which I still need to read). This way we can describe climate change.
  • Citizen scientists (or experts) being asked about difficult cases. I have this idea in my head that people are good at pattern recognition, which Richard didn't rubbish.
No paper notes.

item.title: Chadwick et al., (2013), Spatial Patterns of Precipitation Change in CMIP5: Why the Rich don't get Richer in the Tropics
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Mark asked me why I was going to read this paper. He hasn't, and him and Tim Andrews say they've seen the talk often enough (and, like me, don't necessarily understand it well enough). Anyway, I thought I ought to read it because it will contain many of the same issues as our cloud radiative forcing on atmospheric absorption paper. I feel like I've virtually forgotten how to write a paper, although remember well enough how to criticise other peoples, so it's also good training for that. Overall, unfortunately, I found the paper really dull, which is not Rob's fault -- it has to be that way and so my cloud paper will be too. I will try to follow his lead, though, and not write too much and draw plenty of pictures. They begin by dividing regional tropical precipitation change into familiar "thermodynamic" (actually due to moisture increases) and "dynamic" (convective mass flux decrease, which for me is really thermodynamic). These components almost cancel, leaving little net change. The most important thing that happens is then movement of precipitation due to changes in sea surface temperatures, necessarily the same as what I see for clouds. The paper has an excellent introduction that goes a bit further than I can understand. After all the usual energy budget stuff, he introduces something called the MASC mechanism (Mean Advection of Stratification Change) formulated by Ma et al., (2012) and blamed for quite a lot of what happens in the rest of the paper. I don't understand it and won't without reading that paper. The point is, though, that descent regions warm more under global warming across the tropics, reducing pressure gradients and tending to reduce the Walker Circulation. They investigate integrated convective mass flux, and find that areas of high velocity potential are areas of high velocity potential reduction under climate change. Anomalies in the diagram are explained as movement in those patterns. In dry descent regions, however, decreases in large-scale subsidence don't lead to increases in shallow convection. They claim that this is due to increased (dry static!?) stability. Finally, relating things back to precipitation... Obviously the precipitation follows movement of the convection. The dynamics dominate, rather than "thermodynamics", of course, although reductions in RH over land can also produce substantial changes.

item.title: CWC meeting 14th and 15th May, 2013
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
The CWC meeting turned out to be quite interesting! I have notes in my blue notebook, but the following points, and subsequent discussions with Joe are worth noting.
  • It turns out that different precipitation observations datasets differ from one another rather a lot in the last thirty years or so. NHML trends are significantly different in four datasets discussed by Gabi Hegerl, and the GHCN data being used by Joe show the largest trend!
  • There are four sets. GHCN, Zhang et al. extended (still being extended / fixed-up), GPCC and the infamous VasClimO. We now have all four.
  • Runoff data may indeed be useful. Hunts reckons that it would be "excellent" over Europe at least. The hydrologists would probably trust it more than precipitation. Joe's initial model study doesn't look incredibly promising, though, in terms of how much it picks up in the way of sulphate driven trends.
  • Xuebin Zhang (long time since I've contacted him!) told me that the Russians (presumably actually the whole USSR?) neglected trace precipitation amounts before 1966. He reckons that pre-1966 totals are underestimated by about 10%.. Adding this to Joe's observed analysis makes it give a sensible value for sulphate forcing... What isn't clear to us is how much the observed datasets that we have have been fixed. We need to check old papers by Pasha Groismann, I think.

item.title: Cadule et al., (2010), Benchmarking coupled climate-carbon models against long-term atmospheric CO2 measurements
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A paper I read by Steve Sitch as part of my probably vain hope to get him to sign up to the MAN VERSUS MACHINE grant with Richard Everson. Looks like Steve might spill into the Mark Webb category of suggesting his own papers to read without pointing out he wrote them first! Anyway, it's Global Biogeochemical Cycles. It's an assessment of the seasonal cycle of vegetation in different models and in different parts of the world. GCMs naturally show wide disagreement in which processes are important but good agreement in 20th century atmospheric CO2 concentration. The authors therefore analyse trend, seasonal and interannual variability at 12 stations for 1979-2003 and compare feat. models. The models are C4MIP, and therefore don't include any forcings apart from CO2, which I find a bit odd. The different GCM-coupled-carbon models are good and bad at different things. HadCM3LC, for example, is generally bad, but good at interannual variability. All the models show at least some shockingly bad errors at some stations. The authors point out that multiple time scales are needed in order to properly assess coupled climate carbon cycle models and that the seasonal cycles of both carbon and climate will need to be improved to produce adequate models. Steve has suggested that we need more on the ground observations of phenology (ie when leaves are on the trees etc). That seems sensible given the results of this paper.

item.title: Fereday et al., (2008), Cluster Analysis of North Atlantic-European Circulation Types and Links with Tropical Pacific Sea Surface Temperatures
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
There... he is. Like others before them, David and co-authors attempted to classify daily-mean observed mean sea level pressure fields into different categories. They used cluster analysis rather than fully-subjective types. They find that there is no preferred number of clusters - a projection of their clusters onto leading modes suggests that no parts of the "parameter space" are really preferred over any others and no "loitering" (of the kind associated with the Lorenz (1963) model occurs. The number of clusters that one chooses is then down to personal preference, taking into account that there should be many enough clusters that any one day is never that far from the cluster archetype and few enough that different clusters are distinguishable from one another. (Depending on what it is that you actually want the clusters for, there can be yet other considerations. e.g. Observational error rendering cluster differences insignificant, or links to changes in temperature and precipitation.) It's important to appreciate they classified anomalies rather than totals, which, again, is a choice you make depending on what you decide you want to do. Here, it helps them stop clusters bunching at one end of a season due to the annual cycle. If one is looking at climate change, on the other hand, that might be desirable. They then correlated various things against ENSO and stuff like that. I did not read that bit.

And also a meeting featuring David Fereday and Jeff Knight

which was considerably more positive than I had reason to expect, as I wasn't well prepared and their reasons for doing the things they did (rather than the more subjective weather types I've discussed with Steve Dorling seemed pretty well-justified). Some points:
  • They clearly strongly believe that tracking changes in clusters won't work! Not unless you have a very small number of clusters. I guess I don't know the data as well as they do. I find forming types across the perturbed and unperturbed climate a bit unsatisfactory, though.
  • That doesn't mean we can't try to look across models and identify which clusters / GWL are which.
  • Surprisingly, they provided the strongest reason so far for looking at GWL rather than objectrive types: GWL are defined in such a way to be interesting to meteorologists. Some rarer types might not be well characterised using clusters, but are important for weather impacts - perhaps on small regions.
  • Jeff Knight even suggested that it might be interesting to see what happens if a forecaster composed their own weather types! Probably a bit more than we can do, though.
  • They have done a small amount of work with HadGEM1 (the paper is about observations). It sounds like they could see only small changes in clusters as they went to 4xCO2 (a rather big change), justifying their suspicion of looking at changes in clusters.
  • Finally, to some extent it sounds like their clusters are not very robust if they re-derive using another dataset / part of the same dataset?

item.title: Huth et al., (2008), Classifications of Atmospheric Circulation Patterns
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A review of classifications of atmospheric circulation types published in Ann. N. Y. Acad. Sci. "Most" classification techniques classify daily mean SLP into between about 4 and 40 types using subjective, objective (well - computer calculated) or mixed subjective-objective types. One has the choice of classifying every day (usual with objective types), or looking for persistence and allowing some days to be transitional (more common with subjective types). Previous days are important -- what happened before party determines how temperature and precipitation are related to pressure. They agree with Fereday et al., (2008), that arguments for a given number of types tend to fall a bit flat. In general, the types should be many enough that that "in-class variance" is small enough that the type is sufficiently representative of a given example, and few enough that there is enough discriminatory power to reliably distinguish the types. There are rather a lot of different classifications, and it's pretty hard to say which is better, although many different metrics are shown. (Later on, it is recommended to use several classification techniques in order to check robustness of results.)

Some applications

Future climate change and downscaling of predictions (although types are not always helpful for downscaling). But one runs into problems if one assumes that future climate change is only due to changes in circulation. Beck et al., (2007) looked at European monthly pressure records back to 1780(!) and used this to reconstruct historical temperature and precipitation changes. Around 50% of changes are described by changes in frequency of type. The rest of it is due to changes of weather within a type. (The situation is "improved" to 60% due to changes in frequency for daily data, available for some of the record.) Some original research is actually done within the review on persistence of weather types. Hot and cold spells are linked to persistence of anticyclones, which produce a greater warming or cooling the longer they sit around due to the radiative imbalances they favour. Most of the paper is about observations, but they do eventually move to doing some stuff with General Circulation Models. Such a classification allows comparison with observations, but if one wants to look at large perturbations in climate, then one is faced with a choice (e.g. 4xCO2 vs control, say) and some difficulties:
  • Subjective types, but these might not represent GCM output satisfactorily.
  • Classify one dataset objectively, but how much do we learn about the second dataset if it doesn't fit the scheme well?
  • (Classifying both datasets separately is out if we decide to use cluster analysis, because clusters are unlikely to be stable enough -- something that David Fereday mentioned.)
  • Objectively classify ALL the perturbed and unperturbed data together, but do the types actually represent the weather from either dataset appropriately?

item.title: Hwang et al., (2013), Anthropogenic sulfate aerosol and the southward shift of tropical precipitation in the late 20th century
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Another Frierson stable paper about the intertropical convergence zone, equator-pole gradients and GCMs. It isn't massively insightful. They do something they call an energetic attribution analysis, which fingers sulphate as the cause of the southward shift. As so often, GCMs are found to underestimate observed changes by a factor of two. It's worth remembering the physical processes going on in the Hadley Cell: if you cool the Northern Hemisphere, the Northern Hadley cell intensifies. More heat is moved in the upper branch, but this simultaneously moves rainfall south as the Hadley cell enlarges...

item.title: Zelinka and Hartmann, (2012), Climate Feedbacks and Their Implications for Poleward Energy Flux Changes in a Warming Climate
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
[caption id="attachment_288" align="alignright" width="300"] Haven't had a picture for a while.[/caption] Another Zelinka and Hartmann.
"This study finds that latitudinal gradients in the sum of climate feedbacks reinforce the preexisting latitudinal gradient in TOA net radiation, requiring the climate system to transport more energy to the poles on a warming planet."
A kernel analysis of CMIP3 reveals that pre-existing patterns of clouds and water vapour (especially) are reinforced, increasing the equator-to-pole temperature gradient. Overall:
  • Temperature reduces E->P transport, due to upper tropospheric warming.
  • q and clouds increase it, again due to upper tropospheric warming and FAT. Plus there are increases in extratropical tropopause height.
  • Surface fluxes are of lower importance, but they note that the ocean increases atmospheric E->P by decreasing its thermohaline circulation.

item.title: Wu et al., (2013), Anthropogenic impact on Earth's hydrological cycle
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: I suppose it was inevitable that they would publish on this eventually. A CMIP5 ALL versus GHG only attribution analysis. The basic premise is that the global hydrological cycle (they look at Northern Hemisphere mean observations) has not been accelerating in both river gauge and precipitation data. They draw "that" precipitation versus temperature plot that I've been wanting to publish for sulphates and GHGs and then do some D&A. As usual, the models probably underestimate the observations. The usual surface-based energy budget explanation of precipitation is given. We will have to make sure that our paper is substantially differentiated from this one, but given that we find the opposite result, it shouldn't be too hard.

item.title: Li et al., (2012), Test of the Fixed Anvil Temperature Hypothesis
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A test of the FAT hypothesis in observations. Well - daytime (I don't know if that makes a difference?) MODIS satellite data and strictly on ENSO rather than global warming. They claim that this is better than GCMs at least, because coarse grids prevent one from testing the FAT hypothesis there. They note, however, that cloud resolving models suggest an increase in cloud top (or anvil) temperature (work by Tompkins and Craig, (2009)). Overall, they find that FAT provides a solid theoretical background for diagnosing cloud detrainment altitude altitude, but some subtle differences from a pure FAT response are visible in the satellite data. They tend to see a cooling in cloud top temperature that leads to a more negative cloud feedback than predicted by FAT. Something that I don't always appreciate adequately was reviewed here:
"The consistency of the spatial patterns between cloud fractions and clear-sky v and conv illustrates the fact that in different tropical regions, both cloudy (convective) and clear (subsidence) domains are present in different proportions. A region that shows the strongest radiative cooling in the clear-sky domain has to be accompanied by the greatest diabatic subsidence warming, which is compensated by convergence, thus being associated with the highest cloud fractions in the cloudy domain."
In other words, those convective towers are pretty damn narrow! The biggest subsidence is happening in almost the same region as the biggest convection, although the pattern is more tropically uniform than 200 hPa cloud fraction. They finish up by regressing cloud top temperature onto sea surface temperature. They find a fairly weak negative slope that is enough for them to say that cloud feedback is even more negative than predicted by FAT. They stress that their results are for ENSO and not a more uniform global warming.

item.title: Andrianakis and Challenor, (2011), Super-parameterisation of ocean deep convection
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: An unpublished technical note by Peter Challenor and colleague about how they emulated ocean convection. There's a lot of the old emulator mathematics, which I won't pretend to understand, but there's also some modelling notes and general statistical comments which I did just about get. They start with a high-resolution model of ocean dynamics that they want to speed-up by emulating the small-scale convective processes. Geostrophic-scale eddies continue to be simulated by a coarse dynamical model Fine-scale behaviour is first simulated in vertical columns alone to speed up model performance and build a tractable problem. The up-down fine-scale simulations are then replaced by a fast statistical emulator. Unlike the atmospheric convection scheme problem, the small-scale ocean up-down convective towers see significant "sideways talk" between the fine-scale resolved columns. By taking a first step of only simulating fine-scale processes in the vertical, they actually introduce the largest error. The subsequent emulation of the 1D convection doesn't make things any worse. It's really the problems from being near the edge of a convective plume and "not knowing it" due to only being able to model in the vertical that cause problems. The other thing they do is choose a long enough timestep such that θ is the only initial condition that matters (rather than u etc). In deriving the emulator they point out something I probably ought to have known but didn't realise before... If you've got a linear process, then you could model it by taking simultaneous principle components of the inputs and outputs. To the extent that the input-only PCs are still orthogonal, you can then dot them with inputs you want to make predictions for and find the outputs... I tried this for my toy convection scheme. It didn't work, which I guess is good, because it means that Nathan still has a project... Oh yes - so, in summary, the emulator works really well. It's the super-parameterisation - ie making the fine-scale simulation up-down only that introduces errors. Hence, super-parameterisations ought to be improved, they say. No paper notes.

item.title: Pendergrass and Hartmann, (2013), The atmospheric energy constraint on global-mean precipitation change
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: I met Angie Pendergrass at AGU. This paper records her efforts to understand changes in global mean precipitation using some idealised modelling studies to break down components. The paper doesn't tell me much I don't already know and obviously uses kernels, because that's what everyone loves doing. Essentially, a uniformly warming, constant RH profile explains the majority of the radiative cooling increase with global warming. Lapse rate and accompanying water vapour changes nearly cancel. They did, however, do something quite nice by introducing a couple of idealised clouds... Basically, the high cloud does a lot to longwave radiation and the low cloud does less than a third as much. No paper notes...

item.title: Tompkins and Craig, (1998), Time-scales of adjustment to radiative-convective equilibrium in the tropical atmosphere
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A paper in QJRMS I read to try to help me improve my idealised strategically parameterisable convection scheme. They get a cloud resolving model / large eddy simulation and perturb it with +1K and -1K SST anomalies. They attempt a timescale separation to seew hich processes dominate on which timescales.
  • Convective up and downdrafts. 30 minutes -- 1 hour.
  • Clear-sky mixing of water vapour and subsidence radiative cooling. 30 days.
  • Boundary layer mixing of Θ and moisture. 10 minutes.
  • The above are vertical processes, but it's worth noting that horizontal gravity wave activity can travel 100 km in 15 -- 30 minutes. They don't mix water vapour, of course.
So, imagine warming some SST. On short timescales, convection warms and dries the atmosphere. On longer timescales, clear-sky mixing (driven by descent?) moistens it. You can show this nicely because the processes that conserve equivalent potential temperature are fast (ie convection and downdrafts) and those that don't are slow. There is also a discussion of appropriate resolution for parameterisation of convection as opposed to treating it as a resolved process.

item.title: Johnson and Xie, (2010), Changes in sea surface temperature threshold for tropical convection
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Rob Chadwick recommended I read this paper because it covers the point about tropical convective area not changing much under climate change. This occurs because, as the paper finds, "the tropical troposphere has warmed consistent with moist-adiabatic adjustment, in agreement with global climate model simulations". Similarly, the distribution of SSTs about the mean does not change with warming. That's really all one needs to know. It's interesting that it's tricky to find a good measure of precipitation change in the tropics (of course), but easier to discuss thresholds, because that depends more on surface temperature measurement. Rob also recommended another paper on this topic by Carlos Hoyos and Peter Webster from Climate Dynamics in 2012, but he also said:
"Here's the paper I was talking about. I actually think most of it is complete b*****ks, especially to do with their proposed strengthening of the circulation under warming, but Fig. 9 shows nicely the invariance of the dynamical warm pool under warming in four GCMs."
Interesting that he should recommend it! NO PAPER NOTES.

item.title: Chen et al., (2013), Non-negligible effects of cloud vertical overlapping assumptions on longwave spectral fingerprinting studies
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
This is a paper I read while working on Lambert, Webb, Yoshimori and Yokohata. In the end, it turned out not to be as relevant as I hoped. Anyway, the paper looks across the longwave spectra of clouds and sees how different overlaps affect the OLR.
"Different cloud overlapping assumptions have little effect on the spectral fingerprints of temperature and humidity. However, the amplitude of the spectral fingerprints due to the same amount of cloud fraction change can differ as much as a factor of two between maximum random versus random overlap assumptions, especially for low and middle clouds."
This appears to be a heavy handed way of saying that the spectrum is unaffected by overlap assumption, but the integrated flux is. References on page 7311 support this for other radiation codes. It is emphasised that low clouds are most affected, which makes sense, since these are the ones that get masked... Presumably no paper notes -- well, I can't find any, anyway.

item.title: Byrne and O'Gorman, (2013), Link between land-oean warming contrast and surface relative humidities in simulations with coupled climate models
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Tropical land-sea warming contrast is captured in models if one assumes that equivalent potential temperature change is the same over land and ocean. This is based on a theory expounded by Byrne and O'Gorman, (2013), in J Climate, which I haven't read, although it sounds pretty similar to Joshi et al., (2008). The idea is applied in CMIP5 for 2070-99 - 1975-04. The important thing to remember is that ΘE itself can be 12 K higher over land than ocean. It's the changes that follow the hypothesis. Their idea does quite well.

item.title: Conroy et al., (2010), El Nino / Southern Oscillation and changes in the zonal gradient of tropical Pacific sea surface temperature over the last 1.2 ka
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: I'm slightly concerned that we've been taking an unfair view of the way other people process proxies in Lilo's project. They (specifically Yan et al.) do use weighted measures of different proxies, rather than just adding stuff up that's in the general area. I'm also rather surprised to find that dealing with paleo-temperatures actually seems harder than dealing with paleo-precipitation. This article from Conroy et al. (from the journal PAGES, which I'd never even heard of) describes a large component of the Pacific temperature reconstruction that Yan et al. relied on that Lilo also has. Conroy's record is based on two proxies. One from El Junco lake in the Galapagos (which seems almost like a precipitation proxy, to be honest) and a foraminifera record from the Indo-Pacific warm pool. They combine the two to build the "tropical Pacific zonal SST gradient". They find that it decreases between about 1000 AD and 2000 AD. I pointed out to Lilo that another paper due to Mann et al., (2009), has apparently complementary results / proxy data. No paper notes.

item.title: Soden et al., (2005), The radiative signature of upper tropospheric moistening
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: This paper apparently does a chunk of what I want done for PROBEC, but neither I nor the referees discovered it. Angus pointed it out to me. Satellites, starting in the 80s are compared with models on upper tropospheric moistening. In general, GCMs do a good job of capturing upper tropospheric moistening, and a particularly good job of capturing the associated radiative effect of changes, because one only has to get the fractional change correct to get that right. (This occurs because of the logarithmic effect of increasing water vapour on radiation.) Temperature data are taken from two retrievals from MSU, which show a difference of about a factor of two in warming. HIRS is used to estimate water vapour concentrations. In general, the constant relative humidity paradigm of observations is adhered to by observations, but there are geographical regions of significant departure. I need to remind myself that Mark Webb said that William Ingram was highly critical of this paper. But that's third hand and may not have any real basis. One thing that this paper doesn't really do that well, and that I initially wanted Angus to focus on was just thinking in terms of radiances, rather than taking the intermediate step of going through water vapour and temperature and having to fudge one's way through multiple radiation codes. However, I think one is in fact bound to take the intermediate step to some degree, although Angus is building a linear model using multiple satellite channels to map the effects of changing relative humidities and other departures from moist adiabatic behaviour.

item.title: Armour et al., (2010), Time-varying climate sensitivty from regional feedbacks
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
There seems to be a whole new school of Gerard Roe-driven climate feedback papers expanding earlier stuff on regional feedbacks like Boer and Yu, (2003). Here's one. The basic idea is that
"Here we propose that λeff and Teff are fundamentally liked to the geographic pattern of regional climate feedbacks and the geographic pattern of surface warming at any given time."
Which I'm trying not to interpret as "if you have a many thousands of degrees of freedom, then your statistical model will fit well." OK - fair enough - they don't allow the gridpoint feedbacks to develop in time, and they admit that they miss out on adjustment effects. They test the idea in CCSM4 using the kernel method(!) It does well. Nothing seems all that uncontroversial, despite the alleged newness. They are probably a bit lucky because most non-local effects are probably contained within a latitude band, and areas in a latitude band tend to warm at the same time. (According to Lambert's hand-written notes, anyway.) I don't think anyone disagrees with any of this stuff, but it is dressed up as a bit new. Overall, there is some value here.

item.title: CFMIP / GEWEX 2014
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: I went to both the CFMIP and GEWEX in the Netherlands this summer. They were not too bad at all! The main thing is that having a conference banquet means going to a beach barbecue place that seems ridiculously exotic compared with Britain, even though it's only Holland. CFMIP: Steve Klein has found SUPER MOIST ADIABATIC WARMING in GCMs above the boundary layer. Hideo Shiogama is designing multi-physics ensembles that go some way to getting past structural restrictions of PPEs. Tobias Becker is using Φ! I was reminded to contact Masa Yoshimori about understanding FAT and its effect on feedbacks (or lack of, according to Masa). GEWEX: is a rather different community than CFMIP, and one that I'm even more of a third wheel in. Saw lots of relevant stuff on droughts and floods. That community really needs better estimates of relevant precipitation events. Met Thorsten Mauritsen, who sent me his paper on the Iris Effect that "himself" and Bjorn Stevens have sent to Nature. Quite interesting. Possibly makes a difference to pattern of tropical feedbacks? An interesting aspect was that TM's lapse rate feedback decreases (compensating for the weaker water vapour feedback caused by the Iris Effect in his simulations), while Sandrine Bony's lapse rate feedback increases. Both TM's and SB's simulations have weaknesses, however. TM's has the iris quite crudely applied. SB's is cloud resolving (so better in that way), but only limited area, calling into question the effect on large-scale dynamics.

item.title: Crook et al., (2011), Spatial Patterns of Modeled Climate Feedback and Contributions to Temperature Response and Polar Amplification
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
The other Crook... (2011) paper. This one describes spatial patterns of climate response as well as global mean responses. Perhaps the biggest surprise is that q + LR feedback produces the biggest range of uncertainty across models, contrary to most other similar studies. The ensemble is of eight slab models however, rather than coupled models.

Analysis:

The paper cites some slightly older literature on both the cloud masking effect (Zhang et al., 1994) and a SW APRP method for estimating surface albedo (Winton et al., 2006). The paper also explores the applicability of regression, which doesn't work once one gets down to 10 x 10 degree slabs.

item.title: Lu and Cai, (2009), A new framework for isolating individual feedback processes in coupled general circulation climate models. Part I: formulation
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
AKA The CFRAM paper

This is the CFRAM paper, in which:
"...the isolation of partial temperature changes due to an external forcing or an individual feedback is achieved by solving the linearized infrared radiation transfer model subject to individual energy flux perturbations..."
They write down changes in longwave radiative divergence on levels as a function of all a model's processes and the direct effect of forcing. Because the effect of warming on longwave divergence is almost a clean function of temperature on that level, they write it as a radiative kernel multiplied by temperature change. They then invert the matrix and solve for temperature. The kernel is specified once using a radiation code. You end up with the temperature change on levels "due" to a given process, like convective heating or shortwave radiation or the forcing itself.  Apart from being on levels (there is also a vertically integrated TFRAM), the contrast with PRP is that PRP supposes feedbacks to be a function of global mean temperature change caused initially by forcing. In CFRAM, all perturbations including forcing have equal status. (I guess the one that doesn't is infrared divergence caused by warming, because this relies on a kernel?)

item.title: Burrows, (2014), Spectra as windows into exoplanet atmospheres
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
To quote a man long gone, "many things that I suspected were confirmed."  Burrows is a senior planetary scientist / astronomer. His article describes progress in exoplanetary science over the past twenty years. (Exoplanetary science was more or less born in the early '90s.) One of his major points is that the very detailed conclusions presently being drawn about exoplanets from a very small amount of data will probably not stand up to better observations, which is pretty much what I thought about the exoplanet conference I attended in Exeter a couple of years back. Exoplanets are difficult to observe. Most of the ones that we know about are big, close to their parent stars and very very hot. Smaller, more Earth-like planets are beginning to be found, but this is much more difficult to do. (Virtually?) everything we know about exoplanets comes from spectra of their primary (in front of the parent star) and secondary eclipses (behind the star). It's very difficult to do anything with the isolated infrared spectra of an exoplanet. But despite this: NOTE that transit spectra for "Earths" do exist! Follow references within for more info... Spectra that do exist are low resolution and derived using instruments that are being pushed beyond their design limits. The existence of various kinds of unknown scatterers (clouds and hazes) makes it even more difficult. Apparently, atmospheric inversions can be detected, but I'm not really sure how? (Unless something can be done with various kinds of broadening, but I would have thought the spectral resolution would be too low?) Burrows fairly points out that we don't even understand these things very well on Earth yet. Measurements are consistent with a model studies that make use of a wide variety of inputs.
The important positive point he makes, though, is held in his introductory paragraph: "I suggest that the true function of the recent past of exoplanet atmospheric research has been not to constrain planet properties for all time, but to train a new generation of scientists who, by rapid trial and error, are fast establishing a solid future foundation for a robust science of exoplanets."
No handwritten notes.

item.title: Kaufman, (2014), A Community-Driven Framework for Climate Reconstructions
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
The PAGES consortium are a group trying to build a consistent set of paleoclimate reconstructions for community use. I have been referred to articles in PAGES news in the past. This Kaufman EOS article sets out plans for PAGES 2k, which is a project designed to build a library of paleoproxies for the past 2000 years, a period, he says, for which climate was relatively similar to today and for which relatively plentiful data is available. Some mini-highlights:
  • Statistical approaches for combining data of different temporal resolutions.
  • Multivariate reconstructions! A fairly bleak view of hydrology, but it is suggested that things can be improved using temperature data. The opposite of Lilo's current problems. Forward modelling is also mentioned.
  • Finally he tells us that: "PAGES 2k is committed to providing researchers with high impact multiauthored papers that address big-picture research questions."

item.title: Schaller et al., (2013), The sensitivity of the modeled energy budget and hydrological cycle to CO2 and solar forcing
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I think that this paper does it. It solves the long-standing riddle of why CO2 and solar forcing respond differently during tropospheric adjustment despite each forcing a similar amount of heat to be absorbed by the lower troposphere. (At her request, I think / I hope), I told Angie Pendergrass:
"Schaller's paper: Just finished reading it. It's a bit laboured, flitting back and forth between surface based and atmospheric explanations and with a bit of mixing up forcing and feedback too. Still - my current view is basically in there. Solar forcing is mostly in the tropics, which doesn't lend itself to spinning down the hydrological cycle nearly as well as CO2, reflected in where precipitation changes too. I agree that she has been quite thorough, but it could be majorly cleaned up if we wanted too, though."
Which is not as nice as I could have been. I think Nathalie Schaller is probably one of Angie's mates, so I should be more careful what I say in future. Especially since Schaller cited Lambert and Faull, (2007), the best paper ever, but was more complimentary (ie didn't point out that my explanation is wrong) then she needed to be. The paper points out explicitly that solar forcing is associated with stronger increases in poleward energy transport, which tend to drive increases in large-scale (presumably frontal) precipitation, as well as greater warming in the tropics. The relatively weaker circulation in CO2 experiments is also commented on. Results are slightly hampered by using the 1%/year approach, and as I say above, there's a good bit of mixing forcing and response going on. But it is comprehensive in its analysis. Non-linearity of response at high λ is explored. No paper notes. Not in the paper is the smoking gun for the vertical argument, but Angie has heard about it. Liz Moyer from the University of Chicago has a postdoc who showed a poster with some single column simulations of the response to CO2 and solar forcing. Both show the same thing: a reduction in precipitation due to the direct effect of forcing.

item.title: Two papers about the El Nino-Southern Oscillation
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I've been trying to learn a bit more about observations of ENSO and paleo-variables associated with it for Lilo's project.  

Trenberth and Caron, (2000), The Southern Oscillation Revisited: Sea Level Pressures, Surface Temperatures, and Precipitation

This paper contains relatively recent information about instrumental observations of surface variables associated with ENSO. It seems there are actually relatively few relevant studies, following a chat with Mat and some searching on Web of Knowledge. A summary:
  • ENSO was in a diminished state between about 1920 and 1950. The 1976 climate shift (this was when climate suddenly started warming quickly) altered some teleconnections.
  • The "ENSO year" (ie most sensible way of estimating what's going on in the annual mean) runs from May to April. It's unlikely this means much in our paleo-study, though.
  • A large number of correlation and lag-correlation patterns have been published. There is a "striking" resemblance between the patterns for temperature and precipitation. The decadal variability pattern is a bit broader than the annual pattern, but similar.
 

Kitzberger et al., (2001), Inter-hemispheric synchrony of forest fires and the El Nino-Southern Oscillation

An interesting paper describing co-variability of fire between Patagonia and the Western United States. The data they examine are heavily, heavily processed (and I'm really a bit unsure about what they've done), but it does appear that they find co-variation between Patagonian and US fire occurrences that can be associated with El Nino. A particularly nice point they make is that the best conditions for a fire is (in these regions) a strong El Nino, which is wet and encourages growth of tinder-y materials, followed by a strong La Nina that really dries things out. It is one of several papers I have recently that discusses (and in this case even shows some results from) documentary evidence of past ENSOs stretching back 500 years or so. For some reason, I find this intriguing, but at least one of the papers (maybe Braganza et al., 2009?) cautions against reading too much into it. A final caution is that another complication is the timing of ENSO fluctuations within the year affects their control of fire. No paper notes for either of these.

item.title: Braganza et al., (2009), A multiproxy index of the El-Nino-Southern Oscillation, A.D. 1525-1982
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A rather nice paper by Karl Braganza, that is trying to do something similar to Lilo's work.
"Using tree ring, coral and ice core data, we reconstruct a proxy-based ENSO index between A.D. 1525 and 1982... our network is Pacific basin-wide, using ENSO sensitive proxies from western equatorial Pacific, New Zealand, the central Pacific, and subtropical North America."

Overview!

This is a multi-proxy analysis that focuses on trying to capture behaviour linked to ENSO and is agnostic about what kind of proxy is being analysed (i.e. could be to do with hydrology or temperature or perhaps even something else). Having used "expert judgement", rather than something else, to choose the proxy locations, he then builds his EOFs from the network locations (rather than what Lilo does currently by sampling locations from the "full spatial coverage" EOF). This ensures that the EOF is orthogonal to subsequent EOFs, but doesn't allow for the fact that there may be mixing between ENSO and other things in the EOF itself. In general, I think the paper is thoughtful and takes a very nice approach to everything, with the exception of errors, which as we now know, are very difficult to calculate:
  • He takes the view that we don't need to calibrate to instrumental observations to get ENSO, as it's basically up-and-down, so you might as well just use the proxy network. I agree with this apart from the consequences for mixing ENSO with other stuff when that network is very limited.
  • Issues of seasonality &c. Proxies are more sensitive to some seasons than others. Tree rings, for example, are obviously sensitive to what's going on during the growing season. They also may not provide a good description of long term behaviour, and need to be high-passed filtered. Not sure we're doing that?
  • Non-linearity. Both of the size of response and between hydrological and temperature indicators.
  • Another mention of Quinn (1987)'s documentary evidence work, although largely critical this time.
  • NO ERRORS! (Well - not really.)
No paper notes. As usual.

item.title: Vecchi and Soden, (2007), Global Warming and the Weakening of the Tropical Circulation
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
So, I finally read this paper after years of not doing so! Angus prompted me to do it after he suggested it to Olivia, our project student. In the end it is not nearly as impressive or insightful as I had feared(?), but as Angus says, it contains a number of very useful plots. Overall they find that
  1. The "thermodynamic scaling arguments of Held and Soden" explain basically everything. (Did Held and Soden really come up with this stuff?)
  2. Changes in the Walker circulation dominate weakening of the circulation, rather than the Hadley circulation. This preferential weakening is linked to:
  3. El-Nino like warming is seen in the model simulations they analyse (although the mechanisms are different).
  4. The Hadley circulation, meanwhile, may be forced to be maintained by energy transport requirements, they speculate.
  5. The heaviest rainfall events continue to increase even though heavy and small precipitation events decrease.
No paper notes.

item.title: Johnson et al., (2015), Evaluating uncertainty in convective cloud microphysics using statistical emulation
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: This is a paper that Mark Webb was trying to scare me with. It turns out that it does not steel all our thunder, but it does prevent some relevant ideas and back up the idea that convection could be represented through statistical emulation. The experiment is not very well described for me, but it looks like what they're doing is running a fairly beefy model of the atmosphere in a channel that contains a sophisticated parameterisation of cloud microphysics and convection that even represents aerosol / CCN interaction. As usual, they want to use the emulator in order to speed-up their calculations. They perturb 12 parameters and analyse the sensitivity of the model's simulation of 80 minutes of precipitation (and some other cloud variables) to the perturbations. In this sense, I think it's something more of a Doug McNeall / David Sexton style of emulation rather than a replication of the actual convective process. Still, this probably lends weight to the idea that convective emulation can be done. Of course -- the emulator is not perfect. The important thing is that its fitting error is small compared with the parameterisation error.

item.title: Chadwick et al., (2014), Surface warming patterns drive tropical rainfall pattern reponses to CO2 forcing on all timescales
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Doing a bit of housekeeping of papers I've read lying around on my desk. Another Rob Chadwick paper that tells us that "the rich don't get richer in the tropics" basically because the pattern of SST matters and that means that stuff mostly just moves around. (If you look at percentiles, then I think the rich still gets richer.) I think he is forced to keep banging this drum partly because Sandrine Bony is banging an opposing drum that is backed up by little evidence. A key point is that, even in the first year, model response is similar to centennial response, rather than due to adjustment due to CO2 forcing (Bony). Of course - the adjustment does dominate the mean slowing of the tropical circulation. The last but one page has what I described in my on-the-paper notes as a "Partially correct explanation of land-sea contrast stuff." (I think I'm unhappy about warming of the atmosphere by CO2 versus solar being misattributed to be big in the CO2 case and small in the solar or something). NO PAPER NOTES.

item.title: Roderick and Farquhar, (2011), A simple framework for relating variations in runoff to variations in climatic conditions and catchment properties
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I've been trying to understand what on Earth it is that Joe does with the Budyko framework in order to understand changes in runoff that result from changes in precipitation.  Figure 1: Says it best. The Choudhury-Yang formulation of the Budyko framework showing rivers moving from water limited to energy limited (ie for evaporation) as rainfall increases. The various values of n delineate different sorts of catchment. Snatches of the actual theory are mentioned here, but really the paper begins with an expansion of relevant derivatives to help choose between the effects of catchment and precipitation changes on the runoff amount. The Murray-Darling River basin is analysed using relevant observed data, and impacts of possible future changes are made. The other thing that is worth mentioning is that qualitative descriptions of how the catchment variable n might change due to various factors are discussed. I did not explore this bit of the paper fully.

Some papers by D Yang and H Yang relevant to China are mentioned. Might be good to follow up. NO PAPER NOTES.

item.title: Gedney et al., (2014), Detection of solar dimming and brightening effects on Northern Hemisphere river flow
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
While I have this land surface stuff on my mind, let's get this one filed away. Another study on attribution of runoff changes from Nic Gedney (the previous one has been heavily criticised elsewhere).
