"Here we formally detect and quantify the historical effect of changing aerosol concentrations, via solar radiation, on observed river flow over the heavily industrialized, northern extra-tropics."
In other words, close to the same region Joe was looking at for his runoff paper. They found that solar dimming led to up to a 25% increase in river runoff in the most heavily polluted regions of Europe. In order to do this, they needed to include the effect of diffuse radiation on photosynthesis, which I think TRENDY therefore probably doesn't do. Nevertheless changes due to changes in direct radiation (or overall radiation?) dominate the total response, since they affect both all evaporation, whereas the diffuse component only affects transpiration. Detections are also achieved at European basin level. They cannot detect land use change. A number of relevant comparisons to Joe's paper can be made. A number of basins were ruled out based on irrigation. We didn't do this because we didn't think it was necessary / it didn't seem to have any noticeable effect on the runoff-rainfall relationship. The effect of what they call CLIMATE and indeed AEROSOL are detected with scaling factors that are significantly under 1. We think this fits in with Joe's work because errors in the observed data will tend to mean that models "overestimate" the observed response, which has little aerosol response in it. Having said that, it looks like that although they have the St Lawrence catchment (one of the tell-tale rivers in Joe's analysis), they don't have the Columbia river (the other one). No paper notes.

item.title: Smerdon, (2012), Climate models as a test bed for climate reconstruction methods: pseudoproxy experiments
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A WIRES climate change article by Jason Smerdon (who once asked me something about land-sea contrast that I did not handle very well) about using GCMs to trial proxy reconstructions. Lilo has been doing something similar (albeit using observations / reanalysis data, but the effect is much the same). Perhaps the most immediately useful thing he does for us is provide an estimate of proxy signal to noise ratio for a typical proxy. I.e. the ratio of climate related fluctuations to junk. Interestingly, he doesn't divide this up by proxy type, which is what I expected, instead discussing a general range from which we've taken something sensible. Instead, he mentions that kind of thing in the FUTURE DESIGN IMPROVEMENTS FOR PPEs section. He notes that different proxies are different, are sensitive to different seasons and are functions of multiple climate (among other) variables. It's here that I get a hint that he's really been talking about temperature all along, which is not really the way Lilo's been using the info. I think we've basically been following his methods, but it is worth pointing out that we haven't tested our calibration by checking the strength of the reconstruction outside the calibration period. In order to do this, we would have to use GCMs, as Smerdon does, but we have tried to omit this from Lilo's paper. Hopefully we will not have to bring this into it, but it may be a necessary evil. It will certainly be a necessary evil of her thesis. Relevant to this, I should check out the paper by Emile-Geay. This individual seems to have said something nasty to Lilo about how important he is at a conference. It's an unfortunate way for him to force himself into our plans, but I suppose it's worked. No paper notes.

item.title: Zhai et al., (sub), Long term cloud change imprinted in seasonal cloud variation: another evidence of high climate sensitivity
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Am I allowed to rap (blog) about papers that I've reviewed but that are not out yet? Probably not, but given that no one else reads this, I'm going to do it anyway. ("Here's a song your Principal Skinner didn't

[caption id="attachment_401" align="alignright" width="580"] Los Simpson[/caption]

want us to play...")

OK - so this is one of those emergent constraints papers that describes how contemporary climate features can be related to future climate features in CMIP5. The paper relates changes in subtropical subsidence region marine low clouds in the seasonal cycle to long term changes in clouds and that in turn to equilibrium climate sensitivity. Their results suggest that we bump up CMIP5 climate sensitivity from 3.5 K to 4.1 K. Overall, the paper looks more sensible that Fasullo and Trenberth (2012), which does something similar with upper tropospheric humidity and high clouds, except in this paper there is a clearer physical link between the relevant processes, as subtropical low clouds are the thing that actually cause the uncertainty in climate sensitivity. There was something sloppy about the paper, and I can't help but feel that my nevertheless rather long review will be the "nice" one and they will fall foul of someone grumpier than me. So who knows when or if we'll see it. It's also interesting to note this stuff because Yoko Tsushima already has a paper out that notes that models that don't get that seasonal cycle right are low sensitivity models (Tsushima et al., 2013). Also Mat Collins notes that the succession of process-based emergent constraints papers are all pointing towards a higher than mean CMIP5 climate sensitivity. Of course - there's no paper notes. Because I've just destroyed them in line with keeping the review confidential.

item.title: MOAP workshop on radiative transfer, 13-14th May, 2015
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
The MOAP workshop on radiative transfer brought together a cast of characters, many of whom I haven't seen really since I was a graduate student. I played a small role in establishing the workshop, arguing that we ought to focus on applications of radiation code in order to get funding, because otherwise nobody would be convinced. However, that was thrown out, and it was decided to focus just on radiation codes, their inputs, comparability and code development. Absolutely fair enough, but it didn't look like a route to fund the national capability that everybody kept mentioning, since Keith Shine states that efforts to obtain funding for such have been going on for 15-20 years. Keith also politely reminded us that "All the MOAP partners are involved in radiation, apart from Exeter." So I did the only reasonable thing: I left Angus to attend the rest of the meeting, and went to grab a coffee so that I could get on with MSc referrals and other administration.

Yet, there are still plenty of meeting highlights:

  • James Manners reminded us that current GCM radiation codes typically undersimulate 4xCO2 forcing because their k bands are saturated before that, and (previously) weak lines and line wings that become dominant aren't parameterised at all. Jimmy also managed to get stitched up to write the pre-proposal on developing a national capability for radiation. I can take part of the credit for making his life difficult, or so he says at any rate. Finally, he showed us a Bill and Ted's slide, confirming my view that SOCRATES is pronounced "Sooa-craytes".
  • Alejandro Bodas told Angus and me that a HIRS simulator (Angus's phrase) already exists within the CFMIP's COSP. This means that we can run an online representation of what HIRS ought to see within HadGEM3 to check whether Angus's monthly field based results make sense or not.
  • Keith Shine before he was done with telling me I'm useless reminded us that modern radiative transfer codes simulate infrared scattering.
  • Robin Hogan (ECMWF) is working on 3D radiative transfer and not because he's interested in giant planets. At low solar zenith angle, tall cumulus / cumulonimbus clouds causing scattering from their sides is important. At high solar zenith angle, radiation being scattered out of clouds and back into the clear-sky is important. His approximate model (ie run-able in a realistic amount of time) is called SPARTACUS, in keeping with the meeting's Graeco-Roman theme.

item.title: The Sky at Night; The runaway greenhouse effect
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
So - my outreach is done for about the next two years. I appeared on the Sky at Night to talk about runaway greenhouse effects, mostly getting deflected into a rather interesting discussion of exoplanets. [caption id="attachment_407" align="alignleft" width="300"] Not actually me, but Lucie Green on the Sky at Night.[/caption] In order to do so, I had to read a couple of papers to make sure my knowledge of the relevant ideas wasn't too far out of date:  

Leconte et al., (2013), Increased insolation threshold for runaway greenhouse processes on Earth-like planets

This paper is the first, or at least one of the first?, to run a 3-D GCM from Earth-like conditions through to runaway greenhouse by turning up the Sun. Previous studies tended to use radiative-convective models that only simulate 1-D and therefore miss a host of effects, especially the existence of dry regions in the tropical and subtropical tropospheres that tend to increase the threshold for the planet to leap to runaway. Clouds, as simulated by this GCM, tend to be de-stabilizing, making the runaway occur at lower temperatures than it would do otherwise. The authors make a fair bit of the robustness of their subgridscale parameterisations being robust over a wide range of conditions. They do seem reasonable, but I would hesitate before taking concreting in their conclusions concerning clouds. Overall they find that one would have to turn up insolation to about 375 Wm-2 before runaway sets in. They reckon this gives Earth "at least another billion years" before runaway conditions. Interestingly, Lucie Green, a solar scientist wouldn't be drawn on this on the day. A remaining puzzle is the water loss on Venus. The authors comment that the runaway Earth's stratosphere remains cold and dry, making it difficult for water to make it's way through for ionisation and then to space. Apparently I thought this was obvious when I was scribbling on the manuscript. I was rather distracted though.  

Tian and Ida, (2015), Water contents of Earth-mass planets around M dwarfs

So - a paper about water loss then recommended to me by Nathan Mayne. Not Venusian water loss, but exoplanet water loss. A key place to look for Earth-like exoplanets is around M dwarfs, basically because there are lots of them. Of course, the planet would have to be very close to the M dwarf to sustain liquid water, and that means that the potential for various kinds of planetary water loss mechanisms to kick in is serious. In particular, M stars are expected to start at quite high luminosity in their young lives before declining to allow Earth-like planets in close-in orbits. However, by this point, the potentially Earth-like planets may have had their water blown away by the star's early activity. It took me a while to dig down and understand what exactly they did to conclude all this. It's interesting to see that this paper, unlike the previous which was clearly written from a planetary / Earth-science perspective, was written by astrophysicists. Hence, they plough all their simulation effort into stellar and planetary system formation and none into simulating the atmospheres of the actual planets, which I think are just represented by a few simple escape formulae. Also, as the authors say
"One underlying assumption of the model is that all water on the planets is at the surface during the PMS phase. Earth-mass planets may retain some water in the mantle during the PMS phase and release water to the surface at later time."
(PMS = "pre-main sequence".) There's probably a research gap here. Anyway - the authors come to the interesting conclusion that we should expect bimodality in available water in planets around M dwarfs (not quite sure what they mean by this), but in most cases most water is lost and M stars are not the place to look for Earth-like planets! Time will tell... No paper notes for either paper.

item.title: Romps (2011), Response of Tropical Precipitation to Global Warming
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
He uses a high resolution cloud resolving simulation (LES to the likes of us) to show that "local precipitation fluxes are found to obey Clausius-Clapeyron (CC) scaling". This is in contrast to what happens in  parameterised GCM convection. He begins by defining the local precipitation flux, which is the global mean precipitation flux / average fraction of domain that is precipitating. (Here I think global can be defined loosely to mean the tropical area of interest.) He is aware of various caveats, such as changes in detrainment level of convection, changes in precipitation efficiency etc, but his basic thesis is
  1. Assume that air parcels go from the bottom to the top of the troposphere.
  2. Nothing changes about convection other than the q follows the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
Which he calls a scaling theory. The approach is found to basically work when compared with changes in the cloud resolving model. Some interesting things happen there, like very localised precipitation fluxes of up to 271 m per year! "Global" precipitation is constrained by energetics to 3 %\K. Meanwhile, vertical moisture gradient, "cloud size" (or something related to it in the vertical) and vertical velocity increase by 5 %\K, increasing local precipitation fluxes greatly. The paper is written with the assurance of a 1970s atmospheric dynamicist (and why not), so I was surprised by his comment that
"Since we do not yet understand what sets CAPE in the current troposphere (i.e. why 1000 J per kg and not 100 or 10,000 J per kg?)"
Is CAPE not just a measure of how much radiation is winning over convection? Perhaps I'm being naive. He tells us that "convective vigour" is a function of CAPE increase, but then I would expect precipitation and CAPE to scale together naturally. I'm not sure I see CAPE as really that fundamental?

item.title: Forget and Leconte, (2013), Possible climates on terrestrial exoplanets
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A review article covering the range of climates that might be found on rocky planets by two experienced researchers.
"To first order, climate primarily depends on 1) The atmospheric composition and the volatile inventory; 2) The incident stellar flux; 3) The tidal evolution of the planetary spin, which can notable lock a planet with a permanent night side."
Aquaplanets: a "vast population of aquaplanets" is mentioned, which makes sense given how close the Earth is to being drowned in water. This is likely to happen near, or close to the snow line where much water is available. Aquaplanets are also interesting in the context of weathering. The carbonate-silicate cycle turns atmospheric CO2 into carbonates that are deposited on the ocean floor on Earth. Where there isn't any land to expose the silicate rocks, this process is (probably?) very strongly hampered, possibly making aquaplanets unstable to a runaway CO2 greenhouse. Escape mechanisms are discussed in some detail. The high activity in the X-ray and UV spectra of young stars and their strong stellar winds, particularly young red dwarfs is discussed in the context of how difficult this makes it to keep an atmosphere early on. (E.g. Mars before 4.1 Gya.) Planetary spin evolution is eventually towards tidal locking (or a resonance?) with the parent star. The timescale depends on r-6, hence Earth-like planets close to red dwarfs are much more likely to be tidally locked than the Earth. (Timescale for Earth estimated in the work to be around 20 Gyr, for Venus 3 Gyr and for Mercury 80 Myr.) Thermal tides in a thick atmosphere could even drive a planet (e.g. Venus) somewhat away from tidal locking. Tidal locking introduces lots of interesting possibilities for atmospheric loss, perhaps through the formation of a massive lump of ices on the night-side, or through losses to space at the sub-stellar point.

item.title: Dal Gesso et al., (2015), A single-column model intercomparison on the stratocumulus representation in present-day and future climate
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Was encouraged to look at this as a primer for the single-column model experiments that Ian Boutle will do for "myself" and Rob Chadwick. (Ian is one of the authors.) Basically, SCMs are compared to GCMs are compared to LES. The LES are generally consistent with one another. Everything else is less consistent with each other and the LES. They scan the models across different values of SST and near surface humidity (which is basically what I'm asking for) and watch to see where clouds form. To summarise:
"...the comparison with LES results suggests that the description of the Scu-topped boundary layer in SCMs is still inadequate."
It also doesn't compare terribly well with the "host" GCMs, unfortunately. Sobel and Bretherton (2000) (to be described in a later post)'s SCM did compare quite well with the full model across the tropics. I wonder if the inclusion of moist advection in that study helped. (They were trying to answer the rather different problem of rainfall (i.e. the wet regions were most important) and did it all within the QTCM framework.) There is a bit of science I learnt from this paper too: LES response to +4K perturbation in the stratocumulus region: Liquid water path decreases as near surface relative humidity decreases (although there is no break-up in cloud!) This reduces the shortwave cloud radiative effect. Both the surface latent heat flux and the entrainment flux at the top of the boundary layer (boundary layer moisture -> free troposphere) increase. The entrainment is enhanced by increasing evaporation but by slightly suppressed by radiative feedbacks that reduce cooling of the free troposphere through increases in free tropospheric moisture. The boundary layer deepens, but RH is reduced leading the cloud base to raise more than the cloud top, thinning the cloud layer overall. (I'm not sure if I understand increases in surface latent heat flux with reductions in atmospheric radiative cooling unless the surface temperature is held fixed? Perhaps the reduction in radiative cooling is only in the lower free troposphere?) They obviously focus on the more stable parts of the tropics. The experiments we will do will be more interested in the wet end of things. NO PAPER NOTES. (Also - Los Simpson.)

item.title: Randall, (2013), Beyond Deadlock
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
[caption id="" align="alignright" width="117"] David Randall[/caption] A Geophysical Research Letters opinion piece from Derek Randall that Erasmo gave to me (after a curry or something? No - too dramatic). His thesis is that climate models aren't improving too much, and that the root cause is parameterisations. He writes:
"Randall et al., (2003a) wrote that 'The cloud parameterization problem is "deadlocked" in the sense that our rate of progress is unacceptably slow.' That was 10 years ago."
He focuses on convective entrainment and resolution dependence. Getting the entrainment right is important because it has a strong influence on and adjusts convection's sensitivity to mid-tropospheric water vapour, for example. Entrainment is also very difficult to observe (or even diagnose from high resolution models). The discussion moves to trying to build resolution independent parameterisations. The second topic is the use of global Cloud Resolving Models (CRMs). This is seen as a hope for the next ten years, although it is conceded that these must still parameterise cloud microphysics. In the meantime we have what he calls Multiscale Modeling Frameworks (MMFs). These use a "superparameterisation", embedding a CRM within a GCM column. The model can run satisfactorily quickly because communication between the CRMs in each column is not simulated. There isn't much of a conclusion. He just hopes that further work with CRMs and MMFs will improve our process understanding.

item.title: Voigt and Shaw, (2015), Circulation response to warming shaped by radiative changes of clouds and water vapour
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: One of, according to somebody we interviewed this week, several Aiko Voigt papers out there on circulation response to cloud and water vapour radiative heating. They find that cloud changes tend to amplify poleward shifts of the extratropical jet (and the ITCZ) and water vapour changes tend to reduce the extents. It is the balance between these two processes that gives the differing responses of MPI-ESM and IPSL-CM5A. Frankly, the results are not really as clean cut as described in the text and the discussion is not that convincing. The authors claim that the response to SST perturbations alone is similar between the two models, but it really isn't at all, retaining the basic structure of the overall response they are trying to understand. Their claim that clouds are the dominant factor is "difficult to buy" according to my squiggles on the manuscript, and it still seems so now. In the end, a physical explanation is not really given, but there is some interesting discussion of cloud processes. Tropical ice clouds move towards the poles in IPSL and towards the equator in MPI. This appears not to be due to circulation change and may therefore be down to cloud microphysics. But they do not investigate. More generally, this stuff seems to be the spirit of the times, evident from the huge number of citations this and similar papers are getting... A simplified modelling study that explores robust / non-robust features of CMIP5 output and attempts to link them to a physical process in the model. Is this good? Frankly, it's probably better than the previous generation of work by people like me that didn't bother with the intermediate simple modelling step and used CMIP3 data. Also, it does seem this topic of radiation-circulation interaction has escaped the attention of researchers until recently (really? or is it just that nobody who wrote and reviewed in the 70s is around anymore?) and it seems that Geoff and I are getting into it just slightly too late. NO PAPER NOTES. Oh yeah - Why do the clouds heat the lower stratosphere? After a chat with Angus, we reckon it must be dynamical. The clouds are basically being analysed in an old fashioned PRP way, so heat the troposphere by FATting up to lower temperatures. I would expect slight radiative cooling of the stratosphere due to this.

item.title: Some papers about stable isotopes
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Just a quick note about some delta O18 papers I read in preparation for Dave Mattey's (unfortunately as yet unsuccessful) NERC South Pacific proposal. What we would like to do is some modelling of delta O18 amounts that we would expect to find in various locations, depending on the position of the South Pacific Convergence Zone. I had this idea that we might to be able to do it offline just by relying on the precipitation amount effect. Having edited a paper that got slammed for taking too many liberties with the relationship between delta O18 and climate, I'm now not so sure, but I will revisit if we pull get the band back together. So - there was:

Kurita, (2013), Water isotopic variability in response to mesoscale convective system over the tropical ocean

The paper reminds us that there is no proper explanation for the "amount effect" on precipitation and therefore isotope records. Here, using observations, it is suggested that the type of convective (or stratiform) system is important in determining the delta O18 ratio.

Lee et al., (2009), Sensitivity of stable water isotopic values to convective parameterization schemes

This is a CAM2 study showing that isotopes could be used to understand something about the timescale of convective cloud formation and precipitation. I think there may also have been a paper by Julia Tindall at some point about HadCM3 modelling of this.

item.title: Sobel and Bretherton, (2000), Modeling Tropical Precipitation in a Single Column
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: This paper presents basically what I want to do (unfortunately) with Angus, Rob and Ian on precipitation in the tropics. It is essentially a presentation of a mean field theory (again - what I wanted to call it...) for climatological precipitation in the tropical region, contrasting their QTCM (remember that) with a single column version of the QTCM that has strong success in replicating ocean precipitation. (For land, and I should do this, see Zeng and Neelin (1999).) It should be noted, though, that it ain't quite a mean field theory, because the model is allowed to have winds prescribed from the control run at all times. These control the evaporation rate and the precipitation in a column. Turning surface temperature variations ON or OFF changes relatively little. The relevant behaviour is satisfactorily driven by winds. If the model is slightly further "de-single-column-ised" by allowing prescribed winds to advect moisture, then the transition from shallow to deep convection is delayed by the effect of moisture advection, which tends to transport more of it upstream to areas of strong convergence. Section 4 describes the use of a "genuine" single column model, which has some success at reproducing observations when SSTs are prescribed for a fixed wind speed. Evidently, these two complementary effects are not both needed at the same time. SOME NOT PARTICULARLY MORE THAN THIS ENGLIGHTENING PAPER NOTES.

item.title: Marlon et al., (2013), Global biomass burning: a synthesis and review of Holocene paleofire records and their controls
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
[caption id="" align="alignright" width="655"] Fire![/caption] This is an interesting, informative review article describing the rather complex relationship between fire, climate and humans over the past 10,000 years. It does tail off a little bit in as much as it describes results rather than conclusions, and it is probably written by a team who know more about proxies and particularly fire than they do about climate, but overall very useful. The main conclusions (from the abstract are):
  1. Episodes of high fire were common in the early Holocene, although temperatures were low and biomass burning was low overall.
  2. There is little evidence that humans modified the fire record and therefore the global carbon cycle during the pre-industrial period.
  3. "There was a nearly global increase in fire activity from 3 to 2 ka that is difficult to explain..., but the widespread and synchronous nature of the increase suggests at least a partial climate forcing;" (which I highlighted) (Yes in pink.)
  4. Burning during the past century generally decreased.
Outside of the tropics, temperature (which is probably connected to rainfall too, one imagines?) is probably the controlling factor. Then there's humans, who can even initiate a feedback by causing more warming through CH4 and CO2 emission through fire. (Although this review finds scant evidence of the importance of this.) Within the tropics, precipitation is possibly the controlling factor. In particular, they assert that in moist environments, more precipitation means less fire in the long term. Lilo reminds me that this is corroborated with one precipitation proxy for the Holocene and the results of Krawchuk and Moritz, (2011), who looked at about 10 years of MODIS data. The paper also contains discussion of archaeological, crop, modelling (also described as "processes of elimination") and the fire-driven and non-fire-driven succession of various vegetation types. Population increased throughout the Holocene, but apparently monotonically and at different times in different areas. Hence, coordinated up-and-down behaviour in different regions may be climate related.

Use of proxies

The development of fire proxies is standard / impeccable as far as I know, with appropriate choice of records and "pre-whitening" to a normalish distribution using the BOX-COX TRANSFORM. Still not sure what that really does, but it seems to me that individual records are probably distributed Poisson or something like that? As teased above, however, use of temperature and hydrological proxies is decidedly dodgier. One or two precipitation proxies are used to describe behaviour in vast tropical regions centred on South America, Africa and South-East Asia. Similar regions defined with one or two temperature proxies are not much better. This all links strongly to work Lilo is currently doing on charcoal records, ENSO and fire. As Dan commented, it's impressive that there's actually some signal coming out of what she's doing. (And especially since it's apparently the case that she's fairly robustly found the opposite of what is described in this paper and the cited article, Krawchuk and Moritz, (2011).) This paper should probably be compared with Kitzberger et al., (2001) (from an earlier blog) that does find that to get fire you need to have a strong El Nino (i.e. wetter in the region they analyse) followed by a strong La Nina (i.e. dryer) from documentary records and tree ring records of the past few centuries. This could fit in with Lilo's findings too, providing the El Nino outweighs the La Nina?

item.title: AGU 2015
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
[caption id="" align="aligncenter" width="483"] AGU Fall Meeting![/caption]

 The actual meeting

Planetary science sessions: Rather ominous. Very impressive. These planetary geology / exoplanetary types seem to have their heads screwed on much more than I thought. Doing great work that will be difficult for us to compete with in Exeter. Robin Wordsworth(!) and Ramses Ramirez discussed the problem of Early Mars (which might actually be a much more practical problem than Early Venus for our NatSci students to look into)? Basically nobody knows how to make it warm enough for the liquid water that geologists believe must have flowed, but they have interesting ideas. Posters-wise, the Chicago (now Oxford...) team are understandably looking into the the effect of humidity on atmospheric radiative fins. Hydrological cycle: Another unusually strong session. It really is worth checking back with the notebook. Spencer Hill showed another example of the importance of convection scheme choice. Changing the rather unusual scheme in GFDL 2.1(?) prevented the model from showing Sahel drying. Elizabeth Maroon showed more GFDL AM2 work for idealised continents and aquaplanets. I found her conclusions difficult to follow, but:
  • "Evaporation driven precipitation change" in the Frierson model (presumably linked to RH level over land / elsewhere?)
  • "Radiative feedback" driven changes in GFDL. This presumably explains why we can't predict precipitation changes in it? (I noted also that HadSM3 has no gradient of radiative feedbacks and this may stand for something?)
FIRE! Silvia Kloster reported that 10 CMIP5 models have fire models now. However, precipitation - fire relationships in different models are rather different from each other. There is also FIREMIP, who are looking at 1750-2000. In the RCPs, fire changes sign across models. Robert Field (NASA) has a fire database. item.title: Pierrehumbert (2011), Infrared radiation and planetary temperature
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A review article written by Ray Pierrehumbert for Physics Today. Worth remembering because it's very good for showing to students learning about radiation, particularly infrared, and its importance to climate on terrestrial planets. Pretty standard stuff and linked to traditional physics. A number of things are worth noting for interest:
  • "Simeon Poisson published a nearly identical formulation [to Karl Schwarzchild] of radiative transfer in 1835, but his equations languished for nearly 100 years without application."
  • Continuum absorption is important but not well understood. Partly due to line-wings, partly due to complexes of molecules that form briefly once the pressure is high enough. Nearly transparent Nitrogen provides an important continuum under cold, dense conditions on Titan.
  • Carbon dioxide emission feature in the Earth's stratosphere: occurs at around 667 inverse cm as absorption is so strong that it is the hot upper stratosphere that is seen from space.
  • He claims that the logarithmicity of CO2 forcing comes from the edges of the prime CO2 absorption feature (around 667 inverse cm) narrowing...

item.title: Two papers on LES convection
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Bob Beare coached me a little in what to say about LES simulation of convection before myself's and Peter Challenor's ill-fated (but coffee fuelled) trip to London for a NERC panel interview. Basically, he (Bob) said, there are two cases that need to be considered. Shallow cumulus over ocean and cumulus development and the diurnal cycle over land. Viz:  

Siebesma et al., (2003), A Large Eddy Simulation Intercomparison Study of Shallow Cumulus Convection

I had a hunch that this guy would be the head honcho on this panel, so I even have paper notes for this paper. An ensemble of different LES are compared to observations of cumulus. The observed data comes from the BOMEX study. (Barbados Oceanographic and Meteorological Experiment). This was a study of a calm 500 square km patch of ocean back in 1973 with consistent cumulus cover. The two key issues for researchers are:
  1. "What regulates the flux of subcloud air into the cloud layer, and
  2. the nature of the mixing processes between the clouds and their environment."
There is a (hopefully someday) useful mention of how trying to understand the difference between different LES is difficult unless they are systematically perturbed / based on the same model structure. The LES show quite a wide range of cloud cover 13 +/- 7 % for the same forcing conditions (they force u, v, w and radiation) , but it is all basically "the same regime". Domains internal to the cloud and "core" regions, which are rather close to what would be expected from moist adiabatics are investigated. Reasonable agreement with airplane  observations  is found. The study then moves to discussing convective parameterisation in GCMs. Both entraining plume mass flux schemes and eddy diffusive schemes are discussed.  

Grabowski et al., (2006), Daytime convective development over land: A model intercomparison based on LBA observations

And then this one, which most probably was considered in rather more of a hurry. It compares the development of daytime convection over land in LES and single column models (ie GCM columns) with observations of the rainy season in Amazonia. As stated by previous studies, SCMs produce convection much to early in the day -- around two hours after Sun-up. The LES shows more sensible development over a number of hours, with both cloud base (because of decreasing surface RH) and cloud top moving upwards for about 5 or 6 hours. Why does the too early development happen in SCMs? One possible reason, they say, is that the entrainment in deep convection is about an order or magnitude less because the clouds are so much broader. This may suppress shallow convection from developing into deep rapidly. One fix would be to vary entrainment rate throughout the day. But that is a bit of a bodge. Observations come from the Large-Scale Biosphere-Atmosphere (LBA) experiment in Rondonia, Brazil (a rather deforested area of the rainforest) in February 1999. Also, I think the study was based on relaxation to some state rather than interactive radiation and land surface.

item.title: Houlie et al., (2016), Use of a GPS-derived troposphere model to improve InSAR deformation estimates in the San Gabriel Valley, California
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A paper by Nicolas Houlie, Funning and Roland Burgmann, believe it or not... Their kind use GPS and InSAR measurements to make estimates of crustal deformation, either for creeping events or for sudden movements (i.e. earthquakes). One of the issues with the methodology is water vapour, which also causes changes in the detected phase / delay in arrival time(?) of microwave measurements (that's why we also use it for meteorology of course). Ignoring the meteorology, they say, leads to errors of up to 30% in the groundwater storage terms of interest to this paper. By the looks of things, this is really pertinent for the earthquakes, where there may be some quick movement -- you can't just integrate over time to get rid of random atmospheric effects. In this paper, they looked at the impact of meteorology on an uplift event 30 km north-east over LA. Some details of the basics that I sort of learned:
  • InSAR provides spatially dense but temporally infrequent measurements. GPS provides temporally dense but spatially sparse measurements (basically because you have to have a groundbased GPS receiver available to see how much something has moved).
  • They use a number of meteorological formulae that look a bit drawn from a textbook willy-nilly. They take values of p, T and RH at the surface from meteorological stations / radiosondes(!? More of this in a minute*), then use some crude approximations for lapse rates and allow constant RH through the column.
  • I asked what the horizontal path lengths for GPS are. I.e. over how many meteorological gridboxes the GPS were straying. He says it's about 30-40 km for the lowest zenith angle pathways to the satellite.
* The paper states that radiosonde data were used (but actually I think it means it is just used to estimate the relationship between variables rather than as actual input to their analysis.

item.title: Huang and Bani Shahabadi, (2014), Why logarithmic? A note on the dependence of radiative forcing on gas concentration
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I actually inserted this one because I love "WIPE DOWN THE LAB BENCH FOR VICTORY". But this paper is a reminder of "Loose lips sink manuscripts", I'm told. William Ingram told me that he shared what he knew on the spectroscopy of radiative forcing with these authors at a conference. Next thing he knew, this appeared. Interesting that he doesn't agree with their results, though. It also doesn't seem right based on Ruth's findings. They investigate forcing due to greenhouse gases and why it is logarithmic. They say that they show that, well:
"We show that the phenomenon can be explained by an Emission Layer Displacement Model, which describes the radiance response to gas perturbation under normal atmospheric conditions such as temperature linearly varying with height and gas concentration exponentially decaying with height."
They do what I didn't manage to do and derive an analytic expression that shows than when an emission layer moves upwards with increasing absorber concentration, the forcing generated is logarithmic. CO2 is the focus, but it also works for water vapour. What they don't do -- and they admit to it, is rule out other mechanisms. Hence, they end up going backwards a bit on their main conclusion. What they do won't work for "unsaturated atmospheric absorption, such as in the window region... Continuum absorption..." Hence, it doesn't actually answer the question posed in the title, but nobody cares about that sort of thing anymore.

item.title: Maroon et al., (2016), The precipitation response to an idealized subtropical continent
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: I recommended this paper to Marianne as something to read, and fortunately it didn't put her off applying for a PhD here. I should definitely read things before I recommend them in future. Particularly in these circumstances. Anyway, I wanted to read this as a follow-up to her talk at EGU and to know what's going on in the world of idealised modelling. It didn't really do quite what I was expecting. What they do is test the response when an idealised sub-tropical continent is added to an aquaplanet model for various simplified physics (no cloud, q, or ice feedbacks) and the full GFDL AM2.1 model. They compare adding a light versus a dark continent. It is found that the light continent is not unlike the dark continent in the idealised model, but it is more extreme in terms of being a heat sink for cross-equatorial energy transport. Doing things using the complex GFDL AM2.1 changes the response a little for the dark continent: the precipitation response to introducing the continent is much bigger. There are also some cloud effects. The SW effect of cloud dominates around the ITCZ. Low clouds form west of the continent, sustaining themselves as they promote subsidence. By contrast, there is cloud loss over the continent itself, increasing SW heating. The light simulation is more different from the dark simulation than for the idealised model, at least partly driven by cloud differences that the authors concede are probably "model dependent". As continent albedo increases to very light, the ITCZ shift goes from being longitudinally varying, to a solid zonally-coherent shift to the hemisphere without the continent in it. The whole paper takes an "SST (ie it rains where it's warmest) versus energetic (ie ITCZ is where energy needs to be exported from) perspectives" approach. The energy perspective comes out on top where they predict different locations.

item.title: Bechtold, (2015), Atmospheric moist convection
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Peter Bechtold's convection notes from a training course at ECMWF, helpfully available on the internet. Geoff Vallis describes Bechtold as being someone who knows a lot about convection, but less about other things, and that shows in the focus of the notes and the fairly small description of other things. However, one of the main things I gleaned from this was the relationship between convection and atmospheric kinetic energy. Bechtold states that convection is in fact the main source of kinetic energy in the atmosphere in the introduction. Later on, we learn that shallow convection is triggered more by vertical velocity / kinetic energy, rather than instability. I think this may explain why Ian Boutle doesn't like my proffered convection scheme, which frankly doesn't differ all that much from Betts-Miller, how ever much I'd like it to. Things that should be noted:
  • In ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System (and presumably elsewhere), convective parameterisation robustly dries the tropical atmosphere overall. This is true, even though convection can move moisture upwards. Most of the column wetting comes from resolved dynamics.
  • There are THREE prominent modes of convection. Deep, shallow, and "congestus". Congestus penetrates to the freezing layer -- a shallow layer of stability promoted by melting ice precipitation. It makes up around 50% of all convective cloud over the west Pacific, and is important in pre-conditioning the atmosphere through moistening for subsequent deep convection.
  • There is discussion of the diurnal cycle of convection and the trouble convective parameterisations have in representing it. Over land, peak rainfall is during late afternoon / early evening. Over ocean, peak rainfall occurs during the night / early morning! I did not realise this latter oceanic point...
  • MIXING / ENTRAINMENT: is something that obviously happens during convection. The big thing that my / Betts-Miller get wrong is that very dry air above an unstable layer tend to enhance the effect of convection on the environment. In fact, very dry air can kill off convective plumes through mixing out their buoyancy and evaporation of condensate.
  • He provides a full description of ECMWF's mass flux scheme (I haven't read it) and brief descriptions of a number of idealised schemes: Kuo (moisture convergence based, deprecated), Betts-Miller (Betts-Miller) and the Emanuel scheme (which is actually rather complicated / computationally intense. The generalities of mass flux schemes are discussed. Entrainment / the entrainment parameter are introduced as its Achilles Heel.

item.title: Frierson, (2007), The Dynamics of Idealized Convection Schemes and Their Effect on the Zonally Averaged Tropical Circulation
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Old paper from Dargan Frierson that is important for two reasons. First,

It describes a simplified Betts-Miller convection scheme:

The simplified Betts-Miller scheme relaxes simulated profiles of potential temperature and moisture towards a pseudoadiabat (actually with a chosen RH) over the course of about 1 day. The leading variable is moisture, which is relaxed up to the level of stability for a parcel originating from the surface. (So no multiple convective events.) Cooling of the whole column is performed to conserve enthalpy. IF there isn't much moisture in the column, then the reference profile may in fact be wetter than the input profile. In this case, SHALLOW CONVECTION is performed. One option (three are discussed) is to find the highest possible top of convection for which it is the case that the input profile is wetter than the output. (Actually looks for precipitation value of zero, meaning that non-precipitating convection occurs.)

It has consequences for the runaway greenhouse results of Leconte et al. (2013):

Because it compares the effects of using Betts-Miller, no convection scheme and correction to 7 Kkm-1 ("Moist Convective Adjustment" (MCA)). It is found that no convection scheme and MCA are basically the same: gridpoint or small-scale very intense storms and very dry subtropics. The Betts-Miller runs, meanwhile, produces a much moister subtropics, because the Betts-Miller convection scheme has a shallow convecting mode that can pump surface moisture upwards. This is interesting in regards to the Leconte paper (which I haven't written up yet) because that article pushes back the runaway greenhouse limit for Earth by pointing out that the drier subtropics (not found in previous 1D studies) permit the planet to ship much more insolation before becoming so hot that OLR doesn't increase with surface temperature. A moister subtropics would pull the runaway greenhouse limit back down again I'd wager... WRITTEN NOTES AVAILABLE.

item.title: Ding and Pierrehumbert, (2016), Convection in Condensible-Rich Atmospheres
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
This paper describes an attempt to provide a parameterisation of convection appropriate for the case where water vapour is no longer a trace ingredient of the atmosphere and instead makes up a substantial fraction of atmospheric pressure. The scheme is then applied in a 1D model with the promise to try it in 3D. Missing from ordinary convection schemes:
  1. Accurate form of the moist enthalpy.
  2. Heat lost due to precipitation.
  3. Pressure changes due to precipitation and evaporation.
  4. Accurate specific heat capacities. (Actually right in some schemes, e.g. ours(?) -- well - righter than some, anyway.)
The paper then goes through some relevant thermodynamics. Of interest is the fact that dL/dT is equal to the difference in the specific heats of the two phases under consideration, which is trivial when you think about it*. Providing the initial and final states are hydrostatic, the form of the derived enthalpy is quite simple. I did wonder about this, but I guess if the convection is happening in a small enough part of a vertical column, this is probably reasonable even in 3D. (I.e. all pressure gradients caused by condensation and evaporation are balanced by vertical reorganisation rather than horizontal.) However, the "convection only occupies a small part of the column" approximation may not be accurate at high condensible inventory? Some LES simulations would be nice... Given that their model has p as a vertical coordinate, many calculations also work out more simply than they might otherwise. [caption id="attachment_488" align="alignleft" width="347"] That too is condensation.[/caption] The scheme is then applied in a 1D radiative-convective code. The character of convection and climate are rather different from on a dilute condensible planet. This is well-illustrated by the case of a planet in a highly eccentric orbit with a strong seasonal cycle. First of all, atmospheric latent heat provides a very substantial heat capacity. Planetary temperatures change little over the course of a year; instead, solar heating and radiative cooling go into evaporation and condensation. Although there is an upper layer of radiative cooling balancing latent heating as on Earth higher up in the atmosphere, nearer the surface, evaporation adds moist mass to the atmosphere which drifts upwards to meet the upper traditionally convecting layer. In the extreme case of a STEAM-dominated atmosphere, the adiabat is close to the CLAUSIUS-CLAPEYRON equation, which is just the moist adiabat for a water-only atmosphere. I have slightly more detailled paper notes. * Presumably this statement will be impenetrable in a few years time.

item.title: Mangeon et al., (2016), INFERNO: a fire and emissions scheme for the Met Office's Unified Model
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
This is the INFERNO fire model description paper in Geosci. Model Dev. Discuss. INFERNO is basically a JULES module, which can predict fire emissions and burnt area, but does not yet feed back on the model vegetation and land surface. The paper is also interesting because it reveals "our understanding" concerning fires. Overall:
"Warm and dry climatological condition favour the occurrence of forest fires. These fires then become a significant emission source to the atmosphere... Fuel flammability is simulated using temperature, relative humidity, fuel density as well as precipitation and soil moisture. Combining flammability with ignitions and vegetation, burnt area is diagnosed."
A previous proto version of the parameterisation was controlled by temperature, RH, and precipitation with triggering driven by humans and lightening. It had some success. This updated version adds using precipitation as a "rapid fire deterrent" and soil moisture as a moisture memory. Perhaps most importantly, fuel density was also introduced, dependent on lead carbon and decomposable plant material (i.e. litter). The litter affects flamability but NOT fuel load. Ignition due to humans (and perhaps natural lightning?) can be varied. Unlike other formulations, the model doesn't use windspeed. Also, there is no simulation of peat fires. The authors suggest that this will lead to an underestimate of fire emissions overall. Ignitions are uniform across plant functional types; burnt area is larger for shrubs and grass; however, carbon density is so much higher in a forest that it will produce higher emissions in general. (Lilo has suggested that we use CO2 emissions as our measure of fire as this should relate well to charcoal amounts. Other emitted species simulated by the model are similar, anyway.)

Model performance versus observations

looks decent overall. R = 0.66 for burnt area and R = 0.59 for emitted carbon compared with the Global fire database. Importantly, emitted carbon is underestimated in boreal regions and equatorial Asia, but overestimated in most other places, including southern hemisphere South America. There tends to be an underestimate of emissions during El Nino years. The model performs better than fire indices, unsurprisingly.

item.title: Xie et al., (2010), Global Warming Pattern Formation: Sea Surface Temperature and Rainfall
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A paper that Rob Chadwick kept reminding me about and one that Angus Ferraro (rest in scientific peace) didn't really like either. (I didn't really like reading it.) The paper is worth remembering, though, because in some ways it is a precursor to what we have been doing on tropical precipitation. A large slice of the paper is about SSTs and SST change in the tropics. However, that is then related to tropical precipitation change over oceans. It isn't really clear whether the authors are talking about SST gradients or changes in SST gradients some of the time, but certainly the idea is that SST patterns control precipitation patterns. There is also some discussion of El Nino versus El Nino-like warming.
"Readers may skip to (sub)sections of interest."
Thanks! Anyway:

SST pattern formation

Is analysed in terms of the surface, or surface mixed-layer heat budget. SST is forced by atmospheric forcing, oceanic mixing and "Newtonian relaxation", which is supposed to depend on evaporation. This immediately leads to an explanation of the equatorial peak in SST warming as windspeed is minimum at the equator. A good example of how the mean state affects changes, the authors tell us. Other peaks and troughs in warming are associated with other processes parameterised in the simple model. The differences between the El Nino pattern and El Nino-like warming are discussed. For one thing, El Nino-like warming peaks during May of each year rather than December. Because the mechanisms are somewhat different from El Nino, patterns of El Nino-like warming are different across different models in different ways from El Nino patterns.

Precipitation

I found this section difficult to understand because I did not always know if they were talking about SST or SST change, but it was this that Rob mostly wanted me to see. Results from coupled GCM experiments are compared with uniform SST warming (so-called "Cess experiments"). Precipitation response is very different, leading to the conclusion that patterns of SST change lead to patterns of precipitation change. It is stated that previous work concentrated on Clausius-Clapeyron change in surface specific humidity to a uniform SST change. To me, this sounds like they are making the opposite kind of point to what we were trying to make in our paper. Nowt wrong with that, and seems well-supported, but not really that similar! However, the conclusion does remind us that surface variations are the key process due to the weak temperature gradient in the free atmosphere.

item.title: Craddock and Greeley, (2009), Minimum estimates of the amount and timing of gases released into the martian atmosphere from volcanic eruptions
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
This was a paper found by Liam and Dan who are Natural Sciences students working with... myself and Nathan Mayne on trying to understand early histories of solar system terrestrial planets. There is quite a lot of useful general information on geology, atmospheres and observation for outsiders such as... myself. Anyway. The paper starts from the premise that there was liquid water on Mars at some point in the past, but that the current atmosphere could not support that. Knowledge of volcanism and geology leads them to believe, however, that much stronger greenhousing atmospheres could have existed billions of years ago, perhaps allowing that liquid water. Such atmospheres could have originated from volcanism, meteor impacts or "simple burial". (Not sure what that last one means). The authors use what we know about basaltic lava flows on Earth (e.g. Kilauea!) to speculate about what observed lava flows on Mars may have released. On Earth, volcanic emissions have been measured both in-situ and and remotely. Measuring things like water vapour and carbon dioxide is clearly difficult in Earth's atmosphere; sulphur dioxide is easier. It is certainly the case that Earth's volcanoes vary a great deal in what they emit. Even if we take the most "Mars-like" of Earth's volcanoes, there must have been the possibility for Mars' volcanism to change with time as well as from volcano to volcano. The paper mentions the CH4 controversy: the presence of methane in the Martian atmosphere and whether it could be biogenic given that methane on Earth is biogenic. The authors point out that there are non-biogenic sources of methane, including volcanoes. There is also discussion of water amounts, which would be present in any eruption, but presumably regulated in the atmosphere by the usual processes in the presence of any substantial pressure. There is a huge uncertainty in Mars' former ocean depth (e.g. how much was lost by photo-dissociation), but it would probably be wet enough for observed fluvial features. Nitrogen and argon come from the volcanoes too.
