Where does the CO2 go? What could it be precipitated as? There are some difficulties with carbonate rock formation on Mars, but this is the classic mechanism on Earth (either from silicates or from existing CaCO3, see page 521...). Alternatively it might be adsorbed in the regolith (the smashed up rock that makes up the surface of a vegetation-less planet).

item.title: STFC exoplanet related papers: part I: GCM studies
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Some papers I've been reading relevant to our STFC exoplanet bid. These ones are GCM studies of the atmospheres by and large.

Yang et al., (2013), Stabilizing cloud feedback dramatically expands the habitable zone of tidally locked planets

Short paper from Astron. and Astrophys. on cloud feedback on tidally locked exoplanets. Near the warm edge of the habitable zone, the greenhouse effect (they're using astronomers' version of our language) due to clouds is weak because there's so much water vapour in the atmosphere. Hence, clouds act to cool only, basically, through reflection of incoming shortwave. (There isn't any discussion of cloud absorption of "shortwave", which might not be so short, in this paper.) They note that tidally locked planets might have a much higher albedo than ones with other rotations, because only the "cloudy bit" is seen by the stellar radiation. Also, the greenhouse effect of tidally locked planets is weaker because of the cold, dry nightside radiator. Plus, as Ian has said, the effects of low cloud feedbacks we experience on Earth are not really seen as these are also operating in the night. Finally, they do some sensitivity tests to determine that the James Webb Space Telescope would be able to detecet a transiting "nearby M-dwarf HZ planet". This isn't spectra relevant, though, and they also don't say how far away the planet is, I don't think. However, variation of the phase curve could say whether or not clouds are present (with some caveats). They also show that a dynamical ocean can play a significant role in the absence of barrier continents, possibly reducing convection enough to affect cloud feedback substantially. They are pretty bullish that there isn't much uncertainty in their findings... "This robustness is due to the simplicity of the mechanism: any GCM that produces strong convection at the substellar point should produce a high cloud albedo." There are a couple of papers here about the presence and location of continents I might follow up.

Hu and Yang, (2014), Role of ocean heat transport in climates of tidally locked exoplanets around M dwarf stars

[caption id="" align="alignright" width="514"] Figure 4 from Hu and Yang, (2014).[/caption] Same Yang, different paper. They use CCSM3 to investigate the effect of possible ocean heat transport on tidally locked exoplanets. The specific planet investigated is Gliese 581g. (I guess that's what the title says.) Rather than an "eyeball" planet, they see a "lobster" planet, with melting sea ice to the eastern edge of the day zone due to strong zonal ocean advection. Ocean heat transport increases with increasing CO2 concentration (and atmospheric heat transport decreases). A meridional thermohaline circulation is established by salinity differences between melting and ice forming regions that can be up to 1000 Sv, and have strong associated poleward heat transport. A snowball state is encountered at higher values of stellar flux with a coupled ocean, presumably because the dayside is cooled more efficiently. However, at the hot end, the coupled ocean version also heats up faster. In particular, the cloud feedback is weaker (as in the 2013 paper above) when ocean heat transport is strong, as dayside convection is weaker. (However, the model became unstable above 1400 Wm-2, so no results for the really hot stuff.) Figure 4 (on the right) is definitely worth a look, particularly for panel A, which shows the massive difference in sensitivity of the atmosphere only and atmosphere-ocean simulations. Not using a dynamic ocean model is therefore something of a limitation! However, here we have an aquaplanet, and as the authors concede, the existence of barrier continents would massively reduce the strength of ocean heat transport.

Turbet et al., (2016), The habitability of Proxima Centauri b: II. Possible climates and observability

The paper that had Ian spitting with rage over not getting there first... But it's actually impressively full-featured. Anyway - a paper by the LMD group detailing possible climates using their GCM. They very much take a "parameter space" approach to the problem, recognising that the planet could in fact be rather dry (and might therefore be entirely dry or "lakey" rather than have oceans. An accompanying paper by Ribas et al. describes this). Over a wide range of parameters, it is found that it is warmer than 273 K somewhere on the planet. This is not the deciding factor for habitability, they note,  citing the case of present day Mars. Atmospheric collapse, prompted by CO2 sublimation, happens at higher CO2 concentrations on tidally locked planets, because of the very cold nightside. There is a detailled discussion of where the water goes, starting with a bit (just in the atmosphere) to planets that deposit it in glaciers at the surface, to glaciers that suffer basal melting from geothermal activity or flow for some reason to regions where they melt and return water to the atmosphere. Glaciers that lock away vast amounts of ice (for their Earth-like atmosphere configuration, the figure is 61% of the Earth's ocean), can be found on tidally locked planets. It's much less on asynchronously rotating planets, and possible tidal heating of the planet's interior increasing geothermal activity in close-in eccentric orbits might suppress it even more. It is in section 4.2.2 where it is stated that "The latter [the atmosphere] will always transport water from the hottest to the coldest regions". And this counts even if there is no ice anywhere. I'm reasonably certain this is contrary to the Earth's tropics, so definitely one for research. There is discussion of possible continental regions, which in the case of a tidally locked planet could be correlated or anti-correlated with the substellar point. If there is a basin at the substellar point, then much liquid water might end up here, promoting evaporation and a moist, warm atmosphere. If it's a mountain, the opposite will be the case. Finally, there's an important bit on the planet's detectability (which I think we largely replicate). "Sensitivity should not be an issue to directly detect Proxima b with the E-ELT." Also, they note that convection is a big uncertainty in models and that they do find different results from Yang et al. above. Thing we could advance on: they don't do radiative effect of condensed CO2, even though they do consider CO2 condensation. I have paper notes for this too.

item.title: STFC exoplanet related papers: part II: The legend of Curly's gold (actually Observations)
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Or most of the other papers lying around that I've at least skimmed now that we've submitted the grant.

de Wit et al., (2016), A combined transmission spectrum of the Earth-sized exoplanets TRAPPIST-1b and c

The point about the TRAPPIST planets (TRAPPIST-1 is an ultracool M-dwarf) is that they transit the star, meaning that transmission spectroscopy has already been used to find out a little bit more about them than we can work out for Proxima Centauri b using the HST (in this case unfortunately the Hubble Space Telescope). The spectra found are apparently "featureless". A cloud free hydrogen dominated atmosphere is therefore ruled out. I find myself confused, but the last page tells us something about how atmospheric transmission spectra work. Deeper atmospheres with lower molecular weight (e.g. H2) show up better than shallower high molecular weight (e.g. H2O) atmospheres of the same mass. They look forward to JWST etc being able to do much more.

Anglada-Escude et al., (2016), A terrestrial planet candidate in a temperate orbit around Proxima Centauri

THE paper as far as Proxima b is concerned. They explain how and what was detected in orbit around Proxima Centauri. They used the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher (HARPS) to establish the small Doppler shifting of Proxima Centuari and therefore reveal the existence of a (best guess) roughly one Earth mass planet in the habitable zone of Proxima b. Some fairly involved Bayesian statistics is deployed (oh - and there is a frequentist version also, but I am not allowed to talk about that on this corridor). There may in fact be a second planet too. A number of arguments against habitability are presented, sensibly I guess in order to reduce the hype. Tidal locking, strong ultraviolet or x-ray flux and strong stellar magnetic fields and flares could all destroy the atmosphere of a close-in exoplanet. Particularly its water. The (perhaps less frequently made?) point is also made that where the planet originally formed affects its water content. Planets that form beyond the "ice line" would be much richer in initial water than planets that formed close to the star.

Kreidberg and Loeb, (2016), Prospects for characterizing the atmosphere of Proxima Centauri b

Using future telescopes, the possible methods of finding out something about Proxima b's atmosphere are (i) direct imaging, (ii) measure variations in reflected starlight with orbital phase and (iii) measure variation in thermal emission with orbital phase. Directly imaging is tricky. I think I remembered to remove all reference to this in the grant in the end. The European Extremely Large Telescope should be able to do this, but that won't be available for 10 years. Albedo measurements (ie (ii)) should be possible. This paper, however, focuses on (iii). They use a very simple toy climate model that provides temperature variation from day-to-night of a tidally locked planet that can vary depending on how efficient planetary heat transport is. They then "observe" the "planet" with a hypothetical JWST. They find that a single phase curve observation is good enough to diagnose whether or not the planet has a significant atmosphere. The detection of an ozone feature also ought to be possible, although a lot of orbits of JWST will be needed.

item.title: Visit to Reading Meteorology
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
On monday, I gave the Reading Meteorology departmental seminar. A slim turnout by their standards -- "Where is everybody?" quoth Jonathan Gregory -- due to EGU, but nevertheless the battery of big guns in the front row of Jonathan, Keith Shine and John Mitchell was present. This and a number of meetings led to some useful ideas / leads:

Reinhard Schiemann

Wondered about how extremes would work on my RH-TS bin plot. Presumably they would follow the other precipitation around in space. However, they might show interesting changes on the actual bin plot itself.

Jonathan Gregory

It's a while since we've spoken. His current work with Tim Andrews highlights that the AMIP period was apparently one of low climate sensitivity (really high climate feedback parameter) meaning that future estimates of warming based on this may not pan out too well. This could be linked to longer term Pacific variability of which the hiatus is a symptom. In other news, the UKESM will feature a dynamic ice sheet model. It is not a very significant drain on computing resources compared with other model components.

Richard Allan

I was keen to wonder aloud what grants he may be working on. Not many that need me by the sounds of things, but then which of other people's grants do? (Apart from Mat Collins, obviously.) His group continue to work on refining estimates of heat and moisture budgets and transports using all available model, observed and reanalysed data. He remains interested in the hydrological cycle. He has a reconstruction of TOA flux stretching back to 1985 from satellite data anchored to ARGO float data that he thinks is good. I don't think it would be useful for thinking about (say) land-sea contrast, but was interesting to hear that such a thing now exists. He had unfortunately sustained a knee injury, which cut short our meeting.

Paulo Ceppi

Who kindly hosted my seminar. He has a new paper on jet shifts that decomposes jet responses into "fast" (5-10 year timescale) and "slow" (longer timescale) responses. Typically, the fast pattern causes a poleward shift of jets that is then later brought back equatorward somewhat by the slow pattern.
This was also the day that Jamie Mitchell from the Met Office Knowledge integration team said
"I'll send your schematics down to our design studio and see if they can work them up."
which has the potential to be utterly superb.

item.title: Voigt et al., (2016), The tropical rain belts with an annual cycle and a continent model intercomparison project: TRACMIP
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
[caption id="attachment_520" align="alignright" width="601"] Figure 6: The effect of quadrupling CO2 concentration on precipitation.[/caption]The TRACMIP description paper by the much celebrated Aiko Voigt. Relevant to Marianne's PhD, and in fairness, not nearly as boring as many papers of this type. 13 "comprehensive" and one "simplified" model are taking part.

Relevant details of TRACMIP protocol:

  • Seasonal and diurnal cycles. Today's obliquity but no eccentricity, except in a dedicated orbital experiment.
  • No sea-ice.
  • CONTINENT at 30S - 30N, 0E - 45E. An idealised version of Africa in their thinking. A 0.1 m slab of ocean with increased albedo and reduced evaporation via a 50% suppression of the relevant bulk formula.
  • Ocean heat transport that is a smoothed version of what is found on Earth. The transport is of course suppressed over the continent.

Other commentary, results from the paper:

Good summary quote on model ensembles:
"A model response that is consistent across an ensemble of GCMs carries more weight than results from a single model and is welcomed for that reason. But scatter across models can be just as informative. For example, correlations of anomalies across an ensemble can highlight how changes in two variables are connected to each other in a robust way across all models, even though the magnitude or even the sign of the changes are uncertain; these robust correlations point to robust mechanisms..."
Unless, it's a PPE, of course, as we've seen previously with land-sea contrast. Results are shown. One thing I find interesting is that in the 4xCO2 experiments, in the median model at least, the land gets wetter not drier. So it doesn't fulfill whatever conditions are necessary to preduce Amazonian conditions. Nevertheless, although climate change in different models isn't discussed, the effect of introducing land into the control simulation of different models is, and this is rather different in different models. Introducing the continent mostly causes cooling (lower albedo?) and often drying (with some more rainfall over the continental area in some models). Polar amplification is still mostly present, which is interesting to note. The effects of atmospheric heat transport and particularly local "temperature feedbacks" are more important than the ice feedbacks and land-sea contrast, which are absent. Temperature feedbacks presumably refers to a local positive (ie cooling of the atmosphere) lapse rate feedback.

item.title: Two review articles on early Mars
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Two review articles on early Mars. One general but more geological one (first) from JGR Planets and one more climate specific one from Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci. whatever that is.

Ehlmann, et al., (2016), The sustainability of habitability on terrestrial planets: Insights, questions, and needed measurements from Mars for understanding the evolution of Earth-like worlds

[caption id="attachment_531" align="aligncenter" width="1024"] Wordsworth figure 1. Some useful Mars pics.[/caption] As the title implies, there is something of a lean towards what this all means for exoplanets. The idea is to use Mars to answer a number of questions regarding planetary habitability, including (i) Is small planet size fatal? (ii) Magnetic fields? (iiii) Chemistry initial or changing? (iv) Effects of early bombardment? (v) Stellar evolution? (vi) How important are climate forcings and their timescales? Why do all this on Mars? Because Mars' surface preserves the first 1 Gy of evolution, because plate tectonics didn't ever start, or shut down early. Olympus Mons et al. have been erupting relatively recently, but the whole complex of this and Tharsis have been built over a very long time. The planet has a 4 km deep dichotomy with Northern lowlands and southern highlands. The change is over a lateral distance of only a few hundred kilometres. It has been hypothesised that the NH was an ancient ocean with fans and deltas (although see comments in Wordsworth article below). The fluvial activity declined into the Amazonian period. Atmospheric loss mechanisms are discussed. Not well-understood. Mantle convection may have occurred under a rigid lid (crust). Less outgassing and volcanicity? The lack of plate tectonics certainly suggests that there is no recycling between atmosphere and interior, that volcanism was a source that could flood the atmosphere with CO2 and it was then lost to space. A similar situation to Venus, except the H2O / CO2 wasn't lost to space because Venus is too massive. (Well - the "H" was lost, creating more Co2, but not the other atoms.) One thing I didn't realise is that atmospheric pressure can at least partly determine what is outgassed from volcanoes. A possibility is that Mars was unable to outgass serious CO2, discussed on page 1940 and references given. Magnetic fields can also strengthen or weaken atmospheric loss, depending on their dominant effects. That on Mars probably switched off 4 billion years ago. A mention is made here of ice getting to the equatorial regions by changes in obliquity as mentioned by Wordsworth below. They comment that GHGs could then lead to a melting of the ice later on. This links to Wordsworth's "icy highlands scenario" (below). Section 4 of the review is then dedicated to proposals for how the surface could be explored by future missions. Not much for us here, but it is later mentioned that the surface composition of exoplanets might be worked out in the (far?) future where the planetary atmosphere is relatively transparent. Sounds crazy. Guess it might be possible for a dead planet!  

Wordsworth, (2016), The Climate of Early Mars

[caption id="attachment_532" align="alignleft" width="565"] Wordsworth figure 7. "Phase diagram" of "possible" Martian climates.[/caption] A strong authoritative article for the most part, but I note that it has a tendency to manifesto-ise for his own hypothesis for the climate of Early Mars, the "epsisodically warm icy highlands scenario". Worst offender:
"The opinion of this author is that the second possibility is the correct one."
Not sure I've seen something like that in a scientific journal before. Good to bear in mind that other articles should be inspected. The review above, which is more a geologists perspective does not come down nearly so strongly in this regard (although it isn't focused on quite the same topic, but for example Ehlman  doesn't write off the Northern Ocean). Anyway, we're not here to bash the guy; what can we learn?
  • The topography of Noachian Mars was pretty similar to today. This is important for dynamical simulation of the atmosphere, which he says shows that it can't rain where we find deltas / other fluvial features.
  • Various evidence suggests that fluvial features "valley networks" existed for 10^5 - 10^7 years rather than longer. Mineral carbonates are "conspicuous by its low abundance". These could have been dissolved by SO2 rain, though, plus there may be large subsurface reservoirs... Nevertheless, in contrast to Ehlman he says that surface carbonate formation would be the most efficient atmospheric CO2 loss mechanism. Losing more than a few hundred milibars over the past 4 billion years would be difficult.
  • THE FAILURE OF THE CO2 GREENHOUSE: Starting with James Kasting in 1991 and his radiative-convective equilibrium models, climate modelling has shown the impossibility of CO2 driven warming of the surface producing a warm, wet Mars. CO2 produces too much Rayleigh scattering, condenses into clouds at low temperatures in the upper troposphere and condenses onto the surface at higher pressures...  (The weak lines can't save us can they? The included spectral diagrams indicates some problems for climate models, but perhaps not enough.) Another warmer, or mechanism entirely is needed. Other GHGs mostly have problems, notably sulphates, which are powerful (in our model anyway), but produce loadsa aerosols (we haven't considered them yet). Ray et al. have suggested that high thin CO2 clouds could play a role, but perhaps not enough. In summary, no one really knows what's going on. Still:
  • He introduces his Icy Highlands Hypothesis which links to "where does the ice / water end up on a planet when the water inventory can't flow back to the hot bit by it's own volition?" His hypothesis is that, during periods of high obliquity, martian ice ended up near the equator, facilitated by the nearby highlands. Some kind of episodic melting forced by impacts(?) / periodic GHGs(?) then produces short-lived fluvial action. This hypothesis is favoured by Mars' low water load (the water has to get to the equator), which in turn makes sense given the lack of glaciation on these highland peaks. (Assuming the ice ended up there, of course.) Alternative hypotheses of warm wet Mars is trashed (rain falls in the wrong place even if you are warm enough due to topography / there couldn't have been a northern ocean because the proposed shoreline traverses up and down by several kilometres and basin deposits are inconsistent / Hesperian volcanic ridges come from a different time from the valley networks.)

item.title: Leconte et al., (2013), 3D climate modeling of close-in land planets: Circulation patterns, climate moist stability, and habitability
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Neil wanted me to look into this paper in order to understand some of the thoughts we've been having over whether water on planets should end up at the equator or at the poles (or on the day side or the night side if you're a tidally locked planet). I had thought perhaps that some "tropical" planets might exist whereby water ends up at the warmest bits, just like in the tropical Pacific, but it turns out instead that the cold trap (which is essentially absent in the tropical idea) wins at least usually, because the coldest bit of the atmosphere is really good at squeezing out that last bit of water and dumping it somewhere it won't evaporate very quickly. Viz: Hopefully the pens aren't so faded you can't see. The paper is an investigation of hot planets and which way their hydrological cycles go. In summary, either the greenhouse effect wins, and the planet goes runaway, or the cold trap wins, and the atmosphere dries out. What I'm wondering about on the board is whether a third planet could exist with plentiful evaporation everywhere, a weak cold trap and either a strong equatorial (or day side) hydrological cycle that has the potential to be killed by low RH at the equator if the planet only supports small lakes not able to sufficiently hydrate the atmosphere. There is an interesting discussion of how atmospheric dynamics, even on a dry planet, depends on rotation rate. Clearly, a non-rotating planet (that somehow maintains the same hot spot) has simple dynamics that flow from hot spot to cold side. A somewhat rapidly rotating planet is more Earth-like, with twin upper level westerly jets and a near-surface easterly equatorial flow. The in-between case, though, is that of SUPER-ROTATION. A single, lower level, equatorial jet dominates the flow and pushes air easterly at most altitudes. It looks as if the twin jets slump and join up. Don't know if this is actually what is happening. A semi-theoretical explanation of how to get super-rotation and why it doesn't occur on very slowly rotating nearly stationary planets is given. It would be necessary to follow provided references in order to interpret it, however. Water is then introduced. There is a strong sensitivity to intial conditions whether the planets end up as runaway greenhouses or with ice locked into a cold trap ice cap (when no surface restoring processes are in action). This is a difference from previous 1D work that places a "flux limit" on runaway level. So if an asteroid smashed into a planet and liberated a load of water vapour, a previously ice bound world could be thrust into runaway(? Assuming dust didn't prevent this I suppose.) 3:2 resonant planets are discussed, where the cold trap is polar rather than night side, and therefore rather less efficient. The rate of "water delivery" (e.g. by VOLCANOES) is important. High and the cold trap effect will be overwhelmed and runaway will ensue. Low and the cold trap dominates. NB: The paper also uses the Manabe and Wetherald (1967) moist adjustment. It is also partly cauched around beating up 1D models, which isn't very difficult these days. Atmospheric loss mechanisms are also discussed. If sufficient H is lost in an early runaway greenhouse phase, the planet could collapse to an iceball.

item.title: Papers related to my G4AW bid on Zimbabwe with Vivid Economics
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I am taking part in a Dutch Space Office Geodata for Agriculture and Water bid with Vivid Economics on Zimbabwe.

Two papers by Terence Darlington Mushore

TDM is a researcher into regional agriculture. He makes some good points and his background reading is solid, but he's clearly rather inexperienced, and seems to miss a few things in his analysis particularly on the statistics side. In addition, the second paper is in what I think is a predatory journal. First paper, in Theor. Appl. Climatol., (2017), describes the relationship between maize (a principal crop in Zimbabwe), rain, temperature and number of wet and dry days at one site in Zimbabwe. In general, more rain means a higher maize crop, unless you get absolutely loads, which means less. That makes sense, but the flood statistic is based on only one data point. If temperature increases, then maize increases, however this looks a bit dodge. If the number of wet days increases, the maize yield increases. The reverse for dry days. It is unclear whether it is lack of drought (i.e. dry days) or better rain that is driving these trends. He finishes by emphasising the importance of a local approach. The other paper, in IOSR J. Env. Sci., Tech. and Food Tech., which probably isn't a real journal, nevertheless contains some useful background. He contends that it is not the quality of seasonal forecasts in Zimbabwe that is the problem (claimed by Manatsa et al., 2012 in Natural Hazards), but a lack of good interpretation of them. Better communication between forecasters / researchers and farmers is needed. Again, some of his stats are not very satisfactory as they are based on "normal", "above" and "below". This is very seasonal forecast-y, but it's not clear to me if these are the most useful categories. For once, there are paper notes on this stuff, but not on the below, which was fed to me by Bryan:

Chavez et al., (2015), An end-to-end assessment of extreme weather impacts on food security

A study that takes climate and weather data and the response of crops to it, and feeds it through a fairly sophisticated statistical framework to produce economic impacts on crop yields. The study area is the Yangtze basin, so I ought to understand something about it, even if I feel this probably rather different than what we want for Zimbabwe. Observations are used to provide a statistical description of "weather within climate", ie basically a weather generator. (This is done even though the authors are very upfront about the non-stationary nature of climate.) A physical crop model helps them derive the relationship between weather (particularly extremes of precipitation and temperature) and crop yield. A couple of convolutions later, they have expected yields. Based on earlier work, it is likely that we could probably get away with simpler statistics for Zimbabwe in terms of developing something useful that people could actually understand. They do make some important points that we should build on, however. If one uses drought resistant crops or builds in irrigation rather than relying on rain-feeding, then losses are reduced at all drought return periods. Or on this one on Kenya:

Hansen et al., (2009), Potential value of GCM-based seasonal rainfall forecasts for maize management in semi-arid Kenya

Like Chavez et al., this is a cross-over crops and climate / economic study. The economic bit I definitely didn't completely follow... They estimate that perfect foreknowledge of growing season would be worth about 15-30% of gross product value. Of course - we don't have that. We have GCMs, so how useful are those? Between 9-24 % according to the authors. I know this is Kenya, not Zimbabwe, but it's interesting to see that the view here is that forecasting quality is good. As above, communication does need to be improved. A crop model called APSIM is employed. (It has already been validated in Zimbabwe.) Seasonal forecasts are taken from ECHAM 4.5. The idea is that farmers follow the forecast, fertilise and plant at high "stand" density in good years to maximise profits and plant drought resistant crops with lower stand density in bad years to reduce losses. Of course, fertiliser etc doesn't come free, so the interaction between different variables and profit is complex. Two caveats: (i) Farmers identified very many possible management responses (e.g. methods of planting and weeding) that affect yield. Not really considered here. (ii) The TYRANNY of geography. The study is for two sites only. You mileage may vary. Oh, the tyranny...

item.title: Peyser and Poulsen, (2008), Controls on Permo-Carboniferous precipitation over tropical Pangaea: A GCM sensitivity study
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Marianne's reasonably ludicrous Squareland continent resembles a tropical Pangaea more than it resembles any present-day Earth continent such as Brazil. I asked her to look into possible analogues, and she found this paper, which I like a fair bit. [caption id="" align="alignnone" width="541"] The situation at the beginning of the Permian. Black outlines are the Central Pangaean Mountains (unimportant relatively). Growing white shading are possible ice sheet configurations.[/caption] The Carboniferous-Permian transition is a warming, possibly deglaciating scenario, interesting to us in particular because during that transition, the land becomes increasingly desertified as rain moves away. This is supported by multiple lines of geological evidence presented in the paper's detailed introduction. Two GCM scenarios are then pursued:
  1. Present day -> 8xCO2: Land drying and warming appears to proceed in the way we've been describing. Soil moisture reduces. There are some subtle changes in monsoonal type atmospheric flow.
  2. Very glaciated -> NO_ICE: A series of scenarios that take glaciation from a south pole to 30 degrees south situation to a non-glaciated situation. This also leads to drying, but through a rather different mechanism. The authors state that the existence of a very large ice sheet locks the ITCZ into a relatively small northerly (i.e. warmer hemisphere) regime. Rain falls over the continent. Once the ice sheet goes away, "normal" seasonality and monsoonal behaviour starts. Land regions then have ample opportunity to dry out while the ITCZ is somewhere else during another season. I think that's the idea anyway...
The paper doesn't do a brilliant job of explaining what's going on atmospherically, for me. It is an Earth Sciences perspective I guess. Still, it does show that there may be more than one way that these things can happen though. More study needed! They also talk about the effect of large tropical continental MouNtains, but these are felt to be secondary.

item.title: Vallis et al., (2014), Response of the large-scale structure of the atmosphere to global warming
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
My first ever Geoff Vallis document read fully from start to finish. It has a magnificent Vallis statement in the abstract that can only have been written by Geoff Vallis:
"We present various physical arguments concerning these circulation changes but none that are both demonstrably correct and that account for model results."
People should say more stuff like this in papers. Then they'd be telling the truth more. Anyway, the paper. It takes RCP8.5 and 1% CMIP5 data and tries to identify robust features of circulation change under global warming and explain them. Understandably, it is found that radiative / thermodynamically driven features are quite robust, whereas those that require understanding of circulation are not. It is also notable to me because it presents a formula for predicting tropopause height and changes in tropopause height under global warming. An argument is given for increases in tropopause height and models investigated. It is found that changes in lapse rate and the increasing temperature of the surface both contribute about the same amount to increases in tropopause height with warming (a couple of hundred metres each per degree warming). A limitation of the arguments made here is that OLR is assumed to remain constant with warming, which won't be true if there is something like melting ice. Energy balance of the stratosphere is discussed in the way I understand it, which might be a useful reference in case that comes up. (In fact, they cite Ramaswamy et al., 2001 in Rev. Geophys.) We are reminded of the 15 micrometre CO2 band, which is really saturated in the atmosphere. Upward radiation in this band in the stratosphere is from the upper troposphere. Also the Goody and Yung style OLR from the troposphere must balance with radiative equilibrium above argument is applied. Changes in Hadley cell width / mid-latitude circulation are next. There are some (the authors warn over) simplified theoretical considerations. The upper tropospheric / lower stratospheric meridional temperature gradient increases following changes in the moist adiabatic lapse rate. The low level meridional temperature gradient decreases due to polar amplification of warming. This might interfere with baroclinicity, but the effect is unclear in more sophisticated treatments. A number of other theoretical arguments are also given. THE PHILLIPS PROBLEM for the development of baroclinicity is discussed. (Much used in my fourth year notes.)

item.title: Xia and Huang, (2017), Differential Radiative Heating Drives Tropical Atmospheric Circulation Weakening
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Another paper by one of William Ingram's bete noire Yi Huang. This one seems largely good, but there are some thing swept under the carpet, which gives me the chance for a pretty reasonable summer project with Manoj Joshi and Angus Ferraro and summer student Becky Varney.

Background

Is that we are trying to understand why tropical circulation in SRM runs goes back to zero given that CO2 would be expected to weaken the circulation directly on top of its effect from radiative feedbacks (the latter would be counteracted by strengthening from solar cooling). The leading hypothesis is Angus's: that overcooling of the tropics by SRM produces circulation strengthening and cancels the CO2 direct effect. The alternative hypothesis (mine...): was that the gradient of the forcing in latitude is important, I think following Schaller et al., (2013), although I should check this. This second hypothesis was trashed by a Co2 forced run with a stronger meridional gradient that mimicked solar forcing. Said gradient didn't make any difference.

The actual bit (paper)

[caption id="attachment_562" align="aligncenter" width="831"] (a) Proportional change of circulation against tropical mean temperature change. (b) Circulation against change in diabatic heating.[/caption] It is proposed that differential heating of the atmosphere drives the strength of the tropical circulation (I guess this is Neelin and Held 1987). Drive the convecting region and you'll strengthen the circulation as energy export needs to be increased. Drive the subsidence region and circulation is weakened. Ordinary (or rat-regular) CO2 forcing is concentrated in subsidence regions due to the prevalence of water vapour and cloud in the ascending regions. The authors run a further simulation in which CO2 forcing is made to be as uniform as possible. It is found that the weakening of the circulation is greatly reduced because the direct effect of forcing is much more positive. In fact, the circulation is greatly strengthened!!! by the direct effect of the uniform forcing, which is noted but not really explored. My guess is this is because land is absorbing the forcing on the ascending side and not much on the descending side. (The authors are mostly interested in the forcing. Fair enough - it dominates the response.) The direct effect of ordinary CO2 forcing is about neutral. All this means that the overcooling by solar forcing must be accompanied by a direct weakening of the circulation to compensate for the strengthening due to the temperature response. That implies that positive solar forcing strengthens the circulation, which is interesting, and may be possible given that solar is initially more strongly absorbed at the surface. It really is D-Day for Lambert and Faull, (2007).

item.title: Bretherton et al., (1992), An intercomparison of methods for finding coupled patterns in climate data
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
So, I finally read this old chestnut. I was prompted to do so by my visit to Chris Huntingford at CEH. Chris is interested in techniques that link patterns in different climate datasets to one another. Well - he's specifically interested in one technique, actually, and that happened to be one of the ones looked at in this paper. The authors made some synthetic data and then analysed it in the following ways:
  1. Combined PCA: which is making joint principle components of different datasets. This was what I was suggesting for our Brazil hydrological dataset. The authors consider this the most efficient technique for identifying shared patterns in short datasets, although it does have some limitations.
  2. Single field PCA: Make EOFs of field 1. Correlate the expansion coefficients with the time series of points from the other field. The limitation of this (and combined PCA) is that the patterns found are biased towards EOFs of the individual fields.
  3. Canonical correlation analysis: identifies linear combinations of field 1 variables that are most strongly correlated with linear combinations of field 2 variables. I did not spend much time considering this, but I'm confident that it's not what we want because, although it maximises correlation, it does not maximise variance of individual components as the PCA methods do.
  4. BP: a variant of PCA that is difficult to implement (and difficult for me to understand presumably).
  5. SVD of the cross-covariance matrix: which is what Chris is suggesting. The cross-covariance matrix is the covariance matrix formed when we take A^TB of our two data matrices A and B. A singular value decomposition of this has left and right eigenvectors that are joint patterns for A and B that maximise variance described. If the available dataset is large, or the joint patterns do not resemble EOFs of the individual fields, then this is the best technique.

item.title: CFMIP 2018, Boulder
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I am indebted to Marion Saint-Lu (who is shortly leaving us) for her summary of CFMIP, (which I have added to in blue).
One big topic discussed this year was the importance of the SST pattern of warming in the time-evolution of the climate sensitivity. The pattern of warming affects the feedbacks, especially since clouds differ with the region, so cloud feedbacks depend on the region of warming. Simulating the right pattern of warming should reduce the uncertainty on the ECS.
--> In particular, the strong dominance of the western tropical pacific over the feedback parameter was discussed by a fair few speakers. This means that the time variation of the feedback parameter in the historical record is linked not to radiative feedback but to changes in SST not related very strongly to the feedback outside of the tropical Pacific. If you just use the tropical pacific to define your temperatures, then historical variation of the feedback parameter goes away. What I took away from that is that if we are only interested in the tropical western pacific then we basically know the climate sensitivity... Imagine if it was the continental US, how excited they'd be! It appears that the speakers did not appreciate this, and so I scored an own goal by asking them all about it (I was confused because of the altitude or something...) --> MAT: could there be any application of this for El Nino / tropical pacific climate change?
On another topic, Peter Caldwell gave an interesting presentation (that I unfortunately did not understand well) on a method to evaluate the significance of emergent constraints; Over 5 emergent constraint (in average, from the literature), 4 were found not significant (when for example not longer working when applied to other ensembles).
--> Peter Caldwell has never been afraid to ruffle a few feathers... I also didn't exactly follow what he was doing, but it was least semi-quantitative. At least part of it was seeing whether emergent constraints do the same thing in different ensembles (seems sensible) and another part had something to do with whether the constraints were correlated with more than one feedback. If it was more than one feedback then he deemed them bad constraints I think (not so sure how sensible that is).
Paulo Ceppi proposed a new definition of the climate sensitivity and climate feedback parameter, in which it is no longer the response to the global temperature change only that is considered (as ∆R = lambda*∆T) but it is also the response to the tropospheric stability change (as ∆R = tau*∆T + sigma*∆S). The change in stability affects the radiation (increased stability = more LW emission and more SW reflection because more stratocumuli). He showed that their new scheme worked pretty well.
--> Paulo was also elected to the CFMIP committee. He has a new lectureship at Imperial and will undoubtedly be a key player on the climate analysis side for the forthcoming grant round. Mark and I would like to get him for our proposal, but I think Reading have already gobbled him up. I don't know whether his new stability index could be observed via some kind of proxy? I suppose not. Steve Sherwood presented Maxime Colin’s PhD results (he is a friend of mine, he were together in Masters). One result was on convective memory (that usually lacks in the models) but that they found important if convection is organised. The second result was more relevant to what we experienced with the SCM: they did a few experiments, I think with WRF, fixing what they called the ‘macrostate’ (RH, Cape…) and found that this would make the convection either explode or completely decline. What they deduced from that was that convection is very unstable when interactions with the environment are removed. Their idea was that the microstate (the rainfall I think) would act on the macrostate (Cape etc), as in a predator-prey scheme (I didn’t really get the point of this predator-prey thing but this is how he was referring to it). I found it quite related to the instability we had in the SCM, although I didn’t think that would be an important new result to highlight. Maybe I should emphasize it a bit more in the paper!
--> A commenter stated that Bob Plant wrote this up a decade ago as part of the Plant-Craig scheme (or something similar). Another discussed question was about the resolution at which resolved convection should be used instead of parametrized convection. They did not agree at all on that! --> No, we did not. I found this discussion fatuous. Fiaz Ahmed gave a talk on considering the precip as a function of buoyancy, but I have to admit I could not get it at all (but I know Hugo did get it).
--> I think I largely understood it at the time, but it slips my mind now. He used some ideas from Chris Holloway's PhD to predict convective mass flux in a couple of ways using observations and/or theory from buoyancy. He came up with entrainment / detrainment rates and ended up with a scheme he could use to predict precipitation that didn't look overly dissimilar to mine. --> To your summary I would add that there was a nearly preposterous amount of chat about convective aggregation, and also that it won't be long before cloud resolving models are running as standard globally.

They have released version one. Version two, which will be cloud resolving releases, well, hopefully not before too long. They're rewriting the entire model in C++. I wonder what bugs they'll find. What bugs they'll introduce. Yang Tian: a new postdoc looking at ARM, precipitation and convection with a focus over the Amazon. She wondered if the surface could affect the diurnal cycle (which we can't do). We had an amusing discussion regarding whether the UM can do cloud resolving over a land surface. (I'm sure it can...) Peter Caldwell: which I dreaded unnecessarily. He didn't want to have a go at me, but chat about my hydrological cycle talk which he had to miss. He is now in charge of the cloud resolving stuff for EEESM. Xue Zheng and Cheng Tao: with whom I had general chats about what I've done and they tried to get me to talk about what was important for the future. Felt a bit like a faculty interview. In one of these conversations we talked about land surface control on the hydrological cycle. The commenter seemed to take an almost JT Reager-esque view that it wasn't that important. Mark Zelinka: who was softly spoken and thoughtful as usual. He says that David Romps' new ideas on FAT are probably correct, although don't change the basic conclusions concerning what clouds will DO under climate change. Paul Durack: with whom I bashed out a few ideas on what to do for the water cycle article.

item.title: Colquhoun (2014), An investigation of the false discovery rate and the misinterpretation of p-values
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Finally read something from dcscience's David Colquhoun. Proof that a blog could get you some much needed unwarranted exposure? Anyway, old DC is basically a neuroscientist, medicalist type, but simple statistics lessons are always worth learning. We all know that setting p = 0.05 and using that as a hard barrier to significance via a t-test is silly. However, even quoting the p-value and regarding that as a measure of how unlikely your results are to be due to chance can be misleading. His main point is made by figure 2: 1000 drugs are tested on people. Due to errors / variance in the population, there are some false positives. These are associated with the usual p value (here we assume these errors are understood precisely so we can quantify them -- reality may not be so kind). All well and good. However, what is frequently ignored is that (i) the test also has a statistical power, which is the ability to detect real effects. This is probably below 100%. Here he uses 80%. And (ii) unfortunately most candidate drugs don't do anything (here assumed to be 90%), so in the main we are testing the case where there can be no real effect and the number of false positives compared with true positives will be very large -- even if are test is very statistically powerful. In this case, the probability of finding a false positive is 45 / (80 + 45) ~ 36% and not 5%! Given that it's almost entirely positive results that get published when it comes to drug testing, this means that even in this very idealised case, around 35% of the results are wrong. There are some more detailed considerations, but the above is his main argument. There are some recommendations for how to do tests better in section 13. The most significant (hah) of these is "use p < 0.001 or less stringently a three-sigma rule".
I've always been a fan of letting the author use some pithy language so that papers aren't so dry. Colquhoun quotes a reviewer in the acknowledgements:
"I am particularly grateful to one of them [the reviewers] for allowing that after having 'constructed such a sturdy soapbox it would be a shame not to let the author speak from it.'"
And so he does. And I think it's a bit of a turn off for me. The opinion and the facts get a bit mixed up in the discussion and there are references to newspaper articles. Also, the repeated assertion of researchers "making fools of" themselves. I don't think that's really what I go to the academic literature for. Reminds me of what Mark Zelinka was saying about David Romps' paper. This is as much a lesson as the intended one about statistics. Mind you - I did enjoy his attack on metrics and the publish-or-perish culture.

item.title: One week at ICAS, The University of Leeds
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Another week where I had a heavy cold. Still - at least they had YORKSHIRE TEA, of which I drank about half a box. Sorry Steef. I gave both my current 2019 hydrological cycle seminar and strategic parameterisation talks. I got reasonably good traction, but hit something of a dead-end with the strategic stuff when Leif Denby asserted that coarse averaging of convection resolving models of various kinds results in a product that can't tell you anything about convection. I don't think that's true really, (as someone else said - this is what parameterisations actually do). However, it carried rather a lot of weight in the meeting and sort of ground things to a halt. I spoke to [caption id="" align="aligncenter" width="374"] "I drink YORKSHIRE TEA nowadays. Like tea used to be."[/caption] Tom Richardson, Chris Smith and Paloma Tracasa-Castro: from the Forster group. They are doing pretty standard CMIP5/6 stuff. Tom Richardson has a newish paper that applies simple Allen and Ingram models to precipitation that actually work over land. I should probably look at that just once, because we could never get it to work... John Marsham, Lawrence Jackson, Declan Finney: We spoke about extreme precipitation and resolved convection in the main. Lizzie Kendon has a new paper on extremes almost out that I should anticipate. As you might expect, resolving convection improves representation of extremes. It is unfortunately difficult to draw general conclusions about future evolution of extremes and, for example, their relationship with mean precipitation. They made an important point about the CP4Africa runs (which I am being told I need for the clouds grant), which is that the resolved and parameterised runs also have different cloud schemes, which I view as rather non-ideal -- especially since our interest is the interaction with the large-scale circulation. This meeting and the next one were difficult because I was seriously under the weather, so I may not have all the details right. I keep wondering if Declan is the Declan who emailed Ben Booth all those years ago about working in environmental science. Leighton Regayre and Jill Johnson: from the Carslaw group. They are emulating model ensembles a la David Sexton, and so were clearly a bit disappointed that my emulators are inside the model. Nevertheless, the meeting was rather a good one (with Keano's excellent coffee propping me up just about). They are trying to constrain aerosol parameterisations with observations. I asked about the "but you can always keep picking constraints til you have one model version" thing. They have a way of approaching this, but I didn't get it quite and certainly can't remember it now. I learnt that the Oxford people, Ken Carslaw and Andrew Gettleman (NCAR) are building a first multi-model perturbed physics ensemble, although they can only perturb three parameters across all three models. Leighton encouraged me to engage with PARACON. He is probably right. Dominick Spracklen and Jess Baker: proved that I should probably pay more attention in CSSP Brazil meetings. Jess's work shows that although relevant observations are difficult to interpret, the radiation limited areas of the Amazon show reducing evaporation with increasing precipitation, basically because there is a lot of cloud cover when it is raining. (There is still a positive relationship in space.) Dominick also sent me a paper that shows that introducing plant biology more properly not only reduces the CO2 sequestered by plants, but also reduces the water vapour feedback through reduced land precipitation. It's only 0.5 Wm-2, but it surprised me. Doug Parker, Richard Keane, Steef Boeing, Leif Denby: And so on to the actual bit. This meeting did not go as well as I hoped, due to Leif's intervention described above. Nevertheless, I picked up some useful ideas. First of all, it was pointed out that a super-parameterised model might be a really easy way to obtain data for linked large-scale and small-scale simulations. It might not give as great an answer as looking at LES directly, but the technology for coarse graining is all already there. Second, Doug suggested that, although he didn't believe that large-scale information from one timestep says much about convection, it might be possible to do it using information from multiple timesteps.

item.title: Shi et al., (2019), Neglecting plant-microbe symbioses leads to underestimation of modeled climate impacts
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: Dominick Spracklen shoved this paper under my nose while I was at LEEDS. It shows that neglecting nitrogen cycling causes an overestimate of plant net primary productivity. Dominick wanted me to look at it, however, because it seems to show that this effect not only increases atmospheric CO2, but also reduces the water vapour feedback through its effect in suppressing evapotranspiration. Since I think like an astronomer and believe the Earth to be an aquaplanet that wouldn't really care about a bit of land for evaporation, I was surprised by this. Although, regarding the experimental setup: Hi Dom and Jess, So - I had a read of that paper. It's a bit of an unusual one... Their experimental set-up, to my mind, anyway, is rather strange to say the least. First of all - I think you're absolutely right. They do find that the effect of increasing CO2 concentration is countered by a reduction in the water vapour feedback. However, what I find rather odd about it is: - Their GCM experiment has fixed prescribed SSTs. CO2 concentration then increases. SSTs stay the same, land temperatures presumably increase a bit due to increasing CO2 (although not loads as the fixed SSTs prevent it). The model will tend to export heat from land regions to compensate for CO2 heating and dump it in the fixed SST oceans. This will do weird stuff to the energy transport. It could potentially suppress ocean evaporation too (although it's not clear that it will) affecting water vapour feedback. Although a state a bit like this would occur if we rapidly increased CO2 concentrations in reality, what we're looking at certainly isn't an equilibrium. At equilbrium, assuming that CO2 concentratrion increased, it's fair to assume we'd be looking at a stronger water vapour feedback too. - Secondly, what seems really odd to me (and this may be my turn to get the wrong end of the stick), is that a land surface model with fixed meteorology is used to determine the NPP suppression and then this rate is applied to the GCM atmosphere without interactive feedbacks to balance it. Then after 25 years, the change in CO2 and water vapour forcing is measured and the numbers given. But wouldn't the effect be twice as big if we waited another 50 years (or however the logs stack up). So an interesting read, but I guess we still don't know what the actual effect will be? cheers Hugo It is only a small effect (about 0.5 Wm-2 compared with 1 Wm-2 on CO2 forcing), although due to the odd setup, who knows how big the effect should be? Probably worth investigating for those interested in such things.

item.title: Convection Parametrization: Progress and Challenges 2019
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I went to CPPC, hosted by PARACON, at the Met Office. I was rather more involved in the proceedings than I expected. Not only was my own presentation placed prominently, rather than being hived off into some graveyard poster session as I expected, but I was asked to lead the machine learning discussion groups and report back to the whole group and attend a meeting of people interested in impulse-response methods for characterising convection. I feel like Alison Stirling (who was basically in charge of the whole thing) is testing me. In general, I didn't think there was too much for me to learn from the general parts of the meeting. People are working towards global cloud resolving models, wondering whether we should care about convective organisation and giving many details of improvements to convective parameterisations. I didn't receive any comments on my own work that are likely to influence it's development, although attendees were generally complementary and Bob Plant became the third person to suggest that we use it to upgrade the "tangent linear model", whatever that is. The side meetings were more relevant:

Machine learning discussion group

I finally met Stephan Rasp, a PhD student who is spoken about in reverent tones by everyone (apart from Leif Denby...) because he's actually done all the machine learning stuff on convection that others like to hand-wave ab out. He played an important role in the discussion and was generally very helpful and pleasant in a way I had been led to not quite expect. Basically, Rasp (and Leif Denby) believes that we need to go back to basics and start solving "standard problems" and set them as "challenges" to the machine learning community in the way that they're used to. His opinion is that the early successes look good, but are beset by issues, particularly with stability and extrapolatability. In the second discussion session I demanded that my group provide me with a list of challenges, which they actually did and Leif even went so far as to set up a website from which these things could be resourced. It was telling that this discussion was a distinct group from Steve Sherwood's impulse-response "convection playground" group (I met with a subset of them below). I'm sure they could have used some of the ideas from this group. Small postscript reading this a bit later having looked at some of the papers again: certainly Rasp's own analysis has the problems he describes, but despite his claims, the O'Gorman paper does use a slab ocean and does present stable climates. OK - that's based on a convective parameterisation and not high-resolution. Could be because he chose the random forest algorithm.  

Meeting with impulse-responsers

Steve Sherwood, Roman Roehrig and some of their groups were put in a smallish Met Office meeting room by Alison Stirling along with me and Bob Plant. I wasn't quite sure what Alison's game was, but it seemed that she had told Steve that I was "interested in the 'convective playground'", which is their name for their WRF SCM technology that runs and impulse responses lots of convection schemes in, well, the SCM. SPOILER ALERT: I'm not really that interested in it. And they aren't really that interested in anything I had to say either. Alison eventually managed to persude me to point out that the impulse response method is certainly not optimised for any convection that we actually care about, and would be a lot of work to do with LES, that my method would be cheaper, and unlike impulse-response, has already been demonstrated to be invertible and put-backable in the GCM. They weren't interested. "We're more interested in understanding," or something, said Steve, missing the point of what I was trying to say. "Don't worry," I told Alison and Bob, "they'll be back". [caption id="attachment_589" align="aligncenter" width="480"] "Don't worry," I say, "youu'lll neverrrrr loooose."[/caption] Could be a huge amount of wasted LES time though! In a way I was quite pleased they didn't want to use my method because I'd get washed away under the weight of their resources.  

Meeting with Peter Caldwell

(Which actually happened the week after because Peter was visiting Exeter for a bit.) I had two ideas in this meeting, although I think one of them defeats the other one, but it's the first time I've thought about climate feedbacks "global climate science" for a long time. Peter showed me a new analysis that decomposes CMIP5 global mean climate feedbacks into principle components, giving us a new set of uncorrelated feedbacks for analysis. Perhaps disappointingly, the first EOF is just shortwave cloud feedback (so no correlations removed really). The second one is a lapse rate - longwave cloud feedback see-saw, which will please Mark Webb. What Peter would like to do is build a multi-emergent constraints method that linearly adds effects on feedbacks from different parts of the Earth. The problem is correlation between potential feedback processes. The solution, I pointed out, is to use his principle component decomposition to remvoe said correlations! Obvious, when you think about it (he had only been thinking about the multi-emergent constraints methods for a day or two). My other idea was to test the combinability of emergent constraints by running them within a GCM and seeing how one feedback effects another. I'm confident we could do this with ISCA. The problem is that I think Peter's feedback decomposition combined with his multi-emergent constraints method suggests that this might not be valuable, as the correlation between SW cloud feedback and others is quite weak. (And that's what's going to make a difference to the range.) Of course, that's probably truest near the centre of the distribution, and we may be more interested by what happens near the edge. The other thing that occured to me is that I wonder what the total amount of feedback available is for both subtropical low cloud and sea ice. In other words, if we get rid of all of them starting from climatological values, what's the total Wm-2? Is that an important quantity?
