item.title: Mitchell and Lora, (2016), The Climate of Titan
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
A review article by Jonathan Mitchell in Annual Reviews of Earth and Planetary Sciences. The climate of Titan, or perhaps even the atmosphere of Titan are a bit of a mystery. He provides some up-to-date information from observations and simulations. I feel like it's basically very good, but the final analysis using a model doesn't necessarily seem to fit in very well with the rest of it. Titan has cold traps(? -- are they really?) at the poles that consist of seas and lakes, and apparently fairly dry equatorial regions (although there seems a fair bit of confusion over this, including Mitchell's own newer work wot I saw on a poster at EXOCLIMES V). Some key obs and model pointers he picks out:
  • There are high clouds at the summer pole, probably due to deep convection occurring there. Although 90% of the incoming solar radiation is absorbed in the atmosphere and only 10% at the surface, the hilariously long radiative timescale of the atmosphere (multi-century) and the lack of an ocean and the multi-decadal seasonal cycle means that the polar surface can be very warm and initiate convection. This all means that the atmosphere can also experience a seasonal cycle despite its very long relaxation timescale.
  • Overall, he reckons the equator to pole temperature difference is perhaps 2 - 4 K at the surface, which isn't much. Especially when you consider the moist mixed boundary layer might be 8 km deep (and 8 K colder than the surface...).
  • Other important numbers: It is thought that surface RH ~ 50%. Atmospheric methane reservoir is ~ 5 m when condensed (10 times more than the surface). Remember that although surface pressure is 1.5 bar, the low surface gravity of Titan means that total atmospheric mass is much higher!
  • Planetary-scale Hadley cell due to slow rotation of the planet. Points out that "moist" transport of this cell is actually equatorwards (as on Earth) even though moisture is exported to the coldest pole for trapping (assuming that happens) as well as convecting region (which tracks around and favours the poles). Note that we have to think seasonally to understand what is going on.
  • Warns that weak temperature gradient theory needs a bit of modification since, although the whole atmosphere is in many ways tropical, there is sufficient variation in mid-level moist static energy you wouldn't get on Earth.
They discuss some simulations using the Titan Atmospheric Model. It is notable that moist heat transport is very weak. Surprising when there's so much methane in the atmosphere. Remember that latent heat of condensation is small, though. The simulations have imposed wet poles and a dry equator. Not sure that's a completely fair way to prove that it only rains at the poles. We could do the same with an Earth model. The seasonal varying heat fluxes are above. You can see that the evaporation remains more or less positive upwards at all times and sensible and radiative heat downwards, which is what I've always wanted... They go on to make a polar cold trap argument that doesn't really seem to fit with the rest of what they've just said, but it is standard. If anything, it looks more like a hot trap to me, whereby P-E > 0 during the summer and there is perhaps(?) weak cold trapping during the winter.

item.title: Two papers applying the Herman and Kuang tangent linear convection scheme
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I had thought that no one had implemented a linear convection scheme within a GCM, but it turns out that I'm wrong. Alison Stirling sent me two that Brian Mapes and group have produced with their so-called "Jalopy" convection scheme. (They're joke term for it because they don't regard it as very good.)

Kelly et al, (2017), Tangent linear superparameterization of convection in a 10 layer global atmosphere with calibrated climatology

The quick drying RONSEAL of papers. They put the Kuang matrices in a GCM (they call it "intermediate complexity", but it is a full GCM dynamically with moist processes stripped out and specific humidity re-introduced as a passive tracer), run it, and are a bit disappointed with the results. I'm surprised it even works at all given that they don't have a separate triggering step.  The aim of the paper is to test how convection interacts with tropical waves and how the strength of convection changes this without having to worry about cranking the entrainment parameter (for example) of an actual convection scheme that might strongly change the state. This they manage to do despite some problems with the base climatology.

Mapes et al., (2019), Estimating Convection’s Moisture Sensitivity: An Observation–Model Synthesis Using AMIE-DYNAMO Field Data

Mapes et al. uses observations from an ARM-DYNAMO (!?) campaign to derive the Kuang matrix. This is easier said than done due to various autocorrelations (obvious to us I guess) and the fact that large-scale motion that wouldn't be in a convective parameterization is not cleanly separable from the motion you want. Their tentative overall conclusion is
"At face value, Fig. 8 indicates that AMIE-DYNAMO observations suggest that natural convection’s sensitivity to free-tropospheric moisture may be roughly twice that computed from a small-domain cloud-resolving CCPM. Before asserting this finding too strongly, let us review this paper’s tall stack of logical inference steps and assumptions."
Specifically:
  • The observations are the best guide we have, but are polluted with noise from other variables that aren't related to q or convection.
  • Correlations across vertical layers mean that observed correlations / coefficients are much bigger than model ones derived using their level-by-level perturbation technique. They bridge this using their "observed field campaign" technique, which I guess means putting in appropriately correlated moisture perturbations and forcing the Kelly GCM with it. From this they derive their factor of 2 sensitivity difference (above).
It must be said that both the Kelly and Mapes papers are very reasonable about not overselling their findings. Mapes ends with a lengthy discussion of "why do field campaigns / real experiments when everything is increasingly model led and the two are difficult to compare?" His rough conclusion is that it's more the experience of getting different kinds of researchers together and absorbing the qualitative findings of the experiments and musing on such questions as "what is convection?" et cetera...

item.title: Wordsworth and Pierrehumbert, (2014), Abiotic Oxygen-dominated atmospheres on terrestrial habitable zone planets
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Another one from the Wordsworth stable that Eric suggested as a starting point for Alex's PhD. Typical of the genre, there's much conjecture and less evidence, but as usual it also contains some interesting ideas. In fact, they almost write it as an opinion piece and don't really describe the 1D radiative convective simulations (I think) are being used to generate their results.   The overall point is that molecular oxygen is not necessarily a sign of life, it could be a sign of high atmospheric water concentration being progressively photolysised to oxygen and hydrogen. If background nitrogen, or other inert gases, don't form a very large fraction of the atmosphere, then water can't be "cold trapped" beneath them and photolysis can't be avoided even well under runaway greenhouse temperatures. (Here when the authors say "cold trapped" they mean at the cold point around the tropopause rather than on a planetary surface I think).   They illustrate their point for an initially pure water planet (including interior), Figure 2, and then extend to more complicated planets including surface oxidation and subduction. The oxygen concentration is determined by the balance of photolysis (which is a function of atmospheric non-water pressure ie also oxygen), loss of oxygen to space, surface and subsurface oxidation.
 
Figure 2 (right). Schematic of possible evolutionary pathways for an initially water-dominated planet exposed to stellar XUV and UV. (a) H2O photolysis causes O2 and other oxidized products to build up on the planet's surface regions of low net instellation. (b) Once sufficient O2 has built up, the planet can transition to a state where a stable O2 atmosphere is present and hydrogen escape to space is balanced by oxidation of the interior.

item.title: Review of the Lambert-Lewis Convection Scheme and possible changes
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
It's high time I reviewed the Lambert-Lewis Convection Scheme and considered possible changes. This stems from the recent LLCS port to ISCA and Neil's assertion that we ought to make LLCS always mix moisture during moist convection -- even where q > q_sat. Some investigation (below) suggests that this is not a good idea. We also really need a flowchart for LLCS because it's reasonably complicated (despite it's "simplicity compared with competitor systems") and it's easy to forget what it actually does.

Flowchart

Possible changes and their effects

The following changes are being considered:
  1. Allow DRY_CONVECTION to mix q anomalies upwards even when q(this level) > q(level below). Introducing this doesn't have much effect in Earth-like simulations because the scenario q(this level) > q(level below) is rare, and we're talking about unsaturated mixing. I'm wondering if not fixing this poses a potential gotcha for future planetary scenarios, so my recommendation is to adopt it.
  2. Set q = q_sat in MOIST_CONVECTION even when q > q_sat initially. This sounds like a good idea because LLCS is basically "where a parcel could get from level i to i+j, mix everything across these levels". However, it's only really relevant when the model state begins to get out of hand for Earth-like simulations as we approach the gridpoint storm limit. In this case q > q_sat aloft and setting q = q_sat causes CONSERVE_MOISTURE to mix moisture rapidly downwards into the boundary layer. This is a recipe for a model crash. It is also rather far-fetched to imagine moist convection style plumes doing this at the same rate as moisture is mixed upwards ordinarily. Neil has already put this into the ISCA version of LLCS but I think it should be avoided. Related to this, LLCS identifies separate convective events for moisture conservation by finding where q changes in CONSERVE_MOISTURE. Hence, if there is a level where q = q_sat, then FIND_BOUNDS thinks convection isn't happening there during CONSERVE_MOISTURE and separates an actual convective event into two. This doesn't happen very often, but is probably more common near the gridpoint storm limit.
  3. Calculate gamma_s, the saturated adiabatic lapse rate, using values all from the level below. This currently looks like a code bug. The temperature components of the gamma_s equation use the level below and the moisture part the current level. "Fixing" this leads to strong upper tropospheric heating, model cooling and a big decline in precipitation. The "fix" is also an approximation like the original expression, of course, so I recommend leaving this for now until a better method is devised. A number of apparently small choices like this cause pretty big differences in performance and can lead to gridpoint storms and crashes. Including:
  4. Set q = q_sat last in MOIST CONVECTION. Currently, q is set to the saturation value for temperature before moist adjustment of the temperature itself. This seems like a no brainer fix, but it leads to efficient saturation of the post-convection atmosphere and GPS. (Note: the amount of rainfall is unaffected by this choice because that depends on the increase in temperature not caused by dry mixing.) This shouldn't be done alone. If we implement this, then I would relax moisture towards RHCRIT * q_sat rather than just q_sat but continue to relax temperature towards the relevant saturation value. I think I've convinced myself this is sensible on a cigarette packet but I haven't tried it. Longer term:
  5. Allow dry and moist events to have different timescales. It is probably sensible to slow down dry events with respect to moist events. Ought to be simple enough where these are separate. Ambiguous for mixed events but I wonder what fraction of the total these are. This might be really useful for Jupiter or other giant planets where there is well-separated dry convection and moist convection in a typical convecting column. Haven't tried it in the code yet.
  6. Try to represent convective entrainment in some more controllable way. Difficult because what is actually happening is ambiguous in a moist adjustment scheme and also because LLCS is kind of total entrainment anyway because "everything is mixed-up". The only thing that comes to mind is that a parcel starting from the bottom of a convecting event wouldn't be able to make it to the top if there is lots of mixing with a low enthalpy environment. We could use this to limit the vertical spread of convection when conditions are unfavourable.  It's interesting, but we would need a lot of assumptions and recasting the code to take care of it might necessitate writing something much more complex and get us out of the territory where we want to be. I also see a lot of gridpoint storms in this future. Obviously haven't tried it yet.

item.title: THAI 2020 -- The rocky exoplanet intercomparison project meeting
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
I attended the THAI meeting, when I really should have been attending CFMIP 2020, but I really have heard enough about RCEMIP for one lifetime. It stands for TRAPPIST Habitable Atmosphere Intercomparison and is running some TRAPPIST 1e cases in about 5 different GCMs including the UM. A number of talks were given and discussions had, which brought up a couple of issues worth remembering:
  • Francois Forget gave his convection talk again, as at Exoclims V. The interesting thing to remember is that the buoyancy of the condensible versus the buoyancy of the background gas is potentially rather important. On Earth, the low density of water vapour versus the higher density of molecular nitrogen gives convection a very small push (that we ignore). (Forget behaved as if this and other errors in Earth-like moist adjustment schemes are primary causes of our uncertainty in atmospheric convection. Nonsense.) On volatile-rich gas giants or anywhere with a hydrogen atmosphere, on the other hand, water or ammonia convection could feel a serious brake from the fact that the background is so light. This might have an effect on Jupiter, for example.
  • Ray Pierrehumbert, meanwhile, thinks that everyone should do mass flux because of some reasons to do with non-dilute condensible cases. I pointed out that there are lots of other ways he could push for mass flux, including some that involved planets that other people can actually simulate.
  • Denis led a rather interesting discussion on "what planetary targets should we simulate and what techniques do we need to simulate them?" (And how does this link to what we can distinguish in observations.) There were some hobby horses. There was, however, also a rather compelling case made for the lack of oceans simulated in e.g. the UM being fixed. I wonder if we should re-address the Codron ocean idea. Apparently, salinity could be a big deal too, which sounds fun if very difficult to deal with.
Overall, exoplanet work, despite some increasing sanity, is still delightfully anarchic with various characters trying to tell us "we should all do this" to little avail.

item.title: Hoskins and Ambrizzi, (1993), Rossby Wave Propagation on a Realistic Longitudinally Varying Flow
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A quick note on this J. Atmos. Sci. paper that "explains" the Barotropic model that Jonathan Beverley is using to describe the propagation of teleconnections that move from tropics to extratropics. I say "explains". As is customary for "classic" papers on atmospheric dynamics, symbols are introduced without explanation, making it hard to know what's going on in detail. The introduction explains that many features of tropospheric stationary waves are obvious from analysing the barotropic vorticity equation "linearized about an upper tropospheric zonal flow". However, previous studies have neglected wave -- mean-flow interaction and that's what they'll do here to better represent propagation of waves relevant to teleconnections. ROSSBY WAVES are possible in westerley flow and are refracted by said flow in a similar manner to Snell's Law in Optics. The result is that Rossby waves are refracted towards latitudes with smaller u (zonal velocity) if I followed the logic correctly. When it comes to the Barotropic Model they use, they take the damped barotropic vorticity equation, force it with a fixed vorticity anomaly and see how this adjusts the rest of the global field at a given pressure level. Notably, linearity is enforced by multiplying the forcing by 10-6. Seems a curious way of doing it, but I'm not arguing. The model is tested for a number of waveguides (presumably regions where zonal velocity is high, so maybe I'm wrong about slow u refracting waves into line). Very prominent is the North Africa-Asian jet entrance, where a vorticity anomaly near the western jet entrance produces a propagating stationary wave train that envelopes the globe after 15 days. Reasonable agreement with observed patterns is found. Overall, this paper was a bit tough for me, but not helped by an absence of definitions. MUST TRY HARDER.

item.title: Prive and Plumb, (2007), Monsoon Dynamics with Interactive Forcing, Part I: Axisymmetric Studies
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Finally read this paper, which is important to Ruth and Harry's monsoon studies. In fact, I feel that a fair few of Ruth's ideas are related to this, so it's pretty useful for understanding her point of view. A number of very idealised axisymmetric (ie non-eddy permitting?) aquaplanet simulations are used to investigate the "thermally direct angular momentum conserving circulation" that emerges in the boreal summer that forms the monsoon circulation. When people say "angular momentum conserving", it seems that they mean that the upper branch of the circulation conserves angular momentum and the lower branch is balanced by near-surface friction. The model experiments are very simple (and that should be borne in mind when regarding the results). There is no radiative cooling, only Newtonian relaxation towards atmospheric temperatures of 200 K and prescribed surface radiative heating. SSTs are prescribed in all experiments, but a Manabe-style bucket model is used for land water. Aquaplanet experiments are run in which SST perturbations are applied in more northern tropical / sub-tropical areas to represent seasonal land warming during the monsoon. A rapid onset of the monsoon is seen above a certain warming threshold, as usual, and upper tropospheric absolute vorticity approaches zero, indicating angular momentum conservation. Land cases are a bit muddier. The meridional circulation still strengthens with increasing land surface temperature, but sudden onset doesn't really happen. This could be because the WISHE feedback (Wind-Induced Surface Heat Exchange) is much weaker, which in oceanic cases enhances the strengthening of the circulation or because the location of ascent moves northward (and therefore ascent weakens) when land is brought fully into play. Perhaps most important is the

5. Theory of monsoon location

Emmanuel et al. (1994) show that under statistical equilibrium (ie convective quasi-equilibrium), the zonal wind field is closely related to the distribution of subcloud moist enthalpy. Where there is large-scale ascent (which there will be near a monsoon), the vertical thermodynamic profiles should approach those of a moist adiabat. Thermal wind balance then implies that wind shear is related to the meridional moist static energy gradient. If, simultaneously, the meridional circulation is conserving angular momentum, the circulation boundary must be in a region of zero wind shear, because this is where the ascent is occurring with a flow of constant angular momentum. Hence, the monsoon ascent and therefore precipitation are associated with the maximum of the moist static energy. "Definitely makes sense, although feels a bit circular", I wrote on my copy. Finally, the location of the moist static energy maximum is discussed. P&P say that the maximum occurs over the coastal continent where surface fluxes are largest. I can see this not working over the ocean, which is what Ruth is worried about. Other useful pointers: "Over the ocean, the moist static energy is closely related to surface temperature, while over a land surface, the moist static energy is controlled by a balance between advection by the large-scale flow and surface heat fluxes". Obviously, but good to see it written down.

item.title: CIRCULATES effect of dynamics on cloud feedback
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Here's the original email I sent to Monisha and Geoff about how we might investigate the effect of circulation on cloud feedback in GCMs. It's good to store this somewhere searchable. However, it also needs some updating. (See below.) Hi, As promised, a possible way to get from where we are to a publication. As I said, it may not be the only way, and a bit of work on it may reveal there's something better we could do or it's wrong, but that's research. Would be great to get both your opinions on this. Hypothesis: GCM cloud parameterisations do not respond (or do not respond strongly enough) to changes in larger scale (ie resolved by GCM dynamics) circulation. Question: If the above is true, what is the effect of this on simulation of present day cloud and cloud feedbacks under climate change? (If the above is false, how does circulation control cloud parameterisation? But it's probably true.) Relevant background: - Paulo Ceppi's review paper (you've read that right?) https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/wcc.465 - quasi-equilibrium stuff. (Done!) - the climate sensitivity assessment. https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2019RG000678 - Probably some more papers on cloud feedback. The one I was involved in was: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00382-012-1336-x There are more up-to-date ones now, but this got a tonne of citations and it's the sort of thing people do. Method: 1) Port simple cloud scheme to UM vn11.8. (By far the worst bit.) (Hugo to see if we can get Ian Boutle to adopt the cloud scheme in the UM trunk so we don't have to worry about maintaining it in future.) 2) Run control run with simple cloud scheme and compare with PC2 setup. Do this for both current and, say, 4xco2 to get simulation of climate change. Probably do this for both tropical box continent setup and a more realistic Earth continent case just to see link to real world a bit more clearly. Think about what is being done with the SPOOKIE cloud scheme elsewhere, and their results. Get paper from Mark Webb if not obvious in literature search. 3) Diagnose link between resolved circulation and cloud radiative effect in the simple cloud scheme and compare with St Andrews results for the convection permitting simulations. (in fact, Anna / Mike already have early results and they look pretty good.) The standard way of doing this would be to composite both the GCM and convection permitting data into regimes of resolved vertical velocity and look at how cloud radiative effect, cloud cover, cloud liquid water / ice vary with the vertical velocity. We would then reprogram the simple cloud scheme to follow the convection permitting simulations, and re-run control and 4xco2 to find impact on climate change. (Hugo to have ridiculous argument with Mark Webb again about whether we should use results from 4xco2 convection permitting runs to inform our GCM simulations.) Results: If relationship between circulation and cloud feedback all rather obvious and easy to adopt, then do this and submit paper. If not obvious then use Lambert or other mathematical method to diagnose how RH / T / circulation interact to produce cloud feedback in the convection permitting simulations, SPOOKIE cloud scheme and PC2. Think about how best to get cloud scheme looking like convection permitting simulation. Do and submit paper. (Using Lambert method will need direct input from me almost certainly.) Lambert method paper: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020MS002085 I would highly value any opinions on how to do better than this. For what it's worth, Mark and I think this will actually work better for cloud schemes than convection schemes (what it is applied to in the paper) for technical reasons I can bore you with later. Bonus activities: a) Think about how convection schemes interact with large-scale flow (and possibly cloud too). (As you suggested.) b) Convene with met office to talk about how best to use our results to inform complex parameterisation. c) Use Lambert (or other method) to find out what the minimum set of resolved model variables are we need to know to build cloud schemes based on (i) existing cloud schemes (ii) high resolution modelling such as st andrews / reading simulations (iii) observations (Will need direct input from me most likely, but I should try this at some point anyway.) d) Once the other part of the Exeter project starts, think about how we can use what you find out to inform climate projections using existing GCM data / larger-scale observations. Perhaps also with Imperial. e) Super bonus activity: Try to build a framework in which cloud responses of (i), (ii) and (iii) to our minimum set of variables and their uncertainties can be described, put it back in the GCM and use that to produce a range of uncertainties for climate change based on observations / hi-res. (Very hard but somebody has got to do it at some point.) An attempt at c) and e) is easily another paper. --- This is where I'm at now. Let me know what you think... best wishes, Hugo

Updated

So having looked at Monisha's analysis and talked to Mike Byrne, a bit more cleverness is required. But that explains, perhaps, why this is a problem in the first place. Surface temperature  and circulation (as measured by omega 500) are very well-correlated in global models (and probably at least moderately well-correlated in reality). This makes separating the effects of temperature and humidity from the effect of vertical velocity on cloud radiative effect in the present day very difficult. That wouldn't be important, except for the fact that circulation will, for example, tend to slow down for both unstable and stable regimes in the future, while temperatures continue to increase. What we need is a GCM experiment that has non-correlated surface temperatures and circulation. I'm hoping that something like this may be possible (perhaps based on the dreaded self-aggregation) using flat tropical SSTs and more realistic SSTs elsewhere. That could then be compared to the sort of thing that Mike and others are doing with hi-res models, to the extent that these have an imprint of large-scale circulation. The other thing to investigate, of course, is what climate change experiments do in high-resolution models.

item.title: Emanuel et al., (1994), On large-scale circulations in convecting atmospheres
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Think I must have read this before, or at least attempted it, but results in Prive and Plumb, (2007), and my own attempts to understand the basics of the tropical hydrological cycle over land persuaded me that I should have a go at it again. It's from Kerry Emanuel, David Neelin and Chris Bretherton. Interesting that they chose QJRMS. Was rather a different beast in 1994 I suppose. There's a lot in here, and I still didn't take the time to go through all of the argumentation surrounding the derivation of the wave equation that describes tropical disturbances. Although they at least bother to define their variables unlike many classic papers, the argumentation is often a bit vague - certainly for thickos like me - and it isn't always clear whether claims are theoretical or based on analysis of observations, or what time and spatial scales are being used to make a point.
"The virtual temperature of the convecting atmosphere is uniquely related to the subcloud-layer entropy."
This seems basically OK, although you think these authors would take more time to talk around the weak temperature gradient approximation and the fact that their statement therefore isn't simply true in the tropics. They do talk about the case where a capping inversion forms over colder SSTs, but isn't made 100% clear what happens in the free troposphere in this case. The paper begins with a polemic against various older ideas, pointing out that temperature gradients rather than heating gradients are important. (Forces move the world. In this paper, everything is basically moist adiabatic and in thermal wind balance, which I think presents problems in the tropical troposphere?) The Kuo scheme and concepts related around moisture conservation that forget about energy balance (radiative-convective equilibrium) are also critiqued. It is explained that statistical equilibrium ("quasi-equilibrium" thinking) actually come originally from Arakawa and Schubert, (1974), which I didn't realise. It is pointed out that things like CAPE and CIN don't really exist much in the real world, because the rapid effects of convection hold things close to critical lapse rates. The magnitude of convection is therefore set by the balance of surface fluxes, convergence, and boundary layer temperature (assuming saturation over the ocean...).

Statistical equilibrium thinking. "Are you asking me, or are you telling me?" "I'm telling you Jim."

Under strict quasi-equilibrium, CAPE does not change with time for a given parcel of air. Using the Maxwell relations of classical thermodynamics, hydrostatic equilibrium and entropy conservation, they relate sub-cloud boundary layer entropy to atmospheric temperatures (and therefore later winds). Sub-cloud entropy itself is related to the balance of surface fluxes, radiative cooling (of the boundary layer) and convective downdrafts (which play a key role in the paper). The downdrafts bring low entropy, dry air into the boundary layer and reduce boundary layer entropy. Later it is stated that this has the tendency to kill small disturbances, which can only really amplify if this feedback is killed by saturating the troposphere. Because top of boundary layer mixing depends on convective activity, it is difficult to come up with a universal mixing timescale, which I would do well to remember in my own work. There follows an interesting discussion on how this links to a large-scale circulation that we apply via a temperature gradient. It is stated that "the rate of subsidence in clear air is not affected by the presence of mean ascent." Are you asking me, or are you telling me? It isn't clear if this is somehow derived from the theory on show, or whether it's related to observations somehow. This implies that large-scale ascent in convecting regions goes through the upward cumulus mass flux rather than influencing surrounding subsidence. That doesn't sound right to me (partly from GCM results) and partly because subsidence rates are probably small near convection anyway as radiative cooling is very inefficient. I suppose this paper was one year before Pierrehumbert, (1995). They eventually come round to the statement that  "large-scale ascent in convecting atmospheres is associated with a reduction of temperature, i.e. with a positive effective static stability." And remind us of Lindzen and Nigam's back pressure. The case is made that this is associated with the continuously evolving nature of SST maximum versus convective maximum. Cloud radiative feedback isn't mentioned.

Further points

A quick collection of their examples and other points made in the paper, certainly not all understood by me.
  • A travelling Kelvin wave disturbance that has convection associated with it would experience damping because of the finite timescale for convective adjustment. (ie NOT strict quasi-equilibrium). The general principle is that heating and temperature anomalies are slightly anti-correlated.
  • There is a concise description of tropical cyclones. Dunno if it's right, but I liked it. A weak initial vortex will cool as convection associated with Ekman pumping will inject dry air into the boundary layer. A stronger initial perturbation will partly amplify through surface flux increases but mostly because the atmosphere becomes saturated weakening (eliminating?) the entropy minimum in the mid-troposphere. This is not unrelated to Pierrehumbert arguments concerning radiative cooling either.
  • Prive and Plumb's used result about winds versus boundary layer entropy is presented starting from thermal wind balance. Again, I can't see this being right for the tropical troposphere given WTG? Tropopause u and v are stated, but perhaps the integration could be terminated at lower pressure? (Although friction...).

item.title: A number of items that inform our view of analysis of cloud feedbacks
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
What with the CIRCULATES annual(?) meeting coming up tomorrow, I've been reviewing a few concepts related to large-scale properties and their relationship to cloud feedback. A number of studies have linked cloud to "cloud controlling properties". A number of things are stuck in the regression model typically (including measures of RH at various levels and vertical velocity, and surface buoyancy fluxes). The two properties that come shining through are surface temperature, which may in fact be a proxy for various things and is not well understood, and (something like) estimated inversion strength (EIS), which is understood via what Mark Webb calls the "Klein and Hartmann relationship". The Klein and Hartmann relationship from Klein and Hartmann (1993). The stronger the inversion between the subtropical boundary layer and free atmosphere, the less the mixing between the two and hence the less of dry air into the boundary layer. The boundary layer tends to be shallower and moister and have more stratocumules. K and H examined this for variability in various regions. Analysing this for climate change, e.g. Qu, Hall and DeAngelis (2015), find increasing inversion strength that would lead to increased cloud, but this is overpowered by the effects of upward buoyancy flux and increased moisture gradient at boundary layer top (which effectively enhances the downward flux of dry air). These latter two are associated with SST and likely to be difficult to nail down. More recently, Paulo has cruised in with Ceppi and Nowack (2021), which uses ridge regression on EIS and SST to determine a range of cloud feedback from 20 years of observations. As he points out, that's not a lot of observations, but testing again GCMs suggests that the selection is pretty robust. A mid-range value of climate sensitivity is selected by this study. Meanwhile Mike Byrne is persuading CIRCULATES to look at the relationship between vertical velocity, dynamical regimes and cloud feedback. His point is that GCMs may not simulate the effects of vertical velocity on cloud feedback properly. That seems sensible. Byrne and Schneider (2018) does a Bony et al., (2004) type decomposition of cloud feedback into

cloud feedback = cloud feedback of circulation regime * amount of regime on planet

Because "what goes up must come down" changes in regime amount can't affect cloud feedback very much if cloud feedback of a regime is linear in vertical velocity. However, Monisha points out that this may not actually be the case.

Updated following on from the 13th August CIRCULATES meeting

A couple of things that may change my views of clouds came up in the actual meeting. First of all, my interpretation of Ceppi et al. apparently didn't do it justice, as it contains lots of advanced machine learning type stuff that allows simultaneous consideration of different cloud regimes and a general narrowing of uncertainty according to Mark. Mark's own talk noted that the uncertainty in tropical marine low cloud is NO LONGER the most important one. Narrowing of the tropical marine range means that tropical high cloud is most important. He recommended that CIRCULATES do research here. Simon Proud from RAL reminded us of the properties of HIMAWARI retrievals. The negative is that locations near the edge of the domain may have horizontal resolutions as bad as 7-8 km. (Those near the centre are nearer 2 km.) There were lots of positives, though. We might consider moving our domain to focus more on high clouds, though. Chris Holloway said that the latest RCEMIP-related stuff from Adrian Tompkins perhaps suggests that the ocean isn't necessarily as much as a killer of convective self-organisation as I thought. It does slow it down, though. Secondly, Alison Wing is considering extending the experimental design to something more useful, including interactive oceans and SST gradients.

item.title: Stability, moist static energy and tropical cloud radiative effect
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
Monisha has been wondering about how to classify cloud radiative effects (err) effectively for both stable and unstable regions. The sorts of classifiers we have been using so far (e.g. Ω500) are ineffective at classifying the most stable regimes. (Probably, because as Monisha says, there isn't really much going on at 500 hPa for the most stable stuff.) One possibility is Gross moist stability (GMS), reviewed by Raymond. Another is a sub-cloud layer buoyancy, described by Williams and Pierrehumbert.

Raymond et al., 2009, The mechanics of gross moist stability

GMS is the ratio of some measure of the horizontal divergence of some moist conserved quantity (like moist enthalpy) to the strength of some measure of convection. It basically relates therefore sources and sinks of entropy to P-E. If GMS is known then a measure of convective activity is available. Note - moisture is not conserved I don't think, so convergent flow is implied. Neelin and Held, (1987) invented it in its original form for their two layer model using moist static energy (which isn't conserved near non-hydrostatic actual convection). Other versions are available. Raymond himself has used column RH as the moist variable. (Not sure that would be conserved...?) Raymond, I think, is more concerned with what happens on a short timescale and especially a shorter spatial scale perhaps than I might be. They also discuss boundary layer entropy, convective quasi-equilibrium a la Emanuel et al., (1994). The mass transport doesn't close, I don't think. I.e. convective downdrafts are smaller than updrafts, implying convergence. I think this all makes sense on a local scale? But for larger flows like mine I think it needs to close? They also discuss one of these QTCM-style models. (Specifically Neelin and Yu, 1994). It has Boussinesq momentum, continuity, and buoyancy, moisture and enthalpy source-sink equations. Linearising around a basic state produces modes and produces waves that I've never been able to understand but wonder if I should for my hydrological work. Update: talking to Tim Jupp suggests that indeed the QTCM is probably basically the same as the Matsuno-Gill model in just being a pile of equations that you reduce to a wave equation.

Williams and Pierrehumbert, (2017), Observational evidence against strongly stabilizing tropical cloud feedbacks

They are particularly interested in high cloud / unstable regime feedbacks. Define "sub-cloud layer buoyancy", which is the ratio
B = (h_0 - h*) / (c_p T ( 1 + gamma))
where h_0 is "unsaturated" sub-cloud moist static energy. (Actually moist static energy of air?), h* is saturated moist static energy (because rising air at cloud base can be interpreted as being on a saturated adiabat). h* is calculated in the free troposphere. h_0 in the boundary layer. Important point is that hottest, non-high LW or SW CRE regions are actually *not* high buoyancy. So buoyancy plot looks rather different from SST plot of CRE. They claim that buoyancy much better overall, but it's a pretty strong claim! Still apparently, a comparison against Ω500 suggests it does better. They go on to analyse feedbacks in interannual data. The paper concludes that there is some cancellation between the high cloud effects over unstable and stable regimes. High cloud is lost over unstable but gained over stable. The commentary is sort of on the iris effect.

item.title: CLOUDSENSE, January 2022
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
The inaugural general meeting of the slightly ridiculously named "CLOUDSENSE" programme. The themes were what we would have expected given what I've seen so far, but the meeting was still an eye-opener for the view that the other projects, which are largely concentrated on cloud-aerosol interaction (except DCMEX to some extent), take of us. I'd seen this before, but to have it formalised was an interesting political lesson in whose ideas carry a meeting, regardless of facts. Specifically:
  1. Ken Carslaw was invited to give a talk about how modelling uncertainty is treated and used to make predictions of climate sensitivity. This talk would hardly have been avant-garde in the '90s, but it was hungrily applauded by the non-CIRCULATES participants. He suggested that a range of climate sensitivities is taken just from the ensemble of climate models that exists. This obviously irritated Mark Webb in the extreme. His response was calm. Steve Klein stayed out of it. He also peddled the canard that more model processes means that "your uncertainty can actually go up", which obviously annoyed me, to the extent that it's admissible for a scientific presentation given in good faith to annoy. If the meeting had been face-to-face, this would have been the keynote talk.
  2. Ben Murray challenged me (again...) on how CIRCULATES can collaborate with the other projects given that the other projects are about aerosols. The real response to this, which I have shared with the others only obliquely but perhaps ought to do more plainly, is that the programme is about cloud feedbacks -- the change in cloud radiative effect per unit global mean temperature. CIRCULATES is about cloud feedbacks and is a group of people that collaborate with the relevant international community. The other projects ought to think about how they can collaborate with us. I instead pointed out the methodological synergies between our projects and the others. We do have a lot of modelling expertise after all. Finally, it is now also apparent that the other projects don't know how to handle uncertainties, so I guess we could help them there too.
In terms of upshots of the meeting, it seems likely that there will be a workshop on uncertainties. This might not be a bad idea, but a reading list would be a good start. Having something that is too old-fashioned or too "us teaching them" risks disengagement from CIRCULATES, which wouldn't be good. Hopefully we can put some other stuff into the workshop too. Maybe we can link it up to the early career stuff. Update from CIRCULATES chat afterwards: Yes. Basically.  We think there's a need for a research proposal / project that actually quantifies the effect of aerosols on cloud feedback uncertainty. Specifically, what is the effect of background aerosol on feedback...

item.title: Dinh and Fueglistaler, 2019, On the Causal Relationship Between the Moist Diabatic Circulation and Cloud Rapid Adjustment to Increasing CO2
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
This is a paper that Chris Holloway recommended for understanding how, well, cloud rapid adjustment responds to increasing CO2. The first few sections of the paper seemed, at best, written in a rather odd style, but it grew on me and the explanations seem sensible. Perhaps the only really odd thing is that the said explanations apparently haven't been trotted out before. First of all, cloud rapid adjustment to CO2 forcing takes the form of an increase in boundary layer cloud and a decrease in free tropospheric cloud. If you have an RH-based cloud scheme, the reduction in free tropospheric RH (maybe a bit of warming, but also a reduction in circulation?) will give you the relevant decrease in free tropospheric cloud. (But that isn't necessarily why it happens.) Boundary layer RH increases, but even a half decent representation of what's going on will need some measure of boundary layer top inversion strength / boundary layer shallowing / reduction in entrainment. They focus on the FREE TROPOSPHERIC EFFECT. Their hypothesis is that changes in precipitation and in the mass of cloud condensates is governed by the same physics. Given autoconversion (ok - there's evaporation too) that seems pretty much hard-coded in. As far as the CO2 effect goes, the decrease in radiative cooling with increasing CO2 decreases the moist adiabatic circulation strength, reducing the rate of cloud condensate production. In general, cloud is seen as being a reservoir between condensation / precipitation or evaporation. Seems very sensible... They comment that
"A high correlation between precipitation and CWP [cloud water path] is not guaranteed a priori because (i) some cloud condensates evaporate... (ii) the fall speeds of the condensates affect the rate of precipitation."
Oh come on, it's pretty guaranteed. Poleward of 60 degrees, cloud fraction is somewhat decoupled from precipitation, however. It's also not that well-correlated with RH change, according to them, whereas CWP change is very well-correlated with precipitation change, again according to them. These conclusions seem a bit overstated to me and tellingly the actual numbers aren't stated. (How did they get that past the reviewers!?) Changes in omega are mostly forced by changes in radiative cooling rather than STATIC STABILITY, which is a quantity I don't understand mathematically properly, but is conceptually clear enough. To the extent that the tropical circulation is closed, this seems enough to explain why ascent must decrease as well as descent. However, they also weigh in on the decreasing ascent issue directly, claiming that ascent is "throttled" by the increase in stratification that occurs due to heating at the top of the boundary layer. They have some approximations (page 3845) that show how condensate production is approximately related to radiative cooling. "Extraordinary that it works," I commented. Regarding THE BOUNDARY LAYER.  They say that below the LCL, cloud amount depends on the evaporation of falling condensates. Increasing the RH, which you will do if you ventilate the boundary layer less with increasing stability, reduces the evaporation and increases cloud amount.

item.title: Increases in future land evaporation, or not
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: One of the biggest confusions, fights, whatever you want to call it, on my GEWEX review article is the issue of whether or not increases in evaporative demand actually end up drying land in the 21st century or not. It seems that the answer is probably "very uncertain". On the one hand, you have CMIP5 and 6 models, which have "simplified representation" of land surface hydrology but some representation of the surface carbon and energy budgets, and on the other hand you have the hydrologist's tool, the Global Hydrological Model, which has little representation of carbon and energy but supposedly more sophisticated representation of water fluxes (but not always, and the definition of land surface models and GHMs overlaps a fair bit). [caption id="attachment_691" align="alignnone" width="638"] Figure 3a from Yang et al., (2019).[/caption] Yang et al., (2019), Hydrologic implication of vegetation response to elevated CO2 in climate projections points out that offline GHMs don't do stomatal responses to CO2 that should reduce evaporation changes that would occur in response to increased potential evaporation from a warmer land and a (relative humidity) drier atmosphere. CMIP5 models do. "Correcting" the Budyko relationship with a simple surface resistance formulation that responds to CO2 makes Budyko look like CMIP5 (and with much reduced evaporation and increased runoff). Crucially it is not really possible to differentiate based on historical evaporation and runoff. However, Yang et al., state that they are consistent with field measurements of stomatal change. Kolby Smith et al., (2015), Large divergence of satellite and Earth system model estimates of global terrestrial CO2 fertilization compares CMIP5 and satellite values of net primary productivity change. They find that CMIP5 models tend to produce around double the increase in NPP, meaning that land carbon storage is increased more strongly in CMIP5, but also that the effects of increasing land vapour pressure deficit are not really felt in CMIP5 but apparently are in the observed record, certainly in dry years. They note that CESM-1, which is the only model in the ensemble they analyse that features nutrient limitation of vegetative growth has a rate of NPP increase much more like satellite numbers. So, models and observations clearly differ, but there is no direct mention of evaporation or evapotranspiration in this paper so I'm unclear exactly what it means for land water.

item.title: Behrens et al., (2022), Non-Linear Dimensionality Reduction With a Variational Encoder Decoder to Understand Convective Processes in Climate Models
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded: A paper in JAMES that Mark Webb recommended I take a look at. For once I wasn't disappointed. It uses a Variational Encoder Decoder, which is basically two neural nets. The first neural net takes the input data and  encodes it onto a small number of nodes. The second neural net translates those nodes into a reconstruction of the original input data and desired outputs for prediction. Mark is correct that it is a non-linear version of my rotated space where I use a small number of features designed to correlate with the most convection-controlling bits of the input space to describe the output space. [caption id="attachment_697" align="alignnone" width="1024"] Fig 1. The variational encoder decoder (VED).[/caption] There isn't really a lot to say about the paper as intuitively it makes sense. The main thing is pictures. They use the VED to encode superparameterised CAM3 and identify different regimes globally using their five nodes. As a representation of all the model's parameterisations, it is obviously very good. To make pictures, they do a PCA of the five nodes (latent space) that gives a view of how the regimes appear over the space. I think I am right in saying that this (below) is the non-linear equivalent of Lambert et al., (2020)'s (remember him) rotated space. They compare to other non-VED ways of doing it, including "naive" PCA. The naive PCA doesn't do very well -- they do all parameterisations across the whole planet so not surprising! However - the PCA is naive and doesn't use rotation I don't think. I wouldn't expect it to work that well. [caption id="attachment_699" align="alignnone" width="1024"] Fig 2. PCA of the five node latent space.[/caption] The question is what I should do next if I'm going to make rotated (or latent) spaces for cloud and convective parameterisations across climate models and other representations of convection. My guess is that it may work well enough to stick with linear for now (and with the increase in tractability for everyone else as well as me). The reason for this is that although within one model, I don't see much variation in output properties away from the direction in which the output is linear, it does make a big difference for multiple models where you have to pick vectors that are not "principle" for any of them. It might still be that non-linear is much more discriminating, and I may have to cross that bridge, but to begin with we can find differences very well using linear. Come to think of it, that non-variation, or at least not very clear variation away from the principle linear direction, presumably explains why simple non-linear models that we might get from polynomial regression or genetic algorithms don't arise.

item.title: CLOUDSENSE April 2023, Leeds
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
The "big" CLOUDSENSE meeting in which I had to make my pitch for leading CLOUDSENSE2. Some "highlights": The other projects are all very excited about Ice Nucleating Particles (INP). Took me a while to have some idea what they were talking about. How you parameterise them is tricky. It seems to be done as a function of temperature, by and large. (Different particles activate at different temperatures.) However, the INP number is also proportional to the aerosol concentration. High INP leads to low albedo (with the potential for high mixed phase cloud feedback under climate change). Low INP leads to high albedo (low feedback potential). This is the basis of Mphase, essentially. Not knowing much about INP, particularly in the Southern Ocean is the basis for Floor and Mark Tarn's synergy project. The Uncertainty workshop 2. Steef Boeing made a decent point that the recent Vogel et al., 2022, Nature paper calls for low sensitivity contradicts Paulo's evidence calling for higher sensitivity than shown by models. As Paulo pointed out, this stems from the two studies examining different evidence. Paulo's is pattern effect; Vogel's is cumulus cloud processes. The Vogel thing is hence quite a nice example for our proposed use of the Sherwood framework as we could use it to constrain one piece of the puzzle rather than the entire model sensitivity thing. (I think that Steve Sherwood in fact suggested that Vogel (or collaborators) had done this, but I can't find the evidence. So, the CLOUDSENSE2 pitch. It could have gone worse, certainly. Oddly, everything that was said in the meeting almost seemed to lead up to it. I wonder who believed me when I said I hadn't revised my slides during the meeting. Perhaps the main thing is that everyone wants to do the correlation thing. I manipulated the audience into applause at the end of my talk in order to gauge feelings. Most negative body language was definitely from Paulo, but he assured me it's fine... I can understand his frustration. I also went through some of my stats stuff (with reasonably wild abandon at points). I don't think anyone actually noticed. Some feedback that I will need to consider:
  • Mat Collins: How do we turn an observed study into an estimate of a feedback? Well, we can do it the Vogel way by screening out models. However, we can't do it by incorporating process feedback into models in the time frame. (The UM is only one model for one thing.) As Paulo pointed out, the Sherwood survey is a "meta-analysis" using, for example, previous ensembles of high resolution models to give a range of feedbacks. Hence a further reason to work on "improving models" as well as estimates of feedback. Alison Stirling is obviously ultra-keen.
  • Tom Lachlan-Cope: SOC will need to do an obs campaign in 2024-5. CLOUDSENSE2 will pay for that, but he's happy for it to come out of the SOC "share" rather than being topsliced as I think Alan Blyth feared.
  • Steef Boeing / Alan Blyth and Tom all advocated for the mixing up of people across projects, especially including modelling expertise.
  • Declan Finney (and others) want a "worked example" of how you might incorporate your work into the feedback framework. Sounds reasonable, but there's definitely more than one way to do that.
  • It was suggested that we need "themes". (For writing the grant? For carrying you the work?) Suggested were: - Statistics - Modelling - Mphase / SOC. (Hopefully we can do better than these soon!)
  • A closing international workshop is desired. Alison Stirling suggested doing it sooner.

item.title: CFMIP-GASS 2023
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
CFMIP 2023 in Paris, joint with GASS. Can't say I was very enthusiastic about attending this conference, particularly since it followed on almost directly from EXOSLAM / Exoclimes, which were tiring, and of course fundamentally interesting. However, observation of the mighty buildings of Paris filled me with thoughts of the heavy cultural and intellectual legacy they proudly proclaim. I felt inspired to give at least a satisfactory performance in front of my own poster (Clouds and Continuous Structural Parameterisation). I had interesting conversations with both Robin Hogan from ECMWF / Reading and a representative of Meteo France, who seemed to realise the true import of what I was saying with a shock I found gratifying. Anyway, what about what everyone else was saying...
  • Tim Andrews: Pattern effect. The feedback parameter is changing over time. Now that we're going into an El Nino it's coming down (meaning that naive analyses will predict increasing climate sensitivity and global warming for the time being).
  • Jonah Bloch-Johnson: Non-linear feedback analysis shows that the GREENS FUNCTIONS thing tends to overestimate effects of individual regions. I probably ought to mention this in CLOUDSENSE2? More importantly he managed to get HadCM3 to runaway at 8xCO2! Really!?
  • Robin Hogan: noted the depressing reality that satellite observations following A-train are not as good as they used to be. Earthcare is their next satellite, but it's really scaled back.
  • Da Yang: It's always good to see Da Yang. His current work is about how water vapour buoyancy means that you see colder air in convecting regions at a given level compared with drier non-convecting regions. It's very planetary. Why did I not think of that. He states that cloud liquid and ice water does not have a big enough effect to really change things. (Can't remember if it also accelerates convection or not.)
  • Poujole-Basile: I'm not sure if this was pushing on something I've been wondering about or not. But some theory of Nadir Jeevanjee relates brightness temperature to vertical velocity and in this work it is applied in satellite observations with some surprising (to them) results. Apparently tropospheric waves can be big and are associated with big differences in vertical velocity (just in the waves or when they break?).
Two linked conversations I had with Jonah and Robin may be worth reporting. The GREENS FUNCTIONS feedbacks people were bemoaning how the whole GREENS FUNCTIONS feedbacks thing isn't great. It was on my mind too, but (slightly annoyingly for me!) it was Robin that voiced it in the open session: if you want something that decomposes your feedbacks into optimised patterns that interact as little as possible, then do PCA! Despite Mark Webb's comments, Jonah says he hasn't done that. I wonder if we could use Tim Andrews's feedbacks only simulations to discover how constant the feedback patterns are? Finally, I asked Mark Zelinka to join the CLOUDSENSE Programme Advisory Group. Let's hope he bites. He's a walking continent of common sense.

item.title: EGU 2024
item.dc:creator: fhl202
item.content:encoded:
So I finally got the train all the way to Wien Hbf from Lympstone Village, including the NightJet. Which was really a lot more like a youth hostel on wheels than what I was expecting. Still, travelling in Europe is like being in the future. EGU, then:

TROPICAL METEOROLOGY

  • Davison and Haynes (Cambridge): A simple model of convective aggregation based on the moist shallow water equations. I feel that the moist shallow water equations are something I should look into... Diffusion plays the role of parameterisation. It is actually the f-plane that limits gravity wave dissipation rather than friction?
  • Luca Schmidt: Gave the precipitation "enhancement" over land that I've seen Cathy Hoehnegger give before. Their key conclusion is that land is actually rainier than ocean. It's just the distribution of available land (and near surface RH?) that makes it less rainy.

HYDROLOGY (My first PICO session? I love PICO sessions already.)

  • Haoshan Wei: TRENDY land surface models are too sensitive observed streamflow. A rather interesting interaction this one. He does not really want to publish his results as he fears people won't like them. Happy to talk about them, though, however? They have submitted a paper to Nat. Comm. that says some other stuff about the results, though.
  • Feng Zhang: Evapotranspiration changes are driven by greening, evaporative demand and changes in precipitation. The region you are in decides what dominates the change.
  • Armon, Reider...: The Sahara had lakes in it that were filled by strong extratropical depressions that are also able to suck up moisture from the tropics. But I think you need that extratropical interaction. Could it happen again in future? CMIP models might predict "big" (percentage...) increases in future but they can't get the rain far enough north in paleoclimates.
  • Duethmann, Bruno...: The history of evapotranspiration from flux towers in France and Germany is complicated and there was much interaction with commenters. I noticed the huge increase in the growing season length in the 1980s, following on from some cold winters and pollution (acid rain?) problems. Having climbed, ET is on the way down again more recently as droughts and the bark beetle take their toll.

PLANETARY AND EXOPLANETARY

  • Ralph Lorenz: He's a character, but always interesting. The lifetime of Martian rovers is essentially determined by how long it take dust to get stuck to their solar panels and shut them down. The unexpectedly long life of a large number of rovers points to the ability of dust devils to clean them off.
  • Noack and Brachmann: I saw a couple of presentations about how planetary interiors lead to the secondary atmospheres that we might observe. Those with mobile surfaces (which can be plate tectonics or "other" apparently) are easier to get some things out of compared with stagnant lids? Or something? Also you can have reduced versus oxidised mantles. Someday I'm going to have to understand REDOX balance. Oxidised mobile put out CO2. (Does this have consequences for Venus evolution?) Oxidised stagnant put out H2O.

ATMOSPHERIC CONVECTION. Big session.

  • Becker (ECMWF): Hi-res global models do not have enough convective organisation. Particularly one of them. Also moistening of the atmosphere before deep convection is not adequate No surprises there, I suppose.
  • Bolot (Princeton): 70% of work generated by convection is needed to lift water (rather than being available for kinetic energy). After global warming, the water needs to be lifted higher than it did previously. (I was slightly confused by the splitting of condensation and precipitation heating in this talk.)
  • Da Yang (I think! But didn't note down speaker name): In shallow convecting boundary layers, there is a balance of advective cooling and convective heating with only a small role for radiation. And there is no real storage of buoyancy. A mesoscale circulating picture therefore needs to be recognised. It sort of feels like there's a lot of work being generated here without much dumping of heat...? But I'll allow it as Da norma gets all this stuff.

DRYLANDS

  • Markowska (Northumbria (Is that in Australia? No - apparently it's in the UK!)): During the past 8 million years there have been some much wetter periods in the Arabian desert. Dry periods happen with high NH ice and meridional SST gradient. At times orbital forcing maximises summer sunshine in Arabia, increasing rainfall markedly (according to HadCM3 anyway!).
  • Jerry Raj: Changing oceanic vertical resolution changes atmospheric waves and jets and precipitation over west Africa rather a lot.
  • Min Hui Lo: As you increase an area of irrigation, you first lower rainfall (presumably through cooling?) and then gradually start to increase it (presumably through moistening).

CLOUDS

  • The CLOUDSENSE session. Monisha did well, but I also noticed the talk of Adam Sokol. One of two he gave at the meeting (admittedly couldn't really make head or tail of the other one). I expect that's a name we'll be hearing rather a lot more of. Anyway, he looked at RCEMIP simulations of tropical anvil clouds and found the anvil cloud feedback a lot closer to neutral than the Sherwood assessment did. Mark Zelinka has noted that this is a much needed correction. I was surprised to see it happen through RCEMIP data, though. The explanation is basically that anvil cloud feedback is balanced between thick cloud (mostly reflects SW) and thin cloud (mostly absorbs upwelling LW). RCEMIP has less thick.
I also had some interesting meetings with Anna Ukkola and Da Yang. But I'll note those separately.
